name: Battle of Demotika
commanders: Ottoman forces supporting John VI Kantakouzenos; Serbian-Bulgarian allied forces
result: First major Ottoman victory in Europe
importance: Opened the way for a permanent Ottoman military role in Thrace.

name: Siege of Hatvan
commanders: Christoph von Teuffenbach vs. Sarıalioğlu Tiryaki Arslan Bey and Sokulluzade Hasan Pasha
result: Ottoman victory / Lifting of the siege
importance: A major 1594 siege during the Long Turkish War where the imperial army under Christoph von Teuffenbach was forced to lift the siege of Hatvan and retreat in disorder after a coordinated Ottoman relief effort and successful castle sortie.
casualties: German/Imperial losses estimated at 1,000 to 2,000; Ottoman relief and garrison forces suffered 3,000 to 4,000 casualties, with all imperial artillery abandoned.

name: Capture of Tata
commanders: Koca Sinan Pasha vs. Imperial Garrison
importance: Following the relief of Hatvan, the advancing Ottoman army under Koca Sinan Pasha captured the strategic fortress of Tata as part of their 1594 campaign in Royal Hungary.

name: Capture of St. Marton
commanders: Koca Sinan Pasha vs. Imperial Garrison
importance: The Ottoman army continued its successful offensive across Hungary, taking the fortress of St. Marton (Pannonhalma) shortly after the capture of Tata.

name: Battle of Kulikovo
commanders: Dmitry Donskoy vs. Mamai
importance: Established Moscow as the primary political center for anti-Horde resistance and broke the aura of Tatar invincibility.
casualties: Very heavy losses on both sides.

name: Battle of Lwów
commanders: John III Sobieski vs. Ibrahim Shishman
importance: King John III Sobieski brilliantly used terrain, clever positioning, and dummy forces to decisively defeat a numerically superior Ottoman-Tatar army of 20,000 near Lwów, a victory commemorated on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Warsaw.
casualties: Heavy Ottoman and Tatar losses; light Commonwealth losses

name: Jan Sobieski's Expedition Against the Tatar Chambuls
commanders: John III Sobieski vs. Jiambet Giray, Nurredin-Sultan, and Haci Giray
result: Decisive Polish-Lithuanian victory; rescue of thousands of captives
importance: A brilliant 450-kilometer lightning cavalry campaign by Grand Hetman John III Sobieski that systematically tracked down, intercepted, and destroyed dispersed Tatar raiding groups (chambuls) across southern Poland, freeing roughly 44,000 captives from the yasir.
casualties: Heavy Tatar raiding losses; minimal Polish-Lithuanian losses

name: Battle of Krasnobród
commanders: John III Sobieski and Mykhailo Khanenko vs. Tatar Chambul Forces
importance: Part of Sobieski's lighting autumn expedition where a grueling 52-kilometer night march through heavy rain led to a surprise dawn attack on a Tatar camp, destroying raiding units and freeing 2,500 captive Polish civilians.
casualties: Tatar raiding units destroyed; heavy prisoner liberation

name: Battle of Kalnyk
commanders: John III Sobieski and Mykhailo Khanenko vs. Petro Doroshenko's Cossack-Tatar Relief Force
importance: As part of Sobieski's siege operations, a relief force of Cossacks and Tatars attempted to reinforce Kalnyk; Polish cavalry intercepted and heavily defeated them near the town dam, inflicting 500 casualties on the Tatars.
casualties: 500 Tatars killed or drowned; heavy relief force losses

name: Siege of Kalnyk
commanders: John III Sobieski and Mykhailo Khanenko vs. Kalnyk Garrison
importance: Jan Sobieski besieged the strongly defended Cossack garrison at Kalnyk for over two weeks, but ultimately lifted the siege and retreated to Bratslav upon learning of an approaching major Tatar reinforcement under Nuradin-sultan Safa-Girey.
casualties: Garrison and besieging losses during investment and skirmishes

name: Battle of Brailov
commanders: Sebastian Machowski vs. Petro Doroshenko
importance: The opening engagement of the Polish-Cossack-Tatar war where joint Cossack-Tatar forces decisively defeated Sebastian Machowski's punitive expedition near Brailov, capturing Machowski and driving the Polish-Lithuanian forces into retreat.
casualties: Most of the Polish-Lithuanian army killed or captured; Commander Machowski taken prisoner

name: Battle of Bila Tserkva (1612)
commanders: Zaporozhian Cossacks vs. Crimean Khanate Forces
importance: A decisive ambush by Zaporozhian Cossacks against the largest Tatar chambul returning from a raid in the Kiev Voivodeship. The battle resulted in the liberation of 5,000 captives and served as a significant deterrent to future Tatar raiding parties.
casualties: Tatar unit completely defeated; 5,000 captives freed

name: Siege of Bila Tserkva
commanders: Petro Doroshenko vs. Polish-Lithuanian Garrison
importance: Following his victory at Brailov, Petro Doroshenko pursued his campaign against the Commonwealth by besieging the key fortress city of Bila Tserkva.
casualties: Garrison and regional defense losses during the investment

name: Battle of Bursztyn (1629)
commanders: Stefan Chmielecki and Hryhoriy Chornyi vs. Kalga Devlet-Giray, Aslan-Giray, and Khan Temir
importance: A decisive counter-attack near the Gnila Lipa river where the Polish-Cossack forces surprised a Tatar camp, resulting in a heavy defeat for the Crimean-Nogai forces and the liberation of 10,000 captives.
casualties: Approximately 8,000 Tatars lost during the expedition; 2,000 captured; 10,000 captives freed

name: Battle of Bila Tserkva (1626)
commanders: Stefan Chmielecki and Mykhailo Doroshenko vs. Buhar Kantymirowie
importance: A decisive clash where Stefan Chmielecki's forces intercepted a Tatar invasion force that believed the region was defenseless after the departure of the main Polish army. The victory shattered the Tatar forces, liberated captives, and ensured peace from raids for the following year.
casualties: 1,000–4,000+ Tatars killed, 1,200+ captured; only 40 Polish/Cossack losses

name: Capture of the Chyhyryn Castle
commanders: Petro Doroshenko vs. Commonwealth Garrison
importance: Doroshenko successfully captured the strategic castle in Chyhyryn as part of his ongoing campaign to consolidate control over Right-Bank Ukraine before facing John III Sobieski at Podhajce.
casualties: Garrison losses and transfer of fortress control

name: Battle of Narol
commanders: John III Sobieski vs. Tatar Chambuls
importance: Continuation of Sobieski's sweeping pursuit where two separate Tatar chambuls were intercepted and defeated in quick succession.

name: Battle of Nemirów
commanders: John III Sobieski vs. Jiambet Giray
importance: Sobieski caught up with and crushed Jiambet's raiding forces as they operated between the regional river lines.

name: Battle of Komarno
commanders: John III Sobieski vs. Nurredin-Sultan
importance: Sobieski successfully intercepted and beat the main forces of Nurredin-Sultan, pursuing them onward to Vyshnia.

name: Battles of Petranka and Kalush
commanders: John III Sobieski vs. Haci Giray
importance: Following a strenuous cross-Dniester march, a vanguard of a thousand Polish soldiers caught up with Haci Giray's retreating forces at dawn and decisively smashed them.
casualties: Haci Giray's forces shattered and scattered

name: Great Stand on the Ugra River
commanders: Ivan III vs. Akhmat Khan
importance: Formally terminated two and a half centuries of Tatar tribute and suzerainty over Russian principalities.

name: First Battle of Vajkal
commanders: Skanderbeg vs. Ballaban Pasha
importance: Fought in the Vajkal valley; Skanderbeg's forces defeated Ballaban Pasha's Ottoman army, though heavy losses were sustained on both sides and several prominent Albanian officers were captured during an overzealous pursuit and later executed in Constantinople
casualties: Heavy casualties on both sides; several captured Albanian commanders skinned alive

name: Second Battle of Vajkal
commanders: Skanderbeg vs. Ballaban Pasha
importance: Fought in August 1465 following Ballaban's renewed invasion; an Albanian army of 12,000 men under Skanderbeg utterly defeated a 24,000-strong Ottoman army led by Ballaban Pasha

name: Battle of Otlukbeli
commanders: Mehmed the Conqueror, Prince Bayezid & Prince Mustafa vs. Uzun Hasan (Aq Qoyunlu)
importance: Fought near Tercan/Otlukbeli; Mehmed II's massive Ottoman army decisively defeated Uzun Hasan's Aq Qoyunlu forces, neutralizing the major Eastern threat to Ottoman rule in Anatolia and breaking Aq Qoyunlu regional dominance
casualties: Heavy Aq Qoyunlu casualties, including the death of Zeynel Mirza and the capture of high-ranking commanders

name: Lipka Rebellion (Campaign)
commanders: Aleksander Kryczyński vs. John III Sobieski
result: Initial mutiny and defection to the Ottomans; later suppression and return to Commonwealth service
importance: A mutiny of 2,000 to 3,000 Lipka Tatar cavalry regiments over overdue pay and lost privileges, leading them to serve the Ottoman Empire as scouts and guides before internal dissatisfaction and military defeat led to their reintegration into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
casualties: Internal mutiny casualties; fortress and garrison losses during the campaign

name: Siege of Bar (1674)
commanders: John III Sobieski vs. Lipka Rebel Garrison (Aleksander Kryczyński / Chief Officers)
importance: King John III Sobieski successfully took the fortified town of Bar, which had been given to the rebel leader Aleksander Kryczyński by the Sultan, leading to the unconditional surrender of the chief officers and clearing the way for the Lipkas to return to Polish service.
casualties: Garrison losses and surrender of rebel leadership

name: Battle of Lipnic
commanders: Stephen the Great vs. Ahmed Khan (Golden Horde)
importance: Repelled a major Volga-Tatar invasion of Moldavia, capturing Ahmed Khan's son and strengthening Moldavian sovereignty.
casualties: Heavy Tatar losses; capture of numerous prisoners.

name: Sack of Sarai
commanders: Crimean Khanate (Mengli I Giray) vs. Great Horde (Sheikh Ahmad)
importance: Destroyed the capital of the Great Horde, permanently extinguishing its statehood and dividing its remnants among rival khanates.
casualties: Heavy devastation of the city and surrounding nomadic forces.

name: Battle of the Samara River
commanders: Stephen III & Meñli I Giray vs. Sheikh Ahmed
importance: Catastrophic blow leading to the destruction of the Golden Horde
casualties: Most of the Great Horde army destroyed

name: Battle of the Cosmin Forest
commanders: Stephen III (Moldavia, Wallachia, Ottoman Empire, Crimean Khanate) vs. King John I Albert
importance: Disastrous defeat for Poland, ending King John's attempt to subjugate Moldavia

name: Battle of Kopystrzyń
commanders: Prince John I Albert vs. Tatar Chambul
importance: Defeat of an Ottoman-dispatched Tatar raiding force in Podolia
casualties: Approx. 1,500 to 2,000 Tatars killed or captured

name: Battle of Zasław
commanders: Mikołaj Chodecki & Semyon Olshanski vs. Crimean Khanate
importance: Near-total destruction of a 9,000-strong Crimean raiding force along the Horyn River

name: Battle of Ștefănești
commanders: Stephen III vs. Eminek Mârza
importance: Repelled a diversionary Crimean-Nogai Tatar invasion of northern Moldavia ordered by Sultan Mehmed II
casualties: Very heavy losses for the Tatar forces

name: Battle of Cernăuți
commanders: Stephen III & Sima Boldur vs. King John I Albert & Konrad III Rudy
importance: An ambush on retreating Polish forces crossing the Prut River, completing the devastation of John I Albert's army
casualties: Very heavy losses, finishing the decimation of the Polish expedition

name: Battle of Lențești
commanders: Sima Boldur (trusted by Stephen III) vs. Konrad III Rudy
importance: An annihilation of 600 Masovian knights sent to relieve the retreating Polish army
casualties: All Masovian knights killed / completely wiped out

name: Sacking of Trembowla
commanders: Stephen III vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Captured and sacked as part of Stephen's retaliatory invasion of southeastern Poland

name: Sacking of Buczacz
commanders: Stephen III vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Captured and pillaged during the 1498 Moldavian campaign in Red Ruthenia

name: Sacking of Podhajce
commanders: Stephen III vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Fell to Stephen's advancing forces during the sweeping punitive raids into Poland

name: Battle of Lwów
commanders: Stanisław Jan Jabłonowski vs. Shahbaz Giray
importance: A surprise raid by Crimean Tatars and Nogais on Lwów during an invasion meant to force a separatist peace; after fierce street fighting and defense by townspeople and peasants, the invaders were driven out, rendering the Tatar expedition a failure.
casualties: ~400 Polish-Lithuanian soldiers plus comparable losses among the Tatars

name: Battle of Podhajce
commanders: Feliks Kazimierz Potocki vs. Qaplan I Giray
importance: A 6,000-strong Polish-Lithuanian army under Field Crown Hetman Feliks Kazimierz Potocki successfully repelled an approximately 14,000-strong Tatar pre-emptive invasion near Podhajce during the Great Turkish War.
casualties: Unknown specific casualties, but included heavy fighting and losses during the defense against the Tatar camp assault

name: Tatar Raid on Podkamień
commanders: Crimean Tatar forces vs. Local inhabitants
importance: As part of the final Tatar raid before the Treaty of Karlowitz took effect, the area of Podkamień was plundered after crossing the Dniester.

name: Tatar Raid on Rohatyn
commanders: Crimean Tatar forces vs. Local inhabitants
importance: Rohatyn was subjected to plundering and devastation by retreating Tatar forces carrying captives following the clash at Martynów.

name: Tatar Raid on Bursztyn
commanders: Crimean Tatar forces vs. Local inhabitants
importance: The Bursztyn area was raided and pillaged by the retreating Crimean Tatar expeditionary force just prior to the enactment of the peace treaty.

name: Tatar Raid on Mariampol
commanders: Crimean Tatar forces vs. Local inhabitants
importance: Mariampol suffered plundering during the final wave of Tatar raids across the Halich lands before the Ottoman-Polish border became peaceful.

name: Battle of the Vorskla River
commanders: Edigu and Temür Qutlugh vs. Vytautas the Great and Tokhtamysh
importance: The crushing defeat of Vytautas's crusade blocked Lithuanian expansion to the Black Sea and southern Ruthenia, forcing a re-alliance with Poland and shifting focus toward Moscow and the Teutonic Order.
casualties: Heavy (~20 princes killed out of 50 present)

name: Tatar Raid on Red Ruthenia
commanders: Crimean Tatars vs. Polish defenders
importance: One of the earliest major targeted slave raids into Red Ruthenia, resulting in tens of thousands of captives.

name: Battle of Martynów
commanders: Adam Sieniawski and Michał Warszycki vs. Crimean Tatar commanders
importance: A clash at the Dniester crossing near Martynów where about 600 Polish troops attacked retreating Tatar forces, but were successfully repulsed just days before the Treaty of Karlowitz took effect.
casualties: Unknown specific casualties, with several prisoners taken by the Tatars

name: Raid on Kamieniec Podolski
commanders: Budjak Horde vs. Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
result: Successful raid and retreat with loot and slaves
importance: A strong Tatar group of the Budjak Horde raided the area near Kamieniec Podolski, prompting Hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski to launch a retaliatory pursuit.

name: Capture of Lipova
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Habsburg monarchy
importance: As part of the Ottoman offensive under Sultan Mustafa II, imperial forces captured Lipova in the Banat region shortly before the Battle of Lugos.

name: Battle of Lugos
commanders: Sultan Mustafa II vs. Federico Ambrosio Veterani
importance: Fought near Lugos in the East Banat as part of the Great Turkish War; Ottoman forces defeated the 7,000-man Austrian army, resulting in heavy casualties and the death and beheading of Field Marshal Veterani alongside Serbian militia commanders.
casualties: Heavy casualties on both sides, including the death of General Veterani and Serbian militia leaders Captain Strahinja and Antonije Znorić

name: Battle of Sasowy Róg
commanders: Stanisław Koniecpolski vs. Budjak Horde Tatars
importance: Hetman Koniecpolski crossed the Dniester into Moldavia and caught up with the retreating Tatars at Sasowy Róg, killing and capturing dozens, recovering all loot, captives, cattle, and horses.
casualties: Several dozen Tatars killed or captured; minimal Commonwealth losses

name: Battle of Ustechko
commanders: Stanisław Jan Jabłonowski and Kazimierz Jan Sapieha vs. Şehbaz Giray
importance: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth forces (2,000–3,000 men with 12 guns) defeated a combined Tatar and Ottoman force (10,000–12,000 strong) during the Polish-Ottoman War.

name: Battle of Hodów
commanders: Konstanty Zaborowski, Mikołaj Tyszkowski, and Jan Witosławski vs. Crimean Tatar commanders
importance: Often called the 'Polish Thermopylae', a small force of 400 Polish cavalrymen fortified themselves in Hodów and successfully repelled a massive Tatar force numbering between 25,000 and 70,000 men, forcing them to abandon the raid.
casualties: Fewer than 100 Polish casualties vs. 1,000–2,000 Tatar losses

name: Blockade and Capture of Oradea
commanders: Habsburg Imperial Forces and Serbian Militia vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Following a prolonged blockade by Habsburg and allied forces, the strategic fortress of Oradea (Nagyvárad) was successfully wrested from Ottoman control in the spring of 1692, ending over three decades of Turkish rule established in 1660.
casualties: Unknown specific casualties, though heavy enough to leave lasting records among participating commanders like Jovan Monasterlija

name: Battle of Pererîta
commanders: Hieronymus Lyubomirsky and King John III Sobieski vs. Murza Arslan
importance: Fought near Pererîta during the Moldavian campaign; a Polish-Lithuanian force of 1,500 under Lyubomirsky (later reinforced) broke through a feigned Tatar retreat, inflicting heavy losses—including the death of Tatar commander Murza Arslan—and enabling the main army to cross the Prut River.
casualties: ~40 killed on the Polish side, with multiple wounded and captured; heavy losses for the Tatars, including commander Murza Arslan

name: Battle of Zernest
commanders: Donat Heissler and Mihály Teleki vs. Imre Thököly and Constantin Brâncoveanu
importance: Fought near Zărnești in Transylvania; the combined allied forces of the Ottoman Empire, Tatars, Wallachians, and Kurucs decisively defeated the Habsburg-Transylvanian army, capturing Imperial commander Donat Heissler and killing Transylvanian count Mihály Teleki.
casualties: 1,800 Imperials killed, wounded, or captured vs. 300 allied casualties

name: Thököly's Crossing of the Carpathians
commanders: Imre Thököly and Constantin Brâncoveanu vs. Imperial army
result: Ottoman and anti-Habsburg coalition strategic breakthrough
importance: Led by Imre Thököly and masterminded by Wallachian Voivode Constantin Brâncoveanu, an Ottoman-allied army of 16,000 men bypassed the heavily fortified Bran Pass by utilizing obscure mountain paths through the Carpathians to penetrate Transylvania.

name: Battle of Sasowy Róg (1612)
commanders: Stefan Potocki vs. Ștefan II Tomșa and Khan Temir
importance: Pro-Habsburg magnate Stefan Potocki's second intervention in Moldavia was crushed near Ștefănești by Tomșa and Budjak Horde Tatars, ending in Potocki's captivity.
casualties: Potocki's 7,000-strong army defeated; Stefan Potocki and Constantin Movilă captured

name: Battle of Sasowy Róg (1616)
commanders: Magnate Forces vs. Iskender Pasha
importance: Iskender Pasha defeated the private forces of Polish magnates on the same spot at Sasowy Róg, taking Samuel Korecki and the Movilă family prisoner to Constantinople.

name: Battle of Gurăslău
commanders: Mihai Viteazul and Giorgio Basta vs. Sigismund Báthory
importance: A joint victory against Transylvanian prince Sigismund Báthory, after which general Giorgio Basta assassinated Mihai Viteazul to secure Habsburg control over Transylvania.

name: Battle of Khotyn (Chocim) / Abazy's Offensive
commanders: Abhaz Pasha and Kantymir vs. Stanisław Koniecpolski
result: Commonwealth defensive victory and Ottoman retreat
importance: Abazy crossed the Dniester with Ottoman forces, vassal troops, and Budjak Tatars to attack Koniecpolski's fortified camp near Khotyn, but was heavily repelled, forcing an Ottoman retreat.
casualties: Heavy Ottoman and Tatar losses during the repulsed assaults

name: Battle of Bucov
commanders: Jan Zamoyski vs. Mihai Viteazul
importance: Jan Zamoyski defeated Mihai Viteazul near Ploiești in Wallachia, restoring Ieremia Movilă to the Moldavian throne and extending Commonwealth influence to the Danube.
casualties: Mihai Viteazul's forces defeated and routed

name: Battle of Podhajce
commanders: John III Sobieski vs. Petro Doroshenko and Adil Giray
importance: Polish-Lithuanian forces under John III Sobieski successfully defended against a superior allied force of Cossacks, Tatars, and Janissaries, leading to an armistice and the promotion of Sobieski to Grand Crown Hetman.
casualties: Heavy Cossack-Tatar losses; moderate Commonwealth losses

name: Moldavian Punitive Campaign in Poland
commanders: Stephen III (with Ottoman & Crimean allies) vs. King John I Albert
importance: Widespread devastation of Red Ruthenia and Podolia up to Lwów, Przemyśl, and Jarosław, forcing a Polish peace treaty
casualties: Enormous devastation; up to 100,000 Polish captives taken

name: Raid on Lwów
commanders: Stephen III vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Stephen's army ravaged the lands up to the major regional center of Lwów

name: Campaign in Pokucie
commanders: Stephen III vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Systematic devastation and foraging across the Pokucie region over the Dniester

name: Raid on Przemyśl
commanders: Stephen III vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Deep punitive raid reaching and devastating the city and environs of Przemyśl

name: Tatar Raid into Pokucie and Habsburg-Controlled Royal Hungary (1594)
commanders: Ğazı II Giray vs. Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth forces
importance: A massive raid led by Crimean Khan Ğazı II Giray with 20,000–30,000 men that devastated the Pokucie region before pushing through mountain passes to plunder Habsburg lands in Hungary, bypassing slow-to-gather Commonwealth forces.
casualties: Widespread devastation of Pokucie and Habsburg borderlands

name: Sacking of Radymno
commanders: Stephen III vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Town sacked and burned during the retaliatory sweep through southeastern Poland

name: Sacking of Jarosław
commanders: Stephen III vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Major urban center of Jarosław ravaged by Stephen's advancing coalition forces
casualties: City and surrounding lands heavily plundered

name: Pillaging of Kańczuga
commanders: Stephen III vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Locality pillaged during the wide-ranging Moldavian offensive

name: Destruction of Łańcut
commanders: Stephen III vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Town and estate lands of Łańcut devastated before the Polish army could mobilize at Sandomierz

name: Zhane–Elbrus Campaign
commanders: Sahib I Giray & Khalil Bey vs. Kansavuk (Zhane)
importance: First major expedition into Circassia, reaching Mount Tkhab and the upper Kuban region

name: Zhane Campaign
commanders: Sahib I Giray & Khalil Bey vs. Kansavuk (Zhane)
importance: Punitive expedition against Zhane lands following refusal to pay tribute and Taman raids
casualties: Widespread devastation; ~50,000 civilians captured over 75 days

name: Campaign to Kabardia
commanders: Sahib I Giray vs. Kabardian and Bzhedug Princes
importance: Major clash along the Malka and Belkh rivers involving an army of up to 70,000 Tatars

name: Astrakhan Conflict & Storming
commanders: Sahib I Giray vs. Yamghurchi Khan
importance: Massive mobilization and storming of Astrakhan, devastating the Astrakhan Khanate and deporting Nogais

name: Hatuqay Campaign
commanders: Sahib I Giray & Ghazi Giray vs. Elok & Antanuk (Hatuqay/Bzhedug)
importance: Final major campaign of Sahib Giray into Hatuqay and the foothills of Elbrus before his assassination

name: Battle of Buzhyn
commanders: Grigory Romodanovsky & Ivan Samoilovich vs. Ibrahim Pasha & Selim I Giray
importance: Forced the Ottoman army to lift the siege of Chyhyryn and retreat, securing victory in the 1677 campaign

name: Battle of the Alma
commanders: Mykhailo Doroshenko & Shahin Giray vs. Khan Temir & Ottoman Janissaries
importance: Cossack forces defeated Khan Temir's army to lift the siege of Bakhchysarai
casualties: 100–1,000 Cossacks killed (including Hetman Doroshenko); ~200 Nogai/Ottoman troops killed

name: Battle of the Tyzyl Gorge (Kanzhal Campaign)
commanders: Kurghoqo Hatokhshoqo vs. Qaplan I Giray
importance: Initial guerrilla phase where Kabardian forces trapped and decimated Crimean detachments in narrow gorges using rolling stones and archers
casualties: Heavy losses for the invading Tatar forces

name: Battle of Kanzhal
commanders: Kurghoqo Hatokhshoqo & Jabagh Qazanoqo vs. Qaplan I Giray
importance: Night surprise attack utilizing fire-driven panic, virtually destroying the Crimean-Ottoman army and shattering Khanate influence in the region
casualties: 30,000–40,000 Crimean/Ottoman casualties; Khan Qaplan I Giray barely escapes

name: Battle of the Afips River
commanders: Adil Giray & Devlet I Giray vs. Temruqo Idar & Western Circassians
importance: Fierce engagement along the Afips river where the famous Kabardian leader Temruqo Idar was mortally wounded
casualties: Very heavy losses on both sides; multiple Circassian nobles killed or captured

name: Moldavian Campaign in Red Ruthenia
commanders: Stephen III (with Ottoman and Crimean allies) vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Systematic devastation and slaving raids across the Red Ruthenia region up to Lwów
casualties: Heavy regional devastation and mass enslavement

name: Moldavian Campaign in Podolia
commanders: Stephen III (with Ottoman and Crimean allies) vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Comprehensive pillaging and destruction across Podolian lands during the punitive expedition

name: Advance to Przeworsk (1498 Campaign)
commanders: Stephen III (with Ottoman & Crimean allies) vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Deep invasion following the crossing of the Dniestr, ransacking Red Ruthenia and reaching as far as Przeworsk
casualties: Massive devastation and up to 100,000 people taken captive

name: Construction of the Kraków Barbican
commanders: King John I Albert
importance: Built in haste following the disastrous Moldavian campaign and fear of an Ottoman retaliatory invasion on Kraków

name: Battle of Gyalu (Death of Rákóczi)
commanders: George II Rákóczi vs. Ottoman-backed forces
importance: Rákóczi was mortally wounded in this battle and died shortly after, marking the definitive end of his reign and Transylvania's independent ambitions
casualties: George II Rákóczi mortally wounded, died shortly afterward

name: Battle of the Bityug River
commanders: Muscovite forces vs. Tatars
importance: A key engagement where Muscovite forces successfully intercepted and defeated a Tatar raiding party along the Bityug River.

name: Tatar Raid on Moscow
commanders: Tatars (Mazowsza/Kazan elements) vs. Muscovite garrison
importance: An unexpected Tatar assault reached the walls of Moscow and burned the outer posads, but the defenders successfully held the Kremlin and forced a sudden night retreat.
casualties: Significant property damage in outer districts

name: Siege of Kiev
commanders: Edigu (Golden Horde) vs. Lithuanian garrison
importance: Following the disastrous Battle of the Vorskla River, the victorious Tatar forces besieged Kiev, which was forced to pay a heavy ransom to avoid destruction.

name: Battle of Odoyev
commanders: Grand Duchy of Lithuania vs. Great Horde (Ulugh Muhammad)
importance: Fought near the town of Odoyev, Lithuanian forces defeated the troops of the Great Horde, halting Tatar expansion into the Upper Oka principalities.

name: Ottoman-Tatar Punitive Invasion of Transylvania
commanders: Ottoman/Crimean Tatar forces (Sultan-ordered) vs. George II Rákóczi
importance: Retaliation for Rákóczi's unauthorized 1657 campaign; devastated Transylvania and began the Porte's direct reassertion of control over the principality
casualties: Widespread devastation of Transylvanian towns and countryside

name: Capitulation of Rákóczi's Army
commanders: George II Rákóczi vs. Crimean Tatar forces
importance: Isolated and surrounded during retreat, Rákóczi's remaining forces were forced to capitulate to the Tatars, effectively ending the Polish campaign in disaster
casualties: Large portions of the Transylvanian army killed or taken captive

name: Battle of Kassa
commanders: Aeneas de Caprara vs. Abdi Pasha the Albanian
importance: Regained Habsburg control over Upper Hungary / Košice, which had been lost to Imre Thököly's Kuruc forces in 1682.

name: Siege of Santa Maura
commanders: Francesco Morosini vs. Bekir Agha
importance: The opening battle of the Sixth Ottoman–Venetian (Morean) War; a Venetian fleet and land force under Francesco Morosini successfully besieged and captured the strategic fortress of Santa Maura on Lefkada after intensive bombardment and a negotiated surrender
casualties: 127 Venetians killed, 128 wounded, and heavy losses due to disease; 700 garrison members and 3,000 civilians evacuated safely

name: Siege of Old and New Navarino (1686)
commanders: Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck vs. Sefer Pasa
importance: Königsmarck's forces captured Old Navarino by cutting its water supply and forced the surrender of New Navarino after an accidental explosion killed its commander, securing a vital foothold in Messenia.
casualties: Heavy for the Ottoman garrison (commander Sefer Pasa killed by magazine explosion)

name: Siege of Modon (1686)
commanders: Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Following sustained bombardment and successive assaults, the heavily fortified stronghold of Modon (Methoni) surrendered to Venetian forces, with its population safely transported to Tripoli.
casualties: Moderate to heavy for the defending garrison

name: Siege and Battle of Nauplia (1686)
commanders: Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck and Francesco Morosini vs. Mustapha Pasha and Ismail Pasha
importance: Venetian forces captured the strategic heights of Palamidi, successfully repulsed relief efforts and large-scale attacks by Ismail Pasha, and forced the surrender of Nauplia, establishing it as Venice's major regional base.
casualties: High among the Venetian besiegers due to plague and combat; 7,000 Muslims evacuated

name: Siege of Virovitica
commanders: James Leslie & Trautmansdorf vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: An early major success of the Great Turkish War in the Croatian–Slavonian theater; allied Habsburg and Croatian forces under James Leslie besieged and captured the strategic Ottoman border town of Virovitica after intercepting a relief force and negotiating a surrender, establishing a vital base for future operations in Slavonia
casualties: Garrison and relief force losses; Ottoman forces captured alive during interception

name: Battle of Mohács (1687)
commanders: Charles of Lorraine and Maximilian II Emanuel vs. Sarı Süleyman Paşa
importance: Also known as the Battle of Harsány Mountain, this crushing defeat for the Ottomans completely reversed the outcome of the 1526 battle, precipitating an internal Ottoman political crisis and a major mutiny that led to the deposition of Sultan Mehmed IV and the Habsburg reconquest of Slavonia and Transylvania.
casualties: Light among Imperial forces (~600 killed); heavy among Ottomans (~10,000 dead, 2,000 captured)

name: Siege of Požega (1689)
commanders: Ottoman forces vs. Local insurgent and Habsburg-allied forces
importance: Following the earlier relief of Požega by Ibrišimović's local insurgents at the Battle of Sokolovac, control of the region was further consolidated under Christian forces during the Great Turkish War.

name: Battle of Zenta
commanders: Prince Eugene of Savoy vs. Sultan Mustafa II
importance: A catastrophic defeat for the Ottomans while crossing the Tisza River; Prince Eugene captured the Ottoman treasury and Imperial Seal, leading directly to the Treaty of Karlowitz and ending Ottoman dominance in Central Europe.
casualties: Light among Holy League forces (~429 killed); massive among Ottomans (~20,000 to 30,000 killed, wounded, or drowned)

name: Capture of Doboj Fortress
commanders: Prince Eugene of Savoy vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Following the plundering of Brod and crossing into Bosnia, Prince Eugene's forces utilized artillery shelling to capture the Doboj Fortress after the garrison refused an ultimatum.

name: Sack of Sarajevo
commanders: Prince Eugene of Savoy vs. Gazi Mehmed Pasha and Sarı Ahmed Pasha
importance: After peace envoys were attacked, Prince Eugene ordered an assault that thoroughly looted and burned most of Sarajevo to the ground, devastating the city's population and economy for nearly two centuries.
casualties: Very high; most of the civilian population affected by the fire and destruction

name: Sack of Krapina
commanders: Ahmed Giray vs. Local Croatian garrisons and inhabitants
importance: Conducted concurrently with the larger Ottoman campaign against Novi Zrin, Crimean Tatar forces led by Ahmed Giray raided deep into the Croatian countryside, successfully sacking Krapina as recorded in Evliya Çelebi's Seyahatnâme.
casualties: High among the local civilian population due to raiding and plunder

name: Battle of Samothrace
commanders: Daniele Dolfin vs. Ottoman, Tripolitanian, and Tunisian commanders
importance: An inconclusive naval engagement off Samothrace involving Venetian sailing ships against an Ottoman and North African allied fleet; notable as the last significant battle of the Great Turkish War.

name: Action of 6 July 1697
commanders: Bartolomeo Contarini vs. Ottoman fleet commanders
importance: A series of naval engagements during the Morean War and the wider Great Turkish War, in which the Venetian fleet under Bartolomeo Contarini pursued and fought the Ottoman fleet across the Aegean Sea. The clashes occurred near Lemnos on 6 July, between Andros and Euboea on 1 September, and south of Euboea on 20 September 1697. Both sides deployed around twenty-six major sailing warships supported by smaller vessels. The Venetian fleet successfully challenged Ottoman naval power in the Aegean, capturing or damaging several enemy vessels and maintaining Venetian dominance of key sea routes during the final years of the war.
casualties: Venetian losses: about 262 killed and 679 wounded across the engagements. Ottoman losses: unknown, including damaged and captured vessels.

name: Battle of Olasch
summary: A Habsburg Imperial army under Augustus II the Strong lifted the siege of Temesvár after Sultan Mustafa II's relief army crossed the Danube at Pancsova. The battle near the Bega River ended indecisively with heavy casualties on both sides, but the Ottomans retained Temesvár and achieved their strategic objective.

name: Battle of Timișoara
commanders: Frederick Augustus I, Elector of Saxony, vs. Sultan Mustafa II
importance: The Battle of Timișoara was fought during the Great Turkish War between Habsburg Imperial forces and the Ottoman army near the fortress of Timișoara in the Banat region. The Imperial army, commanded by Frederick Augustus I of Saxony, attempted to challenge Ottoman control of the region but was defeated by Sultan Mustafa II's forces. The victory strengthened Ottoman control over the Banat and demonstrated the temporary recovery of Ottoman military power following earlier Habsburg advances in Hungary and Serbia. The battle occurred shortly before the decisive Ottoman defeat at Zenta in 1697, which ultimately forced the empire toward the Treaty of Karlowitz.

name: Siege of Klis
commanders: Petar Kružić vs. Murat-beg Tardić
importance: Following the death of Croatian feudal lord Petar Kružić and the failure of Christian relief forces, the strategic Klis Fortress surrendered to the Ottomans, becoming the center of the Sanjak of Klis.

name: Osijek Campaign
commanders: James Leslie vs. Ottoman regional garrison
importance: A successful deep raid into Ottoman Slavonia where Christian forces defeated an Ottoman field army near Osijek and destroyed the local palanka and Suleiman Bridge, though they lacked heavy artillery to siege the main fortress.

name: Battle of Sokolovac
commanders: Ibrišimović vs. Ottoman garrison of Požega
importance: Ibrišimović assembled a local insurgent force that ambushed and defeated an Ottoman army besieging Požega, earning him the nickname 'Sokol' and serving as a launchpad for the liberation of Slavonia.

name: Siege of Udbina
commanders: Joseph von Herberstein vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Herberstein successfully forced the dehydrated Ottoman garrison inside Udbina to surrender by cutting off their water source, leading to the liberation of the entire Lika region.
casualties: None killed directly in siege; garrison captured/disarmed

name: Surrender of Lički Novi
commanders: Joseph von Herberstein and Marko Mesić vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The Ottoman garrison at Lički Novi immediately surrendered upon the arrival of Herberstein's army crossing the Velebit mountains, prompting other nearby outposts to withdraw and triggering the broader liberation of Lika.

name: Siege of Bilaj
commanders: Joseph von Herberstein vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Following a two-day cannon bombardment, the Ottoman garrison at Bilaj surrendered and was granted permission to withdraw peacefully.

name: Surrender of Perušić
commanders: Joseph von Herberstein vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The outposts of Budak and Perušić surrendered to Herberstein's advancing Christian army, with the garrison allowed to pull out safely.

name: Skirmish at Udbina
commanders: Joseph von Herberstein vs. Ottoman forces
importance: As the Christian army arrived before Udbina through Pločanski klanac, a small force of about 300 Ottoman troops attempted a brief skirmish before retreating behind the stronghold's walls.

name: Siege of Bihać
commanders: Karl Auersperg and Ivan Andrija Makar vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Planned as a diversionary attack from the main Danube offensive, the Habsburg siege of Bihać was ultimately called off due to strong Ottoman resistance, lack of coordination, and orders from Vienna.

name: Conquest of Coron
commanders: Francesco Morosini vs. Halil Pasha
importance: The opening campaign of the Venetian conquest of the Morea during the Great Turkish War; a Venetian-led allied force successfully besieged and captured the strategic Ottoman fortress of Coron after defeating an Ottoman relief army and breaching the citadel walls
casualties: Garrison massacred following an accidental explosion during surrender negotiations; over 1,336 inhabitants enslaved; unknown Venetian/allied casualties

name: Battle of Kalamata
commanders: Hannibal von Degenfeld & Maximilian William of Brunswick-Lüneburg vs. Kapudan Pasha
importance: Fought during the Morean War; an allied Venetian expeditionary army under Hannibal von Degenfeld attacked and routed an entrenched Ottoman force outside Kalamata, cementing the Venetian foothold in the southern Morea, prompting the destruction of the obsolete local castle, and completing the liberation of the Mani Peninsula
casualties: Heavy Ottoman casualties and retreat; minor Venetian-allied losses

name: Battle of Mani
commanders: Francesco Morosini, Hannibal von Degenfeld & Pavlos Makris vs. Ismail Pasha & Kapudan Pasha
importance: A key phase of the Morean War where Venetian victories at Coron and Kalamata, combined with renewed Maniot uprisings, forced the capitulation and evacuation of Ottoman garrisons from Zarnata, Kelefa, and Passavas, securing the Mani Peninsula for Venice
casualties: Heavy Ottoman garrison evacuations and losses; allied losses from combat and winter disease

name: Night Attack on Herceg Novi
commanders: Hajduks and Montenegrin forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: A short night attack demonstrating the anti-Ottoman intents of the Hajduks and local forces prior to formal Venetian-led campaigns in the region.

name: Battle of Vrtijeljka
commanders: Bajo Pivljanin and Venetian-backed hajduks vs. Suleyman Bushati
importance: Ottoman forces under the Vizier of Shkodër annihilated the hajduk detachment making a last stand, allowing them to penetrate and plunder Cetinje.
casualties: Heavy losses among the hajduks and defenders

name: Siege and Capture of Herceg Novi
commanders: Girolamo Cornaro and Duke Vučeta Bogdanović vs. Topal Hussein Pasha of Bosnia
importance: Following a month-long siege and successful Montenegrin defense against relief forces at Kameno, Herceg Novi surrendered to the Venetians, ending nearly 150 years of Ottoman rule.

name: Battle of Kameno
commanders: Montenegrin forces vs. Topal Hussein Pasha
importance: Montenegrin forces under Venetian alliance successfully defeated Ottoman relief forces attempting to break the siege of Herceg Novi.

name: First Kuči Defense against Suleyman Pasha
commanders: Kuči tribe vs. Suleyman Pasha Bushati
importance: Suleyman Pasha Bushati attacked the Montenegrin Highland tribe Kuči twice, suffering a heavy defeat with 1,500 casualties and losing Medun.

name: July 1691 Expedition against Piperi and Bjelopavlići
commanders: Piperi and Bjelopavlići tribes vs. Suleyman Pasha Bushati
importance: Suleyman was defeated yet again during his punitive expeditions against the Piperi and Bjelopavlići tribes.

name: Ottoman Campaign against Cetinje and Destruction of the Monastery
commanders: Suleyman Pasha Bushati vs. Venetian garrison
result: Ottoman tactical advance / Venetian retreat and sabotage
importance: Suleyman launched a large campaign against Montenegro; Venetian forces retreated to the Cetinje Monastery and, before departing, time-mined and permanently destroyed it, alienating the local population from Venice.

name: Battle of Cape Corvo
commanders: Ottavio d'Aragona vs. Sinari Pasha
importance: A major naval engagement of the Ottoman-Habsburg wars near Samos; a Sicilian-Spanish squadron under Ottavio d'Aragona ambushed and defeated an Ottoman fleet, capturing seven galleys and around 600 prisoners, marking the greatest Spanish naval victory over the Ottomans since Lepanto
casualties: 6 Spaniards killed, 30 wounded; ~400 Ottomans killed, 600 captured, and 1,200 Christian galley slaves freed

name: Battle on Vrtijeljka
commanders: Bošković, Bajo Pivljanin & Antonio Zeno vs. Süleyman Pasha of Scutari
importance: Fought on the hill of Vrtijeljka near Cetinje at the start of the Morean War; an Ottoman force under Süleyman Pasha of Scutari defeated a Venetian irregular force and Montenegrin-Hajduk fighters, resulting in the death of the famed hajduk leader Bajo Pivljanin and the display of severed heads in Constantinople
casualties: Heavy Christian and Hajduk casualties, including the death of Bajo Pivljanin and dozens of fighters; significant Ottoman losses

name: Battle of Párkány
commanders: John III Sobieski and Charles V, Duke of Lorraine vs. Ottoman field army
importance: Crushed the retreating Ottoman forces in northern Hungary immediately after the relief of Vienna.
casualties: Heavy for Ottomans, light for Christians

name: Rákóczi's Invasion of Poland (Treaty of Radnot Campaign)
commanders: George II Rákóczi & Antin Zhdanovych (Cossacks) & Swedish allies vs. Polish-Lithuanian forces
importance: Unauthorized invasion of Poland under the Treaty of Radnot, launched without Ottoman consent, in alliance with Charles X Gustav of Sweden and Khmelnytsky's Cossacks; part of the broader 'Deluge'

name: Abandonment by Sweden and Cossack Withdrawal
commanders: George II Rákóczi vs. Polish-Lithuanian forces & Crimean Tatars
importance: Charles X Gustav withdrew to counter a Danish threat, leaving Rákóczi's army isolated; Cossack support also withdrew, exposing Transylvanian forces to encirclement

name: Crimean Tatar Raids into Poland-Lithuania
commanders: Crimean Khanate vs. Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
result: Frequent Tatar raids and strategic alliance victories
importance: Frequent deep raids into Poland-Lithuania culminated in Tatars fighting alongside the Ottoman army at the Battle of Cecora in 1620, crushing Polish-Lithuanian forces and capturing Hetman Stanisław Żółkiewski.

name: Crimean Tatar Slaving Sweeps during the Khmelnytsky Uprising
commanders: Crimean Khanate (allied with Cossacks) vs. Poland-Lithuania
importance: While allied with Ukrainian Cossacks during their rebellion against Poland, Crimean forces independently launched massive slaving sweeps through Volhynia, Red Ruthenia, and Podolia.
casualties: Tens of thousands of captives taken

name: Opportunistic Border Raids during 'The Deluge'
commanders: Crimean Khanate vs. Poland, Russia, and Cossack Hetmanate
importance: During the Russo-Polish War and Swedish invasions, the Tatar khans switched sides rapidly between Poland, Russia, and the Cossack Hetmanate, raiding whichever territory was momentarily undefended.

name: Battle of Zeytinburnu
commanders: Mezzomorto Hüseyin Pasha vs. Venetian commanders
importance: The Ottoman fleet under Mezzomorto inflicted a devastating defeat on the Venetian fleet off Lesbos after the accidental explosion of the Venetian flagship Battista Piccolo, resulting in thousands of casualties and the capture of several vessels.
casualties: ~5,000 Venetian casualties, including multiple senior officers and captured ships

name: The Last Great Raid
commanders: Qirim Giray vs. Russian-Ukrainian border defense
result: Initial Tatar raid success / Strategic failure
importance: During the Russo-Turkish War, Khan Qirim Giray led the final major Tatar raid in history, bursting across the Russian-Ukrainian border and capturing roughly 20,000 slaves as a dying gasp of the slave-raiding era.

name: Battle of Andros
commanders: Bartolomeo Contarini and Alessandro Molin vs. Mezzo Morto Hüseyin Pasha
importance: An indecisive naval engagement off Andros where the combined Venetian and Papal fleet engaged Mezzo Morto Hüseyin Pasha's Ottoman and Barbary fleet without any vessels being lost on either side.
casualties: 56 Christians killed and 125 wounded in sailing ships, plus ~19 casualties in rowing vessels

name: Battle of Lubieszów
commanders: Jan Zborowski vs. Johann Winkelbruch
importance: A smaller royal army (~2,500 men) decisively defeated a much larger Danzig-mercenary army (~10,000–12,000 men), leading into the Siege of Danzig
casualties: 4,416–4,427 Danzig soldiers killed and 1,000–5,000 captured vs. 58 killed and 127 wounded for the Commonwealth

name: Battle of Cenei
commanders: Frederick Augustus I of Saxony vs. Sultan Mustafa II
importance: Fought in the Banat of Temeswar between the Habsburg army and the Ottoman forces personally led by Sultan Mustafa II, resulting in an Ottoman victory.

name: Siege of Vác
commanders: Charles V, Duke of Lorraine vs. Ottoman-Kuruc outposts
importance: Cleared opposing Ottoman-Kuruc strongholds along the Danube valley during maneuvers leading to Buda.

name: Battle of Eperjes
commanders: General Schulz vs. Imre Thököly
importance: Fought near Eperjes (Prešov, Slovakia) during the Great Turkish War; Imperial Habsburg forces under General Schulz decisively defeated the anti-Habsburg Kuruc and Ottoman allied forces led by Imre Thököly
casualties: Unspecified losses; decisive defeat for Thököly's forces

name: First Siege of Esztergom
commanders: John III Sobieski and Charles V, Duke of Lorraine vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Recaptured the strategic fortress city of Esztergom following the success at Párkány.

name: Siege of Esztergom (1605)
commanders: Lala Mehmed Pasha vs. Wilheim Öttingen and Count Dampierre
importance: A major 1605 Ottoman siege during the Long Turkish War where Grand Vizier Lala Mehmed Pasha successfully captured Esztergom from the Habsburg garrison following intense bombardment, mining, and the collapse of key defenses on Saint Thomas Hill.
casualties: ~1,000 defenders killed during the defense of the town; heavy losses from Ottoman mines and assaults before the final surrender

name: Attack on Kereki
commanders: Colonel Concini vs. Local Forces
importance: Colonel Concini launched a military attack on Kereki during the early stages of regional anti-Habsburg disturbances.

name: Battle of Álmosd
commanders: Stephen Bocskai vs. Imperial Forces
importance: A crucial early victory for Stephen Bocskai's anti-Habsburg insurgent forces that launched his major uprising in Royal Hungary.
casualties: Moderate to heavy combat casualties on both sides

name: Conquest of Debrecen
commanders: Stephen Bocskai vs. Imperial Garrison
importance: Debrecen was successfully captured by Stephen Bocskai's forces immediately following the victory at Álmosd, securing a major regional base.

name: Battle of Tokaj
commanders: Stephen Boczkaí vs. Belgioioso
importance: Bocskai's forces defeated imperial troops under Belgioioso, expanding insurgent control toward the upper Tisza region.

name: Battle of Ostyán
commanders: Balázs Németi vs. Giorgio Basta
importance: Imperial general Giorgio Basta defeated rebel forces, leading to the capture and execution of insurgent leader Balázs Németi.
casualties: Rebel leader executed; moderate insurgent casualties

name: Battle of Edelény
commanders: Bocskai's Forces vs. Imperial Forces
importance: A tactical engagement during the late autumn campaign as imperial forces attempted to check Bocskai's expansion in northeastern Hungary.

name: Fall of Kazan
commanders: Ivan the Terrible vs. Khan Yadegar Mokhammad
importance: The fall of the Kazan Khanate shattered the Turkic-Islamic balance in the middle Volga region and marked the beginning of Russian expansion into the Kipchak steppes.

name: Capture of Aden and Red Sea Campaign
commanders: Hadim Suleiman Pasha vs. Local Yemeni Rulers / Portuguese forces
importance: Secured Aden and the choke point of the southern Red Sea against Portuguese naval hegemony, establishing the Ottoman Eyalet of Yemen.

name: Siege of Jeddah
commanders: Ottoman garrison vs. Portuguese fleet under Estêvão da Gama
importance: Repulsed a major Portuguese expedition aimed at destroying Islamic holy sites and cutting off Ottoman maritime trade in the Red Sea.

name: Battle of Tlemcen / Campaigns in North Africa
commanders: Salah Reis vs. Saadi / Local rivals
importance: Solidified Ottoman-Barbary control across the North African littoral, countering Spanish and local dynastic opposition.

name: War of Parma
commanders: Ottavio Farnese, Henry II of France vs. Charles V, Pope Julius III
importance: Opened the Italian War of 1551–1559 over control of Parma and French influence in northern Italy.

name: Invasion of Gozo
commanders: Ottoman navy vs. Knights of Malta
importance: Preceded the conquest of Tripoli by weeks

name: Ottoman-Adal Campaign against Abyssinia
commanders: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi (supported by Ottoman musketeers) vs. Ethiopian-Portuguese forces
importance: Marked the high-water mark and subsequent check of Muslim-Ottoman aligned expansion in the Horn of Africa and the southern Red Sea basin.

name: Siege / Blockade of Kamianets
commanders: Jan III Sobieski / Stanisław Jan Jabłonowski vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Repeated Polish attempts to blockade and starve out the major Ottoman fortress wedge in Podolia following the victory at Vienna, which ultimately held out until the 1699 Treaty of Karlowitz.

name: Siege of Kamenets
commanders: James Louis Sobieski, Stanisław Jan Jabłonowski, Andrzej Potocki, and Andriy Mohyla vs. Huseyin Pasha
importance: A Polish-Cossack army of 27,000 led by James Louis Sobieski attempted to recapture the Ottoman fortress of Kamenets, but the arrival of a 10,000-strong relief force caused the Polish troops to retreat in failure.

name: 1688 Siege of Kamenets
commanders: Polish-Lithuanian commanders vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: A second consecutive failed Polish expedition involving an 18,000-man army attempting to capture Kamenets, followed by a retreat and subsequent Crimean raids on Polish lands.

name: Skirmishes of Göllersdorf and the Austrian Marches
commanders: Habsburg border garrisons vs. Ottoman Akinji raiders
importance: Represented the penetration of Ottoman raiding parties deep into Lower Austria along the Morava and Danube river valleys, checked by Habsburg border defense forces.

name: Siege of Buda
commanders: Charles V, Duke of Lorraine vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The massive Habsburg attempt to capture the vital Ottoman stronghold of Buda failed due to stubborn garrison defense and winter conditions.

name: Siege around Érsekújvár
commanders: Habsburg Imperial forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Targeted operations and blockades to isolate key Ottoman regional strongholds in upper Hungary.

name: Battle of Vezekény
commanders: Ádám Forgách and Ladislaus Esterházy vs. Bey Mustafa
importance: A notable 17th-century engagement where Hungarian forces secured a victory against Ottoman raiders, though at the cost of notable noble leaders of the Esterházy family.

name: Capture of Gallipoli
commanders: Suleyman Pasha; Byzantine local defenders
importance: Established the first durable Ottoman base on the European side of the Dardanelles.

name: Battle of Jiliște
commanders: John III the Terrible & Ivan Svirhovsky vs. Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, Peter the Lame & Alexander II Mircea
importance: Major Moldavian-Cossack victory during the Moldavian campaign of 1574 against combined Ottoman, Crimean, and Wallachian forces.
casualties: Heavy Ottoman-Crimean losses; entire enemy force routed.

name: Battle of Cătlăbuga
commanders: Stephen III of Moldavia & Jan Karnkowski vs. Ottoman forces
importance: Moldavian-Polish victory near Chilia during the Moldavian campaign of 1484–1486, though Stephen ultimately ceased attempts to retake Chilia.

name: Battle of Dubica
commanders: Petar Berislavić, Nikola III Zrinski & Mihovil Frankopan vs. Junuz-aga (Ottoman forces)
importance: Fought near Dubica between the Sava and Una rivers; a Croatian army under Ban Petar Berislavić decisively defeated an Ottoman raiding force from the Sanjak of Bosnia, inflicting heavy losses and freeing numerous Christian captives
casualties: Heavy Ottoman casualties (estimated between 2,000 and 7,000 killed, drowned, or captured, including several commanders)

name: Battle of Plješevica
commanders: Petar Berislavić vs. Ottoman Empire forces
importance: An engagement on Mount Plješevica during which the veteran Croatian Ban Petar Berislavić was ambushed and killed after years of relentless campaigning against Ottoman incursions
casualties: Croatian forces defeated; death of Ban Petar Berislavić

name: Battle of Botoșani
commanders: Stephen III of Moldavia vs. Bayezid II
importance: Major Moldavian victory during the Moldavian-Ottoman War (1498–1500), resulting in a disastrous rout of the Ottoman army.

name: Battle of Ștefănești
commanders: Stephen III of Moldavia vs. Eminek Mârza
importance: Moldavian victory during the Moldavian-Ottoman War (1475–1476) against invading Crimean-Nogai Tatar forces.

name: Battle of Cahul
commanders: John the Terrible & Ivan Svirhovsky vs. Ottoman-Crimean forces
importance: Decisive suppression of the Moldavian Revolt following noble betrayal; resulted in the execution of Prince John the Terrible and the capture of Cossack hetman Ivan Svirhovsky.

name: Capture of Yazlovets
commanders: Jan III Sobieski vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Marked the opening success of the first phase of the Moldavian campaign.

name: Battle of Boiany
commanders: Stanisław Jan Jabłonowski vs. Sulieman Pasha, Constantin Cantemir, and Crimean forces
importance: Defeated the invading Polish army in Bukovina, forcing a grueling retreat and stalling Polish expansion aims.

name: Skirmish at Bukovina Forest
commanders: Stanisław Jan Jabłonowski vs. Ottoman, Moldavian and Crimean pursuers
result: Indecisive tactical engagement / Strategic Ottoman pursuit
importance: A fierce rearguard action during the retreat back across the Prut River, successfully protecting the remnants of the Polish army.

name: Capture of Iași
commanders: King Jan III Sobieski vs. Moldavian garrison
importance: As part of the 1686 campaign, King Jan III Sobieski's army captured Iași to use as a strong garrison and base of operations after the Moldavian prince and boyars abandoned the city.

name: Engagement at Iași (Fire and Retreat)
commanders: King Jan III Sobieski vs. Anti-Polish local populace / Ottoman-Crimean pressure
importance: Following a devastating city-wide fire and rising anti-Polish sentiment, the Polish forces were prompted to abandon Iași and begin their retreat.

name: Capture of Soroca
commanders: King Jan III Sobieski vs. Ottoman-Moldavian garrison
importance: Captured by King Jan III Sobieski's army during the initial successes of his final Moldavia campaign in late August 1691.

name: Capture of Suceava
commanders: King Jan III Sobieski vs. Ottoman-Moldavian garrison
importance: Successfully captured by Polish forces alongside Soroca during the opening phase of the 1691 Moldavian campaign.

name: Battle of Novoselka
commanders: Stefan Dymidecki vs. Yamman Saidak and Tatar-Ottoman forces
importance: Fought on June 6, 1688, near Kamianets during the Polish-Ottoman War, where a Polish detachment under Stefan Dymidecki was intercepted, overwhelmed, and routed by a superior force of Crimean Tatars and Ottoman janissaries.
casualties: Several hundred Polish soldiers killed and 18 banners captured

name: Capture of Neamț
commanders: King Jan III Sobieski vs. Ottoman-Moldavian garrison
importance: Captured by the poorly supplied Polish army on October 14, 1691, as the campaign pushed deeper before being forced to retreat due to a lack of promised Austrian aid and constant enemy harassment.

name: Engagement against Crimean Cavalry
commanders: King Jan III Sobieski vs. Crimean forces
importance: A notable clash during the grueling Polish retreat where Polish forces successfully routed a detachment of 2,000 Crimean cavalrymen.
casualties: Unknown specific numbers (2,000 Crimean cavalry engaged and routed)

name: Final Rear-guard Battle of the 1686 Campaign
commanders: King Jan III Sobieski vs. Ottoman-Crimean pursuers
importance: The last major defensive battle fought by the exhausted Polish army against harassing Ottoman-Crimean forces shortly before crossing back over the border near Sniatyn on October 13.
casualties: Contributed to overall campaign losses of 20% to 30% of the Polish force

name: Capture of Adrianople (Edirne)
commanders: Murad I and Lala Sahin Pasha; Byzantine defenders
importance: Gave the Ottomans a major Thracian capital and road hub.

name: Battle of Maritsa (Sirpsindigi)
commanders: Ottoman raiding forces; Balkan coalition
importance: Early victory consolidating Ottoman power in Thrace.

name: Adrianople officially becomes capital
commanders: Murad I
importance: Marked the European orientation of the expanding Ottoman state.

name: Capture of Serres
commanders: Ottoman Rumelian forces; Byzantine/Serbian local defenders
importance: Strengthened Ottoman control of eastern Macedonia.

name: Capture of Sofia
commanders: Lala Sahin Pasha; Bulgarian defenders
importance: Secured a key road junction into the western Balkans.

name: Capture of Nis
commanders: Murad I; Serbian defenders
importance: Opened the Morava corridor toward Serbia.

name: Capture of Thessaloniki (temporary)
commanders: Ottoman Rumelian forces; Byzantine defenders
importance: First Ottoman occupation of the major Aegean port before its later permanent conquest.

name: Campaign into Bosnia
commanders: Ottoman frontier commanders; Bosnian forces
importance: Extended Ottoman pressure into Bosnia before later conquest.

name: Battle of Kosovo
commanders: Murad I; Prince Lazar
result: The Ottoman forces delivered a devastating and decisive triumph, shattering the Serbian host and securing the realm, though both Sultan Murad and Prince Lazar fell in the fierce clash.
importance: Reshaped Serbian-Ottoman relations and Balkan power politics.

name: Capture of Skopje
commanders: Pasa Yigit Bey; Serbian local authorities
importance: Made Skopje a major Ottoman base in the Vardar corridor.

name: Siege of Tarnovo
commanders: Ottoman forces; Bulgarian defenders
importance: Crippled the Second Bulgarian Empire.

name: Battle of Rovine
commanders: Bayezid I; Mircea the Elder
importance: Demonstrated the contested nature of Ottoman suzerainty over Wallachia.

name: Battle of Nicopolis
commanders: Bayezid I; Sigismund of Hungary
importance: Destroyed a major anti-Ottoman crusade on the Danube.

name: Sack of Patras (Spanish)
commanders: Spanish Fleet vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Part of anti-Ottoman naval operations; the city was significantly damaged by fire.

name: Pillage of Patras (Maltese)
commanders: Knights of Malta vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: A destructive naval raid highlighting the vulnerability of Peloponnesian coastal cities.

name: Siege and Storming of Hainburg
commanders: Ottoman Advance Forces vs. Imperial Garrison
result: Ottoman victory / Destruction of the town
importance: As the main Ottoman army advanced toward Vienna during the 1683 campaign, advance forces stormed and captured the strategic Danubian town of Hainburg in Lower Austria, overcoming fierce resistance.
casualties: Heavy loss of life among the defenders and townspeople

name: Ottoman and Tatar Raids on Silesia
commanders: Ottoman and Tatar Light Cavalry vs. Regional Garrisons
importance: Following the fall of Érsekújvár (Nové Zámky) during the 1663-1664 war, Ottoman and allied Tatar irregular cavalry pushed deep north into Moravia and Silesia, burning towns, villages, and taking thousands of captives far beyond the main theater.
casualties: Thousands of civilians captured or killed; widespread regional devastation

name: Raid on Wiener Neustadt
commanders: Ottoman and Tatar Raiders vs. Imperial Garrison
result: Ottoman raiding success / Town besieged and bypassed
importance: During Suleiman the Magnificent's 1529 campaign against Vienna, Ottoman and Tatar light cavalry raided, besieged, and subjected Wiener Neustadt to heavy attacks before the main forces moved on toward Vienna.
casualties: Severe surrounding devastation and local garrison losses

name: Raid and Occupation of Klosterneuburg (1529)
commanders: Ottoman Advance Forces vs. Imperial Garrison
importance: During the 1529 campaign against Vienna, Ottoman troops raided and occupied the strategic town and abbey complex of Klosterneuburg just north of Vienna, using it as a forward base and staging area.
casualties: Local garrison and civilian casualties; extensive looting

name: Raid and Operations at Klosterneuburg (1683)
commanders: Ottoman Forces vs. Imperial Outposts
importance: During the 1683 Ottoman advance on Vienna, Klosterneuburg was once again targeted, raided, and occupied by Ottoman detachments to secure the Danube approaches north of the capital.
casualties: Surrounding area devastated; regional outpost losses

name: Raid of Moravia
commanders: Ottoman and Crimean Tatar forces; Habsburg forces
importance: A major tactical raid disrupting Habsburg supply lines during the Austro-Turkish War.
casualties: Significant disruption and material losses in the Moravian region.

name: Siege of Ioannina
commanders: Ottoman forces; Byzantine/local defenders
importance: The surrender of Ioannina marked a significant step in the Ottoman consolidation of Epirus.

name: Battle of Romhány
commanders: Habsburg vs. Ottoman Empire
importance: An early engagement of the Long Turkish War on the northern Hungarian front.

name: Battle of Guruslău
commanders: Michael the Brave and Giorgio Basta vs. Mózes Székely
importance: One of the final major military successes for Michael the Brave in Transylvania.

name: Battle of Humenné
commanders: Walenty Rogawski & George Drugeth vs. George Rákóczi
importance: Polish-Habsburg allied forces under Walenty Rogawski defeated George Rákóczi's Transylvanian corps, forcing Gábor Bethlen to lift the siege of Vienna and retreat
casualties: Heavy losses for Transylvanians during the unexpected counterattack

name: Siege of Stuhlweissenburg (1601)
commanders: Habsburg forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The strategic fortress was briefly recaptured by Christian forces.

name: Siege of Székesfehérvár (1602)
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Habsburg forces
importance: The Ottomans successfully reclaimed this critical stronghold.

name: Siege of Buda (1603)
commanders: Habsburg forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: A failed attempt by Habsburg forces to reclaim the administrative heart of Ottoman Hungary.

name: Naval Battle of Preveza
commanders: Hayreddin Barbarossa; Andrea Doria
importance: Consolidated Ottoman naval dominance in the Mediterranean for decades.
casualties: Heavy losses for the Holy League fleet.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Sudak
commanders: Gedik Ahmed Pasha
importance: Consolidation of Ottoman control over the Crimean coast.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Balaklava
commanders: Gedik Ahmed Pasha
importance: Further reduced Genoese coastal strongholds.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Kerch
commanders: Gedik Ahmed Pasha
importance: Secured the strategic entrance to the Sea of Azov.

name: Ottoman Conquest of Azov (Tana)
commanders: Gedik Ahmed Pasha
importance: Established Ottoman dominance over the northern Black Sea and the Don River trade route.

name: Battle of Giurgiu
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Wallachia & Habsburg allies
importance: Part of the Long Turkish War, checking Ottoman expansion in the Danube region.

name: Battle of Cecora (1620)
commanders: Stanisław Żółkiewski and Gaspar Graziani vs. Iskender Pasha, Khan Temir, and Gabor Bethlen
importance: A catastrophic defeat for the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in Moldavia during the Polish-Ottoman War, resulting in the death of Grand Hetman Stanisław Żółkiewski, the capture of Hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Bohdan Khmelnytsky, and serving as a direct catalyst for the major campaign of Khotyn in 1621.
casualties: Most of the Commonwealth army killed or captured (only 1,000–1,500 survivors); moderate losses for Ottoman-Tatar forces

name: Battle of White Mountain
commanders: Habsburg/Catholic League vs. Bohemian Protestant Estates (with participation by Lisowczycy)
importance: A decisive early battle of the Thirty Years' War where imperial forces crushed the Bohemian revolt, with Polish Lisowczycy mercenaries participating following their campaigns in Hungary.

name: Battle of Zhovti Vody
commanders: Cossacks & Crimean Khanate; Poland-Lithuania
importance: First major victory of Khmelnytsky's Uprising.

name: Greek Uprisings in the Peloponnese and Aegean
commanders: Francesco Morosini, Joannicius II, and Maniot Leaders vs. Ottoman Provincial Forces
result: Initial rebel and Venetian successes followed by Ottoman suppression
importance: A series of Venetian-fostered Greek uprisings and rebellions against Ottoman rule across the Peloponnese, Mani Peninsula, and Aegean islands—including the capture of Kalamata—which ultimately collapsed when Venetian support was withdrawn, forcing rebels to surrender or flee to Italy.
casualties: Heavy rebel and civilian losses, displacement, and migration to Corsica

name: Siege of Šibenik
commanders: Leonardo Foscolo vs. Ottoman Forces
importance: A grueling month-long Ottoman siege of the key Venetian stronghold of Šibenik, which was successfully repelled by the defenders under Leonardo Foscolo.

name: Ottoman Offensive in Dalmatia (Capture of Novigrad)
commanders: Ottoman Commander vs. Venetian Garrison
importance: Major Ottoman offensive along the Dalmatian front that captured the islands of Krk, Pag, and Cres, alongside the supposedly impregnable fortress of Novigrad after a brief two-day bombardment.
casualties: Garrison losses and surrender of Novigrad

name: Ottoman Raid on Cerigo (Kythera)
commanders: Francesco Morosini / Venetian Garrison vs. Ottoman Raiders
importance: An attempted Ottoman amphibious raid on the island of Cerigo (Kythera) during the prolonged struggle for Crete, which was successfully repelled by the Venetian defenders as the sole allied success of 1667.
casualties: Ottoman raiding forces repulsed with losses

name: Recapture of Novigrad
commanders: Leonardo Foscolo vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: As part of the Venetian counter-offensive on the Dalmatian front led by Leonardo Foscolo, Venetian forces successfully retook the fortress of Novigrad from the Ottomans.

name: Capture of Knin
commanders: Leonardo Foscolo vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Venetian commander Leonardo Foscolo temporarily captured the strategic inland fortress of Knin during the successful 1647 Venetian counter-offensive in Dalmatia.

name: Raid on Aigina and Volos
commanders: Francesco Morosini vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Francesco Morosini initiated a more aggressive campaign, successfully raiding the Ottoman supply depot at Aigina and razing the port town of Volos in a surprise night attack.
casualties: Ottoman supply depot and port town severely damaged

name: Action of 21 June 1655
commanders: Francesco Morosini vs. Mustapha Pasha
importance: A clear Venetian naval victory against a large Ottoman fleet under Mustapha Pasha near the Dardanelles, securing temporary freedom of action for Venetian forces.
casualties: Ottoman fleet defeated and forced to avoid action for the rest of the year

name: Siege of Malvasia (Monemvasia)
commanders: Francesco Morosini vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Following his naval success, Francesco Morosini undertook a siege of the strategic island fortress of Monemvasia off the Peloponnese, which ultimately proved unsuccessful.

name: Battle of Patras
commanders: Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck vs. Mehmed Pasha
importance: Königsmarck's army assaulted the entrenched Ottoman camp outside Patras, routing Mehmed Pasha's forces and triggering a panic that led to the swift abandonment of Rio, Antirrio, and Naupaktos.

name: Capture of Acrocorinth
commanders: Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The Ottoman garrison abandoned the formidable fortress of Acrocorinth after torching the town upon Königsmarck's approach, effectively completing the main conquest of the Peloponnese.

name: Siege of Monemvasia
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The last remaining Ottoman stronghold in the Peloponnese was placed under a prolonged blockade and siege, ultimately holding out until its surrender in 1690.

name: Capture of Tenedos
commanders: Barbado Doer vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Capitalizing on the massive victory at the Second Dardanelles, Venetian forces seized the strategic island of Tenedos to establish a tight blockade.
casualties: Garrison losses and transfer of control

name: Siege of Kelefa
commanders: Ottoman forces vs. Kelefa garrison
result: Ottoman withdrawal upon Venetian fleet arrival
importance: The Ottomans seized the initiative early in the year by attacking Kelefa, but lifted the siege and withdrew when a Venetian fleet under Venieri arrived.

name: Capture of Arkadia
commanders: Venetian squadron and Dalmatian troops vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Captured by a Venetian squadron and Dalmatian troops further north in Messenia concurrently with the operations around Navarino and Modon.

name: Assault on Argos
commanders: Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck vs. Ismail Pasha
importance: Venetian forces successfully launched an assault against the Ottoman relief army under Ismail Pasha, taking Argos and forcing the pasha to retreat to Corinth.

name: Battle of the Venetian Camp at Nauplia
commanders: Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck and Francesco Morosini vs. Ismail Pasha
importance: Ismail Pasha's large-scale attack on the Venetian camp was heavily defeated after Morosini landed 2,000 men from the fleet on his flank, directly precipitating the surrender of Nauplia.
casualties: Heavy for the attacking Ottoman forces

name: Capture of Klis
commanders: Leonardo Foscolo vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Venetian forces under Leonardo Foscolo captured the heavily fortified stronghold of Klis, near Split, as part of their major counter-offensive to turn the tide against the Ottomans in Dalmatia.

name: Capture of Azov
commanders: Don Cossacks; Ottoman Empire
importance: Temporarily severed the Ottoman hold on the Don-Volga trade route.

name: Siege of Azov
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Don Cossacks
importance: Failed Ottoman attempt to regain Azov.

name: Ottoman Recovery of Azov
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Don Cossacks
importance: Cossacks withdrew, returning the fortress to Ottoman control.

name: Ottoman–Polish Border Campaigns
commanders: Ottoman & Crimean forces; Poland-Lithuania
importance: Series of raids destabilizing the Dniester border region.

name: Destruction of the Great Horde
commanders: Crimean Khanate; Great Horde
importance: Ended the remnants of the Golden Horde, clearing the way for Crimean hegemony.

name: Capture of Arta
commanders: Ottoman forces; Local rulers
importance: The capture of Arta expanded Ottoman administrative control across Epirus.

name: Siege of the Hexamilion Wall
commanders: Murad II; Constantine Palaiologos
importance: Ottoman forces breached the defensive wall at the Isthmus of Corinth, opening the Peloponnese to invasion.

name: Siege of Astrakhan
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Tsardom of Russia
importance: Failed Ottoman attempt to capture Astrakhan and control the Volga trade route.

name: Conquest of Thessaly completed
commanders: Ottoman Rumelian forces; Thessalian local powers
importance: Extended direct Ottoman authority into central Greece.

name: Capture of Vidin
commanders: Ottoman Danube forces; Bulgarian defenders
importance: Ended the last major Bulgarian political center.

name: Expansion into Albania
commanders: Ottoman frontier forces; Albanian lords
importance: Laid groundwork for the later Albanian campaigns.

name: Battle of Ankara
commanders: Bayezid I; Timur
importance: Outside the Europe-only frame but essential to the pause in European expansion.

name: End of Ottoman Interregnum
commanders: Mehmed I
importance: Restored dynastic unity after the civil war.

name: Capture of Valona (Vlora)
commanders: Ottoman forces; Albanian/Venetian local authorities
importance: Improved Ottoman access to the Adriatic coast.

name: First Siege of Constantinople
commanders: Murad II; Byzantine defenders
importance: Early failed Ottoman attempt against the Byzantine capital.

name: Capture of Thessaloniki
commanders: Murad II; Venetian defenders
importance: Secured the major Macedonian port for the Ottomans.

name: Albanian campaigns
commanders: Ottoman Rumelian forces; Albanian rebels and lords
importance: Part of the long contest for Albania before Skanderbeg's revolt.

name: Capture of Smederevo
commanders: Murad II; Serbian Despotate defenders
importance: Temporarily eliminated Serbia as an independent barrier.

name: Siege of Belgrade
commanders: Ottoman forces; Hungarian defenders
importance: Showed Belgrade's continued strength as Hungary's southern gate.

name: Battle of Niš (Long Campaign)
commanders: Janos Hunyadi and Wladyslaw III vs. Kasim Pasha / Ottoman commanders
importance: Major Christian victory during the Long Campaign, opening the Balkan offensive before Varna.

name: Battle of Râmnic
commanders: Stephen III of Moldavia vs. Basarab IV and Ottoman forces
importance: Moldavian invasion of Wallachia resulting in the rout of Wallachian-Ottoman forces following the death of Mehmed II.
casualties: Entire Wallachian army annihilated; significant Moldavian losses.

name: Battle of Chițcani
commanders: Stefan Kunicki & Ștefan Petriceicu vs. Yala-Pasha & Ali, bey of Tighina
importance: Cossack and Moldavian allied victory during Kunicki's campaign at the opening of the Polish-Ottoman War (1683–1699).

name: Battle of Reni
commanders: Stefan Kunicki, Andriy Mohyla & Ștefan Petriceicu vs. Haci II Giray & Ottoman forces
importance: Major engagement during the Great Turkish War that effectively ended Kunicki's campaign following initial Christian successes.

name: Skirmishes at the Dniester Crossing
commanders: King Jan III Sobieski vs. Crimean troops
importance: Battles fought against Crimean troops during the construction and protection of bridges across the Dniester River near Zhvanets and Gródek, complicated further by storms and fierce resistance before the campaign was abandoned.
casualties: Heavy due to battles, famine, and disease

name: Siege of Negroponte
commanders: Francesco Morosini and Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck vs. Ottoman garrison and Ismail Pasha
importance: Morosini launched a major campaign to capture Negroponte (Chalkis), but faced a determined Ottoman defense, successful resupply across the Euripus Strait by Ismail Pasha, and heavy losses from the plague—including General Königsmarck—forcing a costly Venetian retreat.
casualties: Roughly 9,000 Venetian and allied losses, largely from disease and combat

name: Attempted Capture of Karystos
commanders: Nikolaos Karystinos vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The warlord Nikolaos Karystinos led an uprising in southern Euboea and attempted to capture the castle of Karystos, but was unsuccessful and later joined the retreating Venetians.

name: Unsuccessful Attack on Monemvasia
commanders: Francesco Morosini vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Morosini attempted an unsuccessful attack on the fortified stronghold of Monemvasia shortly before his failing health forced him to return to Venice.

name: Battle of Varna
commanders: Murad II; Wladyslaw III and Janos Hunyadi
importance: Destroyed the crusade of Varna.
casualties: King Wladyslaw killed; heavy Christian losses.

name: Capture of Nemyriv
commanders: Stefan Kunicki; Ivan Draginich
importance: Removed the local Ottoman-backed administration and re-established Cossack control in Right-bank Ukraine.

name: Capture of Mohyliv
commanders: Stefan Kunicki
importance: Secured a strategic foothold prior to crossing the Prut River into Moldavia.

name: Capture of Yampil
commanders: Stefan Kunicki
importance: Facilitated the coalition's southward advance into the Budjak steppe and Moldavia.

name: Raid on Bilhorod (Akkerman)
commanders: Stefan Kunicki
importance: Stormed surrounding settlements and disrupted regional Tatar power, though the main fortress held due to a lack of heavy artillery.

name: Storming of Izmail
commanders: Stefan Kunicki
importance: Demonstrated deep penetration into Nogai and Tatar territory along the Black Sea coast.
casualties: Garrison losses unrecorded; tactical success for the raiders.

name: Storming of Kiliia
commanders: Stefan Kunicki
importance: Contributed to the widespread disruption of Ottoman supply lines and local defense structures in the Budjak region.

name: Battle of Obreška
commanders: Croatian Ban Petar Erdody vs. Bosnian Sanjakbey Mustafa Pasha Sokolović
importance: Successfully checked the Ottoman advance following the fall of Krupa, leading to the ennoblement of Petar Erdody as a count.

name: First Siege of Dubica (1685)
commanders: Croatian Ban Erdödy vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Croatian forces pushed the line of defense toward the Una River by capturing Dubica after setting the fort's interior ablaze, subsequently defeating arriving Ottoman reinforcements.

name: Capture of Krupa (1685)
commanders: Croatian Ban Erdödy vs. local Ottoman forces
