importance: The town and fortress of Krupa were captured following a successful skirmish against local Ottoman troops as part of the broader Pounje offensive.

name: First Siege of Kostajnica
commanders: Croatian Ban Erdödy vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Croatian forces under Ban Erdödy attempted to capture the fortress of Kostajnica as part of their Pounje campaign, but failed to breach the walls due to a lack of artillery.

name: Siege of Negroponte
commanders: Francesco Morosini and Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck vs. Ismail Pasha
importance: Following the successful Venetian conquest of most of the Peloponnese and the capture of Athens, Venice attempted to seize Negroponte (modern Chalkis), the principal Ottoman fortress in Central Greece. Although the Venetians invested the city with a large multinational force and fleet, they failed to fully blockade it, allowing Ismail Pasha to reinforce and supply the garrison by sea. A devastating plague ravaged the besieging army, killing around 4,000 soldiers—including the experienced commander Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck—and the withdrawal of Florentine, Maltese, and German contingents forced Doge Francesco Morosini to abandon the siege. The Ottoman victory preserved one of the empire's most important Aegean strongholds.
casualties: Venetian coalition: heavy losses, including about 4,000 dead from plague. Ottoman Empire: unknown.

name: Battle of Batočina
commanders: Louis William, Margrave of Baden-Baden, and Pavle Nestorović vs. Arap Recep Pasha
importance: Fought during the Habsburg advance into Serbia in the Great Turkish War, the battle saw the Serbian Militia under Pavle Nestorović serve as the vanguard of the Imperial army. The Habsburg-led force decisively defeated a much larger Ottoman army near Batočina, capturing its artillery, mortars, camp, and baggage train. The victory secured the route toward Niš and contributed to the rapid collapse of Ottoman defenses in central Serbia during the 1689 campaign.
casualties: Holy Roman Empire: about 400 killed or wounded. Ottoman Empire: about 3,000 killed; 108 guns, 3 mortars, and the entire camp and baggage captured.

name: Battle of Niš
commanders: Louis William, Margrave of Baden-Baden, Enea Silvio Piccolomini, and Pavle Nestorović vs. Ottoman field commanders
importance: One of the most significant Habsburg victories of the 1689 campaign, the battle resulted in the defeat of a much larger Ottoman army and the capture of Niš, opening the route into Macedonia. During the engagement, Pavle Nestorović led the Serbian Militia in a successful flanking maneuver around the Ottoman right wing after discovering Vinik Hill was undefended, contributing decisively to the Imperial victory. Following the battle, Louis William continued to capture Vidin while Enea Silvio Piccolomini advanced deep into Macedonia, marking the greatest extent of the Habsburg advance into the central Balkans during the Great Turkish War. The Ottomans, however, recaptured Niš in September 1690 after the Imperial withdrawal.
casualties: Holy Roman Empire: about 400 killed or wounded. Ottoman Empire: unknown.

name: Siege of Vidin
commanders: Louis William, Margrave of Baden-Baden vs. Ottoman garrison commander
importance: Following the decisive victory at Niš, Louis William advanced eastward to the important Danube fortress of Vidin. The Imperial army invested the city on 14 October 1689, and after a brief siege the Ottoman garrison capitulated on 19 October. The capture of Vidin secured a major Danubian stronghold, extended Habsburg control across much of Serbia and northwestern Bulgaria, and represented the furthest eastward advance of the Imperial army during the 1689 campaign before the Ottoman counteroffensive of 1690.

name: Capture and Burning of Skopje
commanders: Enea Silvio Piccolomini vs. Ottoman local garrison
importance: Following the Imperial victories at Niš and Vidin, General Enea Silvio Piccolomini advanced into Macedonia and occupied Skopje on 25 October 1689 with little resistance after the Ottoman garrison withdrew. Unable to hold the city against an imminent Ottoman counteroffensive and facing severe logistical difficulties, Piccolomini ordered Skopje to be burned. The fire raged for two days (26–27 October), devastating much of the city and destroying its commercial infrastructure. The destruction marked the end of Skopje's prominence as one of the Ottoman Balkans' leading trade centers, causing a dramatic population decline and long-term economic decline. Piccolomini himself died shortly afterward during the campaign.
casualties: Unknown; extensive destruction of the city by fire.

name: Capture of Kaçanik Pass
commanders: Enea Silvio Piccolomini vs. Ottoman forces
importance: During the Habsburg Balkan offensive of 1689 in the Great Turkish War, General Enea Silvio Piccolomini captured the strategically important Kaçanik Pass, a narrow mountain corridor connecting Kosovo with Macedonia. Control of the pass allowed the Imperial army to advance southward from Kosovo into the Skopje basin, bypassing major natural barriers and opening the route for the subsequent occupation of Skopje on 25 October 1689. The seizure of Kaçanik represented one of the furthest points of Habsburg penetration into the central Balkans during the war.

name: Battle of Štip
commanders: Johann Georg von Holstein vs. Ottoman commanders
importance: The Battle of Štip was one of the largest and most significant clashes of the Habsburg 1689 Macedonian campaign during the Great Turkish War. After the capture and burning of Skopje, Austrian forces under Johann Georg von Holstein, who had assumed command after the death of Enea Silvio Piccolomini, advanced against an Ottoman concentration at Štip. Launching a rapid attack from their camp near Kumanovo, the Imperial troops surprised and defeated the Ottoman army at dawn. The defeat forced the Ottomans to retreat from eastern Macedonia, while the Habsburg forces captured large quantities of supplies and temporarily extended their influence deep into Ottoman territory. The battle represented the peak of the Habsburg advance into Macedonia, although Štip was later recovered by the Ottomans in 1691.
casualties: Holy Roman Empire: unknown. Ottoman Empire: about 2,000 killed; additional reconnaissance force of 300 men destroyed during the Austrian withdrawal.

name: Battle of Mytilene
commanders: Daniele Dolfin vs. Ottoman and Barbary fleet commanders
importance: A major naval engagement of the Morean War within the wider Great Turkish War, the Battle of Mytilene was fought between the Venetian fleet under Daniele Dolfin and a combined Ottoman–North African Muslim fleet near the island of Lesbos. Despite being temporarily isolated and heavily outnumbered during the early stages of the battle, several Venetian ships including the Redentor, Sacra Lega, and San Domenico inflicted severe damage on the enemy flagship division before the Venetian fleet regrouped and forced the Muslim fleet to withdraw to Mytilene. The defeat exposed weaknesses in the Ottoman reliance on Barbary corsair support and encouraged Sultan Suleiman II to expand the Ottoman battle fleet and reduce dependence on North African auxiliary forces.
casualties: Venetian: heavy losses, including Admiral Giovanni Buggie killed and Daniele Dolfin wounded. Ottoman–Barbary fleet: heavier losses; several ships damaged, with up to two galleys possibly sunk.

name: Attack on Crete
commanders: Domenico Mocenigo vs. Ottoman defenders of Candia
importance: During the Great Turkish War, Venice attempted to reopen a major front in Crete, targeting Candia (modern Heraklion), the former Venetian stronghold captured by the Ottomans after the long Cretan War (1645–1669). A Venetian fleet of 34 galleons and 27 other vessels, supported by an expeditionary force and a local Greek uprising against Ottoman rule, besieged the city in 1692. However, the operation failed due to Venetian strategic hesitation, logistical problems, and defections among Christian forces. Domenico Mocenigo abandoned the siege, evacuated around 2,000 Cretan supporters, and returned to the Peloponnese. The failed expedition confirmed Ottoman control of Crete for the remainder of the war.

name: Naval Action in Andros
commanders: Bartolomeo Contarini vs. Ottoman commanders
importance: Part of the 1697 campaign where the Venetian fleet under Bartolomeo Contarini hunted down and engaged the Ottoman fleet in the Aegean Sea around Andros (notably resulting in the accidental explosion of the Venetian ship San Sebastiano).
casualties: Unknown specific casualties for this individual clash, alongside material loss of the San Sebastiano

name: Gerakaris's Raid on Western Central Greece
commanders: Limberakis Gerakaris vs. Venetian garrison and local forces
importance: Limberakis Gerakaris led a mixed force of 2,000 men to seize and torch Missolonghi, plunder Valtos and Xiromero, and attack Aitoliko and Vonitsa.

name: Defense of Salona (Amfissa)
commanders: Dimitrios Charopolitis and Elias Damianovich vs. Limberakis Gerakaris
importance: Local inhabitants under Dimitrios Charopolitis and Elias Damianovich successfully repulsed Limberakis Gerakaris in his attack on Salona.

name: Venetian Campaign and Raiding in Acarnania
commanders: Venetian forces and Greek irregulars vs. Ottoman forces
importance: Following the fall of Lefkada, Venetian forces and Greek irregulars crossed to the mainland, raiding the opposite shore and bringing most of Acarnania under Venetian control.

name: Capture of Preveza
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The capture of the Ottoman stronghold of Preveza in late September 1684 eliminated one of the final Ottoman bastions in the region and secured Venetian communications.

name: Capture of Vonitsa
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The fall of the fort of Vonitsa in late September 1684 removed the last Ottoman bastion in the operational theater, securing the Ionian Sea approaches.

name: Ottoman Campaign in Central Greece
commanders: Ottoman forces vs. Venetian garrison at Lepanto
result: Venetian defensive victory (partially offset by Ottoman re-establishment of hinterland control)
importance: Reinforced Ottoman forces swept through Central Greece and though repulsed in an attack on Lepanto, they re-established control over the hinterland east of it.

name: Gerakaris's Invasion of the Peloponnese
commanders: Limberakis Gerakaris vs. Venetian defenders
importance: Gerakaris spearheaded an Ottoman invasion, taking Corinth and unsuccessfully besieging Acrocorinth and Argos before Venetian reinforcements forced a withdrawal.

name: Sack of Arta
commanders: Limberakis Gerakaris vs. local inhabitants
importance: Following his defection to the Venetians, Gerakaris carried out a brutal and savage sack of Arta, which led directly to his arrest and imprisonment at Brescia by Venice.

name: Capture of Kanina
commanders: Venetian expeditionary forces vs. Ottoman garrison of Kanina
importance: During Venice's western Balkan offensive in the Great Turkish War, Venetian forces landed near Valona (Vlorë) to support the Greek uprising in Himara and attack Ottoman positions in Epirus. After the Ottoman field forces withdrew toward their fortified positions, the Venetians invested the inland fortress of Kanina, which dominated the approaches to Valona. The fortress surrendered on 17 September 1690, giving Venice control of a key strategic position overlooking the Bay of Valona and opening the way for the capture of Valona the following day.

name: Capture of Kostajnica (1687)
commanders: Croatian Ban Erdödy vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Following the earlier failed attempt due to lack of artillery, Ban Erdödy successfully captured the strategic fortress of Kostajnica in 1687, helping restore the defense line to the Una River.

name: Capture of Valona
commanders: Venetian naval and land forces vs. Ottoman garrison of Valona
importance: Following the surrender of Kanina, the Venetian expedition captured the Ottoman port city and fortress of Valona (modern Vlorë) on the Albanian coast. The Ottoman garrison evacuated the city rather than fight, allowing Venice to establish a temporary foothold along the coast of Epirus and Albania. The capture expanded Venetian influence into the surrounding regions of Himara, Souli, Argyrokastron, and toward Arta, but the gains proved temporary as Ottoman forces under Fazıl Mustafa Pasha launched a counteroffensive and recovered Valona in March 1691.
casualties: Unknown; Ottoman garrison evacuated the city.

name: Capture of Zrin (1687)
commanders: Croatian Ban Erdödy vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The ancestral fortress of the Zrinski family at Zrin was retaken by Croatian forces in 1687 as part of the successful offensive along the Una River.

name: Siege of Belgrade
commanders: Köprülü Fazıl Mustafa Pasha vs. Habsburg garrison of Belgrade
importance: The fifth siege of Belgrade during the Great Turkish War resulted in the Ottoman reconquest of the fortress only two years after its capture by the Habsburgs in 1688. Following the outbreak of the Nine Years' War in Western Europe, Emperor Leopold I was forced to divert much of his army away from the Balkans, allowing Grand Vizier Köprülü Fazıl Mustafa Pasha to launch a major counteroffensive. After recovering Niš, the Ottoman army reached Belgrade in October 1690 and quickly besieged the city. The siege ended after an Ottoman shell struck the main Austrian powder magazine, causing a devastating explosion that forced the defenders to surrender. Belgrade remained under Ottoman control until its capture by Austria in 1717.

name: Second Battle of Niš
commanders: Ottoman forces under Köprülü Fazıl Mustafa Pasha vs. Habsburg forces
importance: The Second Battle of Niš was part of the Ottoman counteroffensive during the Great Turkish War that reversed many of the Habsburg gains of 1689. After the death of Enea Silvio Piccolomini and the collapse of the Imperial position in Macedonia, the Ottoman army advanced northward to recover Serbian territories. Niš, which had been captured by Louis William, Margrave of Baden-Baden, in September 1689, was retaken by the Ottomans in 1690. The victory reopened the route toward Belgrade and enabled the Ottoman army to continue its successful campaign that culminated in the recapture of the capital fortress in October 1690.

name: Siege of Vlorë
commanders: Koca Halil Pasha, Küçük Cafer Pasha, and Süleyman Pasha vs. Giralomo Cornaro, Giovanni Matteo, and Charles Sparre
importance: The Siege of Vlorë was part of the Ottoman counteroffensive during the Great Turkish War to recover territories lost to Venice in western Albania. After Venetian forces captured Vlorë and nearby Kaninë in September 1690 following the weakening of the Ottoman garrison, the Ottoman government organized a major expedition under Koca Halil Pasha to retake the strategically important port. A force of around 6,000 Ottoman troops, including Janissaries and regional contingents, surrounded the Venetian-held fortress in February 1691. A Venetian relief attempt launched from the sea on 4 March was defeated, and after suffering heavy losses the defenders evacuated the fortress on 6 March. The victory restored Ottoman control over one of the most important ports on the Albanian coast and reversed Venetian gains in Epirus and southern Albania.
casualties: Ottoman Empire: light losses. Venice: about 4,000 casualties; Venetian commanders Giralomo Cornaro, Giovanni Matteo, and Charles Sparre were killed.

name: Battle of Slankamen
commanders: Ludwig Wilhelm of Baden (Türkenlouis), supported by Jovan Monasterlija and Serbian Militia vs. Mustafa Köprülü Pasha and Emeric Thököly
importance: The Battle of Slankamen was one of the most decisive Habsburg victories of the Great Turkish War and effectively ended the Ottoman resurgence on the Hungarian front. After the Ottoman reconquest of Belgrade in 1690 and the temporary recovery of momentum under Grand Vizier Köprülü Fazıl Mustafa Pasha, the Ottoman army advanced into Syrmia to challenge Imperial control. Ludwig Wilhelm of Baden assembled a force of around 33,000 troops, including a large Serbian militia contingent under Jovan Monasterlija, and forced the Ottomans into a major battle near the Danube–Tisza region. Despite initial Ottoman advantages, including the destruction of Imperial supply wagons, the Habsburg army counterattacked and routed the Ottoman forces. The death of Grand Vizier Köprülü Fazıl Mustafa Pasha during the battle caused the Ottoman army to collapse. The victory secured Habsburg control of Hungary, Croatia, and Transylvania and paved the way toward the eventual Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699.
casualties: Holy Roman Empire: heavy losses, estimated several thousand killed and wounded. Ottoman Empire: catastrophic losses, with thousands killed; artillery, treasury, and baggage captured.

name: Siege of Belgrade
commanders: Duke of Croy vs. Ca’fer Pasha, with Ottoman relief forces under Bozoklu Mustafa Pasha
importance: The Siege of Belgrade in 1693 was an unsuccessful Habsburg attempt to recapture the fortress during the Great Turkish War. After the Ottomans had regained Belgrade in 1690 and strengthened its defenses, the Habsburg commander Duke of Croy launched a campaign against the strategically vital city in an effort to divert the Ottoman grand vizier's army away from Transylvania. The Imperial army of around 28,000 troops crossed the Sava and established siege positions, but delays in receiving artillery and naval support prevented an effective assault. Ottoman defenders under Ca’fer Pasha successfully resisted, while the approaching relief army under Bozoklu Mustafa Pasha forced the Habsburgs into a desperate night assault on 17 September. The attack failed with heavy losses, and the Imperial army withdrew toward Petrovaradin. The failed siege confirmed Ottoman control of Belgrade, which remained in Ottoman hands until the Habsburg conquest of 1717.
casualties: Holy Roman Empire: heavy losses during the failed assault and retreat; exact numbers unknown. Ottoman Empire: unknown.

name: Capture of Novi (1687)
commanders: Croatian Ban Erdödy vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Novigrad na Uni (Novi) was captured alongside Kostajnica and Zrin in 1687, successfully pushing the Habsburg-Croatian border back to the Una River as planned.

name: Battle of Gorjani
commanders: Habsburg Monarchy (Johann Katzianer) vs. Ottoman Empire (Governor of Belgrade forces)
importance: A decisive defeat for the Habsburgs that saw the annihilation of their 24,000-man army, halting imperial offensive ambitions in the region following the broken Treaty of Konstantiniyye.

name: Siege of Buda
commanders: Suleiman the Magnificent vs. Ferdinand I
importance: Suleiman successfully captured Buda after intensive artillery bombardment, restoring and installing John Zápolya as an Ottoman vassal king over Hungary before marching on Vienna.

name: Battle of Srebrenica (1411)
commanders: Kingdom of Bosnia (Tvrtko II, Hrvoje Vukčić) vs. Hungary (Sigismund of Luxembourg, Stefan Lazarević)
importance: Sigismund of Luxembourg seized the city, granting it to Serbian Despot Stefan Lazarević, establishing long-term Hungarian influence over the silver mines.

name: Battle of Srebrenica (1444)
commanders: Kingdom of Bosnia (Stjepan Tomaš) vs. Ottoman Empire / Serbian Despotate
importance: King Stjepan Tomaš successfully reconquered the city, ending a long period of Hungarian-Despotate administration.

name: Battle of Srebrenica (1445)
commanders: Kingdom of Bosnia (Ivaniš Pavlović) vs. Serbian Despotate (Đurađ Branković)
importance: The Bosnian forces pushed back the Despotate of Serbia to maintain control over the Podrinje mining region.

name: Battle of Srebrenica (1449)
commanders: Kingdom of Bosnia (Stjepan Tomaš) vs. Serbian Despotate
importance: A final re-conquest by Stjepan Tomaš against the Despotate, cementing control shortly before the intensifying Ottoman offensive in the region.

name: Battle of Bileća
commanders: Kingdom of Bosnia (Vlatko Vuković) vs. Ottoman Empire (Lala Shahin Pasha)
importance: A significant early defensive success for the Bosnian Kingdom, halting an Ottoman plundering raid into the Hum region.

name: Siege of Ključ
commanders: Ottoman Empire (Mahmud Pasha Angelović) vs. Kingdom of Bosnia (Stephen Tomašević)
importance: Led to the capture and execution of the last Bosnian King, Stephen Tomašević, and the rapid collapse of Bosnian resistance across 70+ towns.
casualties: Heavy (Bosnian forces fled or were captured)

name: Battle of Una
commanders: Kingdom of Croatia (Matthias Geréb, Vuk Grgurević) vs. Ottoman Sanjak of Bosnia
importance: One of the first major Croatian victories against the Ottoman Empire; it successfully checked Ottoman incursions and led to a 7-year truce.

name: Battle of Vrpile
commanders: Kingdom of Croatia (Ladislav of Egervár, Bernardin Frankopan) vs. Ottoman raiding force
importance: A successful ambush of an Ottoman raiding party returning from Carniola; it demonstrated effective frontier defense tactics.

name: Battle of Novigrad
commanders: Kingdom of Croatia (Petar Berislavić) vs. Ottoman Bosnia Eyalet forces
importance: A heavy defeat for the Croatian forces led by Ban Petar Berislavić, illustrating the increasing military pressure on the Adriatic coastal defenses.

name: Battle of Hrastovica
commanders: Kingdom of Croatia (Local castellan) vs. Ottoman Empire (Malkoč-beg)
importance: A tactical defensive success for the newly formed Hrastovica captaincy, demonstrating the effectiveness of localized garrison fortifications in halting Ottoman incursions into the Banija region.

name: Relief of Jajce
commanders: Kingdom of Croatia (Petar Berislavić) vs. Ottoman Empire (Gazi Husrev-beg)
importance: Although the attempt to capture nearby Ottoman forts failed, the relief expedition successfully reprovisioned the Jajce garrison, extending the lifespan of this critical Christian defensive salient by several years.

name: Siege of Knin
commanders: Ottoman Empire (Ghazi Husrev-beg) vs. Kingdom of Croatia (Mihajlo Vojković)
importance: The loss of Knin, the royal capital of the Kingdom of Croatia, was a devastating blow that forced the redistribution of Ottoman forces and established a permanent Ottoman administrative seat in the region.

name: Battle of Belaj
commanders: Habsburg/Croatian forces (Ivan Karlović, Bernardin Ričan) vs. Ottoman Empire (Gazi Husrev-beg)
importance: A significant defensive success that routed an Ottoman raiding force returning from Carniola, though marred by the friendly-fire incident that nearly killed the Croatian Ban.

name: Battle of Stephaniana
commanders: Serbian Empire (Preljub) vs. Emirate of Aydin (Umur Beg)
importance: The first major military engagement between Serbian and Turkish forces, though it did not stop Dušan's expansion into Macedonia.

name: Siege of Mirandola
commanders: Piero Strozzi vs. Papal-Imperial commanders
importance: The defenders successfully resisted the Papal-Imperial siege, preserving Parma's French-backed position.

name: Treaty of Chambord
commanders: Henry II of France; Maurice of Saxony and German Protestant princes
importance: France allied with the German Protestant princes against Charles V, paving the way for French expansion into Lorraine.

name: Truce ending the War of Parma
commanders: Charles V; Henry II; Ottavio Farnese
importance: Ended active fighting in the War of Parma while leaving broader Franco-Habsburg tensions unresolved.

name: Second Schmalkaldic War (Princes' Revolt)
commanders: Maurice of Saxony, Henry II of France vs. Charles V
importance: Forced Charles V to accept the Peace of Passau while France secured Metz, Toul, and Verdun.

name: Siege of Metz
commanders: Francis, Duke of Guise vs. Charles V
importance: France successfully defended Metz, frustrating Charles V's attempt to recover the Three Bishoprics.
casualties: Heavy Imperial losses from combat and disease.

name: Siege of Thérouanne
commanders: Emmanuel Philibert, Imperial commanders vs. French garrison
importance: Thérouanne was captured and deliberately destroyed on Charles V's orders.

name: Battle of Demotika
commanders: Serbian/Bulgarian forces (Gradislav Borilović) vs. Ottoman Beylik (Süleyman Pasha)
importance: A landmark engagement marking the first major victory of Ottoman troops on European soil, leading to the occupation of Gallipoli.

name: Battle of Sırpsındığı
commanders: Serbian/Bulgarian/Wallachian forces (Mrnjavčević brothers) vs. Ottoman Empire (Hacı İlbey)
importance: The 'Rout of the Serbs'; a major Ottoman success that solidified their presence near Adrianople (Edirne).

name: Battle of Samokov
commanders: Serbian/Bulgarian forces (Uglješa Mrnjavčević, Ivan Shishman) vs. Ottoman Empire (Lala Shahin Pasha)
importance: The swift Ottoman victory left the Serbian and Bulgarian forces disorganized and fleeing, opening the path for further Ottoman penetration.

name: Battle of Hațeg
commanders: Kingdom of Hungary (Miklós Csáki) vs. Ottoman Empire
importance: Marked the beginning of the War of the South Danube (1420–1432), where Ottoman forces devastated the Transylvanian frontier.

name: Battle of Szőlős
commanders: Jovan Nenad vs. Péter Perényi
importance: A significant engagement where the forces of the 'Black Man' Jovan Nenad defeated the Hungarian nobility, establishing a short-lived autonomous Serbian entity.

name: Battle of Sződfalva
commanders: Jovan Nenad vs. Péter Perényi and Imre Czibak
importance: The decisive defeat of Jovan Nenad's army, leading to the collapse of his autonomous principality and his death.

name: Battle of Tarcal
commanders: John Zápolya vs. Archduke Ferdinand of Austria
importance: Ferdinand's success at Tarcal solidified Habsburg claims to the Hungarian throne and forced Zápolya into a defensive posture.

name: Battle of Szina
commanders: John Zápolya vs. Bálint Török and Johann Katzianer
importance: A major blow to John Zápolya, pushing him to seek Ottoman military assistance against Ferdinand.

name: Battle of Feldioara
commanders: Petru Rareș (Moldavia) vs. Bálint Török and István Majláth
importance: Demonstrated the reach of Moldavian influence under Petru Rareș, who briefly exerted control over Transylvanian regions after the defeat of Habsburg forces.

name: Second Battle of Kosovo
commanders: Murad II; Janos Hunyadi
importance: Confirmed Ottoman dominance in the Balkans.

name: Fall of Constantinople
commanders: Mehmed II; Constantine XI
importance: Ended the Byzantine Empire and created the Ottoman imperial capital.

name: First Siege of Novo Brdo
commanders: Mehmed II's forces; Serbian defenders
importance: Captured one of the Balkans' richest mining centers.

name: Siege of Belgrade
commanders: Mehmed II; Janos Hunyadi
importance: Delayed Ottoman advance into Hungary for decades.

name: Capture of Athens
commanders: Mehmed II; Duchy of Athens
importance: Brought Athens into the Ottoman sphere.

name: Capture of Smederevo
commanders: Mehmed II; Serbian defenders
importance: Ended the Serbian Despotate as an independent state.

name: Conquest of the Morea
commanders: Mehmed II; Palaiologos despots
importance: Ended Byzantine successor rule in the Peloponnese.

name: Conquest of Trebizond
commanders: Mehmed II; David Komnenos
importance: Outside the Europe-only frame but included as the final Byzantine successor conquest.

name: Wallachian campaign
commanders: Mehmed II; Vlad III
importance: Reasserted Ottoman pressure over Wallachia after Vlad's raids.

name: Conquest of Bosnia
commanders: Mehmed II; Stephen Tomasevic
importance: Created the foundation for Ottoman Bosnia.

name: First Siege of Kruje
commanders: Mehmed II; Skanderbeg and Albanian defenders
importance: Major failed Ottoman attempt to break Albanian resistance.

name: Second Siege of Kruje
commanders: Mehmed II; Albanian defenders
importance: Albanian resistance continued despite heavy pressure.

name: Capture of Caffa
commanders: Gedik Ahmed Pasha; Genoese defenders
importance: Brought the Genoese Black Sea colonies under Ottoman control.

name: Third Siege of Kruje
commanders: Ottoman forces; Venetian-Albanian defenders
importance: Broke the most famous Albanian fortress resistance after Skanderbeg's death.

name: Siege of Shkoder begins
commanders: Mehmed II's forces; Venetian defenders
importance: Opened the final phase of Ottoman conquest in northern Albania.

name: Capture of Shkoder
commanders: Ottoman forces; Venetian defenders
importance: Confirmed Ottoman control after Venice ceded the fortress.

name: Siege of Otranto
commanders: Gedik Ahmed Pasha; Neapolitan defenders
importance: Demonstrated Ottoman ability to project power into Italy.

name: Capture of Kilia
commanders: Bayezid II; Moldavian defenders
importance: Cut Moldavia away from a key Danube-Black Sea outlet.

name: Capture of Akkerman
commanders: Bayezid II; Moldavian defenders
importance: Completed Ottoman seizure of Moldavia's Black Sea access.

name: Battle of Zonchio
commanders: Kemal Reis; Venetian fleet
importance: One of the first major naval battles using shipboard artillery decisively.

name: Battle of Karpathos
commanders: Kemal Reis vs. Nicolas Centurione
importance: Kemal Reis defeated the Knights Hospitaller fleet between Karpathos and Crete, capturing five ships and the enemy commander
casualties: 1 Hospitaller ship sunk, 5 captured; light Ottoman losses

name: Battle of Adana (1486)
commanders: Hersekzade Ahmed Pasha vs. Mamluk Sultanate
importance: Combined Ottoman-Janissary forces were defeated before Adana, forcing Karagöz Mehmed to flee and Hersekzade Ahmed into captivity, restoring Cilicia to Mamluk control
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses and capture of Hersekzade Ahmed Pasha

name: Battle of Ağaçarıyı
commanders: Hadim Ali Pasha vs. Mamluk Sultanate
importance: Major open-field clash near Adana where the Ottoman right flank collapsed and Karaman soldiers fled, forcing a full Ottoman retreat
casualties: Heavy Ottoman casualties; field conceded to Mamluks

name: Siege of Adana (1488–1489)
commanders: Hadim Ali Pasha vs. Mamluk Sultanate
importance: Mamluks successfully besieged and captured Adana following the Ottoman defeat at Ağaçarıyı, cementing Mamluk control over Cilicia

name: Mamluk Offensive against Kayseri
commanders: Mamluk Sultanate vs. Hersekzade Ahmed Pasha
importance: Mamluks advanced into Karaman and laid siege to Kayseri before retreating upon the approach of Hersekzade Ahmed Pasha's relief army, leading to the 1491 peace treaty

name: Defeat in Bukovina
commanders: John I Albert vs. Moldavian and Ottoman forces
importance: Subsequent rout of retreating Polish forces in Bukovina shortly after the Cosmin Forest disaster, resulting in thousands more killed

name: Battle of Modon
commanders: Kemal Reis vs. Venetian Fleet
importance: Ottoman fleet defeated Venice again, allowing Kemal Reis to bombard and capture the vital fortress town of Modon
casualties: Heavy Venetian losses; fall of Modon and Coron ('two eyes of the Republic')

name: Siege and Capture of Cephalonia
commanders: Gonzalo de Córdoba vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: A joint Spanish-Venetian force captured Cephalonia, temporarily halting the Ottoman offensive on Venetian eastern territories

name: Capture of Durazzo
commanders: Feriz Beg vs. Republic of Venice
importance: Feriz Beg captured the strategic stronghold of Durazzo in Venetian Albania

name: Capture of Coron
commanders: Ottoman forces; Venetian defenders
importance: Consolidated Ottoman gains in the southwestern Peloponnese.

name: Siege of Belgrade
commanders: Suleiman I; Hungarian defenders
importance: Opened the Danube road into Hungary.

name: Siege of Rhodes
commanders: Suleiman I; Philippe Villiers de L'Isle-Adam
importance: Ended Hospitaller rule on Rhodes.

name: Battle of Mohacs
commanders: Suleiman I; Louis II
importance: Collapsed the medieval Kingdom of Hungary.
casualties: King Louis II killed; heavy Hungarian losses.

name: First Siege of Vienna
commanders: Suleiman I; Wilhelm von Roggendorf
importance: Checked Ottoman advance into Austria.
casualties: Attrition from weather and siege fighting.

name: Siege of Güns (Kőszeg)
commanders: Suleiman I; Nikola Jurisic
importance: Delayed Suleiman's march and protected Vienna.
casualties: Heavy siege losses not securely recorded.

name: Capture of Klis
commanders: Ottoman Bosnian forces; Croatian defenders
importance: Strengthened the Ottoman-Venetian-Habsburg frontier in Dalmatia.

name: Capture of Buda (1541)
commanders: Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent vs. Wilhelm von Roggendorf
result: Decisive Ottoman victory / Annexation of Buda
importance: The crushing defeat of the Habsburg relief and withdrawal forces outside Buda by Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, which effectively ended the 1541 siege and led to the bloodless Ottoman occupation and annexation of Buda via strategic ruse.
casualties: Thousands of imperial troops killed or drowned in the Danube; commander Wilhelm von Roggendorf mortally wounded.

name: Siege of Buda (1541)
commanders: Wilhelm von Roggendorf vs. Ottoman Garrison and Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent
result: Ottoman defensive victory / Failure of Habsburg siege
importance: A major Habsburg attempt by Archduke Ferdinand I to capture Buda following the death of John Zápolya. The poorly managed siege was broken by Sultan Suleiman's relief army, paving the way for the subsequent Ottoman annexation of the city.
casualties: Heavy imperial losses during failed assaults and subsequent routing by Ottoman relief forces

name: Capture of Buda (1527)
commanders: Ferdinand I vs. John Zápolya's forces
importance: Ferdinand I captured Buda during the Hungarian Civil War (1527–1528) to enforce his claim to the Hungarian throne after Ottoman withdrawal.

name: Fall of Dvore
commanders: Stojan Janković and Ilija Smiljanić vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The fall of the Ottoman outpost of Dvore near Split marked the beginning of anti-Ottoman operations and countryside raids in Dalmatia during the early stages of the Great Turkish War.

name: Siege of Knin
commanders: Girolamo Cornaro and Zaviša Janković vs. Mehmed-pasha
importance: Following intensive Venetian artillery bombardment, the Ottoman garrison under Mehmed-pasha surrendered Knin, leading to Venetian control and the deportation of prominent Ottoman captives.

name: Battle of Sinj (1686)
commanders: Girolamo Cornaro vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Venetian forces under General Girolamo Cornaro successfully captured the strategic fortress of Sinj from the Ottomans in September 1686 during the course of the Great Turkish War.

name: First Siege of Sinj
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The Republic of Venice besieged the town and fortress of Sinj as part of the Morean War, but the attempt was unsuccessful.

name: Second Siege of Sinj
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Venetian forces launched a second siege against Sinj following their earlier attempt, but were once again repulsed without success.

name: Rebellion of Poljica
commanders: Local militia of the Republic of Poljica vs. Ottoman forces
result: Poljica rebellion and alignment with Venice
importance: During the second Venetian siege of Sinj, the local militia of the Republic of Poljica openly rebelled against their nominal Ottoman suzerainty (held since 1513) to aid the Venetian armies.

name: Ottoman Attack on Zadvarje
commanders: Ottoman forces vs. Local defenders / Poljica militia
importance: The Ottomans launched an retaliatory attack against Zadvarje following the rebellion of Poljica, but were pushed back with major casualties.

name: Ottoman Attack on Dolac
commanders: Ottoman forces vs. Local defenders
importance: As part of retaliatory operations against Poljica, Ottoman forces attacked Dolac but were successfully repulsed with significant casualties.

name: Ottoman Attack on Srijane
commanders: Ottoman forces vs. Local defenders
importance: The Ottomans carried out a retaliatory assault on Srijane, which was beaten back by local defenders suffering major losses.

name: Capture of Győr (1527)
commanders: Ferdinand I vs. John Zápolya's forces
importance: Ferdinand I seized Győr during his western Hungarian campaign against John Zápolya.

name: Capture of Komárom (1527)
commanders: Ferdinand I vs. John Zápolya's forces
importance: Komárom fell to Ferdinand I's forces as they pushed back the Ottoman vassal John Zápolya across royal Hungary.

name: Capture of Esztergom (1527–1528)
commanders: Ferdinand I vs. John Zápolya's forces
importance: The strategic fortress of Esztergom was captured by Ferdinand I's army during the 1527–1528 civil war campaign.

name: Capture of Székesfehérvár (1527–1528)
commanders: Ferdinand I vs. John Zápolya's forces
importance: The traditional coronation city of Székesfehérvár fell to Ferdinand I as he consolidated control over central Hungary.

name: Capture of Esztergom
commanders: Suleiman I; Habsburg defenders
importance: Secured a major Danube fortress north of Buda.

name: Capture of Szekesfehervar
commanders: Suleiman I; Habsburg defenders
importance: Captured the traditional coronation city of the Hungarian kings.

name: Capture of Visegrad
commanders: Ottoman Danube forces; Habsburg defenders
importance: Strengthened Ottoman control along the Danube bend.

name: Campaign in Transylvania
commanders: Ottoman commanders and Transylvanian factions; Habsburg forces
importance: Reinforced Transylvania's role as a contested vassal-buffer state.

name: Battle of Brest
commanders: Ivan Drašković vs. Achmed Hafis Pasha
importance: A key defensive victory that successfully halted the advance of the Ottoman force led by the Beylerbey of Vidin into Croatian territory.

name: Battle of Brest
commanders: Hasan Pasha Predojević vs. Tamás Erdődy & Kristofor Peuchel
importance: Fought near Brest in the Kingdom of Croatia during the Ottoman-Habsburg wars; Ottoman forces under Bosnian beglerbeg Hasan Pasha Predojević crushed combined Croatian and Styrian forces led by Ban Tamás Erdődy, leading to the capture of Brest and setting the stage for the subsequent siege of Sisak
casualties: 800+ allied casualties; heavy defeat and rout of Croatian and Styrian forces

name: First Siege of Bihać
commanders: Ferhad Pasha Sokolović vs. Franz Horner
importance: The Bihać garrison utilized heavy artillery to inflict severe casualties on Ottoman attackers, forcing Ferhad Pasha to quickly lift the siege.

name: Battle of Ivanić
commanders: Habsburg-Croatian forces vs. Ali-beg (Sanjakbey of Pakrac)
importance: Fought in Slavonia after local Sanjakbeys shifted northern attacks; resulted in the death of Ottoman commander Ali-beg.

name: Siege of Sisak (1591)
commanders: Telli Hasan Pasha vs. Thomas Erdődy
importance: Hasan Pasha launched an offensive to capture the strategic city defending Zagreb, but was forced to retreat, triggering an escalation of hostilities.

name: Siege of Temesvar
commanders: Kara Ahmed Pasha; Istvan Losonczy
importance: Created Temesvar Eyalet.

name: Siege of Eger
commanders: Kara Ahmed Pasha; Istvan Dobo
importance: Famous Habsburg-Hungarian defensive success in northern Hungary.

name: Great Siege of Malta
commanders: Serdar Lala Mustafa Pasha (Ottoman, ~25,000 men) vs. Knights Hospitaller & Don Garcia's Spanish relief force
importance: Saved Malta and the Knights Hospitaller, a key Spanish ally protecting southern Italy; Spanish relief force of 8,000 forced Ottoman evacuation
casualties: Heavy losses on Ottoman side (not quantified in source)

name: Battle of Călugăreni
commanders: Michael the Brave vs. Sinan Pasha
result: Tactical Wallachian victory, strategic Ottoman advance
importance: A major defensive stand by Wallachian forces against the Ottoman campaign aimed at occupying Bucharest and Târgoviște.

name: Battle of Leobersdorf
commanders: Sebastian Schertlin von Burtenbach, Johann Katzianer vs. Kazim Bey
importance: Habsburg forces trapped and destroyed Kazim Bey's Ottoman light cavalry raiding party after they were forced into a narrow valley, securing the southern approach to Vienna.

name: Siege of Drégelypalánk
commanders: György Szondi vs. Ottoman Empire
importance: A legendary symbol of heroism; Szondi and his small garrison fought to the death against overwhelming odds.

name: Siege of Szolnok
commanders: Ottoman Empire (Pasha Ahmed Ali) vs. Lőrinc Nyáry
importance: The rapid collapse of the fortress due to mercenary desertion caused widespread panic in the region, directly impacting the morale of the defenders at the upcoming Siege of Eger.

name: Siege of Eger
commanders: Ottoman Empire (Mehmed III) vs. Habsburg garrison
importance: The fall of Eger provided the Ottomans with a critical strategic stronghold in Upper Hungary, following the surrender of the demoralized garrison.

name: Battle of Palást
commanders: Erasmus von Teufel vs. Arslan Bey
importance: The Ottoman victory, catalyzed by a gunpowder explosion in the Habsburg camp, shattered Christian resistance in the region and forced the abandonment of Central Slovakia.

name: Capture of Nógrád
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Habsburg garrison
importance: Consolidated Ottoman control over the northern territories of the Eyalet of Buda.

name: Battle of Khotyn
commanders: Jan Karol Chodkiewicz vs. Sultan Osman II
importance: The combined Polish-Lithuanian and Cossack army successfully halted the Ottoman advance near the Dniester River.

name: Battle of Martynów
commanders: Stanisław Koniecpolski vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: Renowned for tactical innovation, effectively neutralizing a massive Tatar mobile force.

name: Battle of Krbava Field
commanders: Ottoman Empire (Bayezid II) vs. Kingdom of Croatia
importance: A catastrophic defeat for the Croatian nobility that accelerated the collapse of central military resistance against Ottoman expansion.

name: Siege of Buda (1530)
commanders: Habsburg (Ferdinand I) vs. John Zápolya
importance: Unsuccessful Habsburg attempt to reclaim Buda, highlighting the deep division of the Hungarian throne.

name: Siege of Buda (1602)
commanders: Hermann Christoph von Russwurm vs. Grand Vizier Yemişçi Hasan Pasha and Ottoman Garrison
result: Ottoman defensive victory / Habsburg capture of Pest only
importance: The second major Habsburg attempt to capture Buda during the Long Turkish War. While Habsburg forces under Russwurm successfully seized Pest across the Danube, the main siege of Buda failed due to fierce Ottoman defense, sorties, relief forces led by Grand Vizier Hasan Pasha, early winter weather, and supply shortages.
casualties: Heavy losses among the besiegers due to disease, cold, failed assaults, and Ottoman sorties; significant defender casualties

name: Siege of Novi Zrin
commanders: Ottoman (Köprülü Fazıl Ahmed Pasha) vs. Croatian forces (Nikola Zrinski)
importance: The destruction of the border fortress of Novi Zrin removed a key defensive bastion for northern Croatia.

name: Siege of Castelnuovo
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: A month-long siege of Castelnuovo (Herceg Novi) led by Venetian forces that successfully ended in a Venetian victory, concluding at the end of September 1687.

name: Capture of Vrgorac
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Venice successfully captured Vrgorac, which opened up strategic military routes towards Imotski and Mostar.

name: Battle of Nagyszőllős
commanders: George II Rákóczi vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: A decisive defeat for Rákóczi's forces that ended his ambitions for the Polish throne and severely weakened Transylvanian influence.
casualties: High; Rákóczi's army was largely destroyed or captured.

name: Venetian Capture of Čitluk
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Venetian forces successfully captured Čitluk north of the Republic of Ragusa during the 1694 campaign.

name: Venetian Capture of Gabela
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Venetian forces successfully captured the strategic stronghold of Gabela north of the Republic of Ragusa in 1694.

name: Venetian Capture of Zažablje
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Venetian forces captured the Zažablje region north of the Republic of Ragusa during their 1694 offensive.

name: Venetian Capture of Trebinje
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Venetian forces captured Trebinje north of the Republic of Ragusa as part of their territorial expansion in 1694.

name: Venetian Capture of Popovo
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
result: Venetian victory (later relinquished in peace treaty)
importance: Venetian forces captured the Popovo region north of Ragusa in 1694, though the area was later relinquished in the final peace treaty to preserve pre-existing demarcation.

name: Venetian Capture of Klobuk
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Venetian forces captured Klobuk north of the Republic of Ragusa during the 1694 campaigns.

name: Venetian Capture of Metković
commanders: Venetian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Venetian forces successfully captured Metković north of the Republic of Ragusa in 1694.

name: Studenica Campaign / Skirmish
commanders: Habsburg / Serbian Militia forces vs. Ottoman Empire
result: Habsburg-allied operations during the Balkan campaign
importance: Operations surrounding the Studenica area during the deep incursions of the Great Turkish War into the central Balkans following the advance toward Niš and Kosovo.

name: Siege of Szigetvar
commanders: Suleiman I; Nikola Subic Zrinski
importance: Suleiman died during the campaign.

name: Peace of Adrianople
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Habsburg Monarchy
importance: Confirmed the central Hungarian settlement after Suleiman's wars.

name: Invasion of Cyprus
commanders: Lala Mustafa Pasha; Venetian Cyprus
importance: Opened the Ottoman-Venetian war over Cyprus.
casualties: Heavy siege casualties during the campaign.

name: Capture of Famagusta
commanders: Lala Mustafa Pasha; Marcantonio Bragadin
importance: Completed Ottoman conquest of Cyprus.

name: Battle of Lepanto
commanders: Muezzinzade Ali Pasha; Don John of Austria
importance: Major Holy League victory over the Ottoman fleet.

name: Battle of Molodi
commanders: Devlet I Giray and Ottoman-supported Crimean forces; Mikhail Vorotynsky and Dmitry Khvorostinin
importance: Checked Crimean-Ottoman pressure on Muscovy after the 1571 burning of Moscow; included as a northern frontier reference outside the core Ottoman Europe frame.
casualties: Heavy Crimean-Tatar losses reported; exact totals vary by source.

name: Battle of Sisak
commanders: Hasan Pasha Predojevic; Habsburg-Croatian forces
importance: Sparked the Long Turkish War.
casualties: Ottoman commander killed; heavy Ottoman losses.

name: Siege of Shkodra
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Venice and League of Lezhë
importance: A landmark siege of the Rozafa Castle that effectively ended Venetian influence in Albania and secured Ottoman dominance in the region.

name: Siege of Kraków (1657)
commanders: Jerzy Lubomirski & Melchior von Hatzfeldt vs. Paul Wirtz & János Bethlen
importance: Combined Polish and Holy Roman Empire forces besieged and successfully recaptured Kraków after a two-year Swedish-Transylvanian occupation
casualties: Garrison capitulation following the destruction of Rákóczi's army at Czarny Ostrow

name: Conquest of Chios
commanders: Piyale Pasha vs. Genoese rulers of Chios
importance: Removed a Genoese (Spanish-allied) possession in the Aegean

name: Strike on the Pula Coast (1566)
commanders: Ottoman fleet vs. Kingdom of Naples
importance: Continued pressure on Spanish-allied Italian coasts following the Chios conquest

name: Kılıç Ali Pasha's Attempted Fleet to Almería
commanders: Kılıç Ali Pasha
importance: Attempted to bring soldiers, provisions and weapons to aid the Morisco rebels of Granada

name: Ottoman Aid Landed near Almería
commanders: Kılıç Ali Pasha
importance: Managed to deliver 400-500 soldiers and provisions/weapons to the Morisco rebels

name: Battle of Mezokeresztes
commanders: Mehmed III; Habsburg-Transylvanian army
importance: Followed the fall of Eger and helped shape Egri Eyalet.

name: Uprising in Banat
commanders: Bishop Teodor of Vršac & Sava Temišvarac vs. Ottoman Empire forces
importance: A rebellion by local Serbs numbering around 5,000 during the initial stage of the Long Turkish War in the Eyalet of Temeşvar; rebels successfully captured several towns before being crushed by the Ottoman army, leading to severe reprisals including the burning of Saint Sava's relics

name: Kuruc Uprising (Thököly's Uprising)
commanders: Imre Thököly vs. Imperial Forces (Habsburg Monarchy)
result: Initial rebel success / Ultimate collapse of Upper Hungary
importance: A major anti-Habsburg uprising led by Imre Thököly that swept across Royal Hungary, culminating in the establishment of the Ottoman-vassal Principality of Upper Hungary before collapsing following disastrous military defeats and Ottoman arrests in 1685.
casualties: Widespread regional devastation, heavy military losses on both sides, and subsequent imprisonment or submission of rebel forces

name: Capture of Szendrő Fortress
commanders: Imre Thököly vs. Imperial Garrison
importance: Imre Thököly captured the strategic border fortress of Szendrő during the early insurgent invasion of Royal Hungary.

name: Capture of Murány Castle
commanders: Imre Thököly vs. Imperial Garrison
importance: Thököly successfully captured the heavily fortified Murány Castle, securing a vital stronghold in northern Royal Hungary.

name: Battle of Barsszentkereszt
commanders: Imre Thököly vs. Imperial Relieving Army
importance: Thököly's rebel and Slovak peasant forces were defeated by imperial troops at Barsszentkereszt (Žiar nad Hronom), forcing them to temporarily abandon the occupied mining towns along the Hron river.

name: Siege of Nagykanizsa (1601)
commanders: Tiryaki Hasan Pasha; Ferdinand's forces
importance: Secured Kanije Eyalet against Habsburg counterattack.

name: Siege of Nagykanizsa (1600)
commanders: Damat İbrahim Pasha and Tiryaki Hasan Pasha vs. Georg Paradeiser
importance: A critical 1600 campaign during the Long Turkish War where the Ottoman army under Damat İbrahim Pasha and Tiryaki Hasan Pasha captured the strategic fortress of Nagykanizsa (Kanije) after a gunpowder explosion destroyed a major tower and a relieving Christian force was repulsed, establishing Kanizsa as a new Ottoman province.
casualties: 170 defenders killed in the gunpowder explosion; Habsburg garrison evacuated freely but faced severe political backlash upon returning to Austria

name: Siege of Székesfehérvár (1605)
commanders: Stephen Bocskai vs. Imperial Garrison
result: Anti-Habsburg Hungarian victory / Alliance with the Ottoman Empire
importance: Stephen Bocskai's anti-Habsburg Hungarian insurgents, allied with the Ottoman Empire during their major uprising, successfully besieged and captured Székesfehérvár, wresting it back from Habsburg control during the final phases of the Long Turkish War.

name: Herzegovina uprising of 1596–1597
commanders: Vojvoda Grdan and Patriarch Jovan Kantul vs. Dervish Bey
importance: Organized by Serbian Patriarch Jovan Kantul and led by Duke Grdan of Nikšić in the Sanjak of Herzegovina and Montenegro during the Long Turkish War, the uprising broke out following the burning of Saint Sava's relics, but was ultimately defeated at Gacko due to a lack of foreign support.
casualties: Heavy insurgent defeats and subsequent significant Serb migrations to the Bay of Kotor and Dalmatia

name: First Tarnovo Uprising
commanders: Theodore Ballina, Ivan Shishman II, and Dionysus Rallis vs. Ottoman Authorities
importance: A Bulgarian uprising against Ottoman rule based in Veliko Tarnovo, sparked by Wallachian incursions under Michael the Brave during the Long Turkish War. The rebels briefly proclaimed Ivan Shishman II as Tsar before being brutally crushed, prompting 16,000 Bulgarians to flee across the Danube.
casualties: Suppressed with severe reprisals; 16,000 refugees fled to Wallachia

name: Battle of Velika Monastery
commanders: Habsburg-Allied forces vs. Ottoman forces
importance: An engagement during the operations to secure Slavonia following the earlier anti-Ottoman uprisings and campaigns in the region.

name: Battle of Osijek (1690)
commanders: Habsburg forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: An unsuccessful attempt by Habsburg forces to capture the heavily fortified strategic hub of Osijek during the counter-offensives of the Great Turkish War.

name: Peace of Zsitvatorok
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Habsburg Monarchy
importance: Ended the Long Turkish War and altered Ottoman-Habsburg diplomatic relations.

name: Entry into Kassa
commanders: Stephen Bocskai vs. City Authorities
importance: Stephen Bocskai triumphantly entered and secured the major strategic city of Kassa (Kosice) during his rising anti-Habsburg rebellion.

name: Siege of Kassa and Operations in Upper Hungary
commanders: Giorgio Basta vs. Kassa Garrison / Ferenc Rhédey
importance: Kassa successfully resisted an imperial siege by Giorgio Basta, who subsequently marched to Eperjes, while Ferenc Rhédey's insurgent army looted West-Felvidék (Western Slovakia) and severely compromised Basta's supply lines.
casualties: Unspecified garrison and imperial supply losses

name: Assassination of Balázs Lippai
commanders: Stephen Bocskai vs. Balázs Lippai
importance: Rebel leader Balázs Lippai was assassinated on the orders of Stephen Bocskai amid shifting political alignments and internal power struggles within the anti-Habsburg movement.

name: Conquest of Szatmár (1605)
commanders: Stephen Bocskai's Troops vs. Imperial Garrison
importance: Stephen Bocskai's insurgent forces successfully conquered the strategic fortress and town of Szatmár (Satu Mare) early in 1605, expanding their territorial control in northeastern Royal Hungary.

name: Bocskai's Expedition to Transdanubia
commanders: Stephen Bocskai's Forces vs. Imperial Forces
importance: Stephen Bocskai's troops pushed westward into Transdanubia (Dunántúl), significantly expanding the reach of the anti-Habsburg uprising across Royal Hungary.

name: Imperial Counterattack in Western Hungary
commanders: Rudolf II's Forces vs. Bocskai's Forces
importance: Forces loyal to Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II launched a counterattack in Western Hungary to stem the territorial gains of Bocskai's rebellion.

name: Assembly in Korpona
commanders: Stephen Bocskai and Hungarian Estates
importance: A major political assembly held in Korpona (Krupina) where leaders of the anti-Habsburg movement and the estates gathered to coordinate military and diplomatic strategy.

name: Muscovite Garrison Takes Guard of Kyiv
commanders: Muscovite voivode Vasily Sheremetev and Cossack authorities
importance: Muscovite troops entered Kyiv following the Pereiaslav agreement and assumed responsibility for guarding the city. This marked the beginning of a permanent Muscovite military presence in Kyiv, although the city remained within the Cossack Hetmanate rather than being directly incorporated into the Tsardom of Russia.

name: Meeting of Bocskai and Lala Mehmed Pasha
commanders: Stephen Bocskai and Grand Vizier Lala Mehmed Pasha
importance: Stephen Bocskai met directly with Ottoman Grand Vizier Lala Mehmed Pasha in Pest County to solidify their military alliance and political coordination against the Habsburgs.

name: Treaty of Vienna (1606)
commanders: Stephen Bocskai and Archduke Matthias
importance: A landmark peace treaty signed between Stephen Bocskai and Archduke Matthias that guaranteed religious freedom for Protestants in Royal Hungary, restored constitutional rights, and recognized Bocskai as Prince of Transylvania.

name: Death of Stephen Bocskai and Execution of Mihály Káthay
commanders: Stephen Bocskai and Mihály Káthay
result: Death of Bocskai / Assassination of Káthay
importance: Stephen Bocskai died suddenly under suspicious circumstances in Kassa (Košice). Believing he had been poisoned, his outraged soldiers blamed, lynched, and killed his chancellor, Mihály Káthay.
casualties: 1 leader died of illness/suspicious causes; 1 chancellor executed by soldiers

name: Capture of Oradea
commanders: Kose Ali Pasha; Transylvanian-Habsburg defenders
importance: Created Varat Eyalet.

name: Capture of Nove Zamky (Ersekujvar)
commanders: Koprulu Fazil Ahmed Pasha; Adam Forgach
importance: Created Uyvar Eyalet in Upper Hungary.

name: Battle of Saint Gotthard
commanders: Koprulu Fazil Ahmed Pasha; Raimondo Montecuccoli
importance: Checked Ottoman advance after Uyvar.

name: Fall of Candia
commanders: Koprulu Fazil Ahmed Pasha; Venetian commanders
importance: Completed Ottoman conquest of Crete after a long siege.

name: Siege of Kamianets-Podilskyi
commanders: Mehmed IV and Koprulu Fazil Ahmed Pasha; Polish defenders
importance: Led to the creation of Podolia Eyalet.

name: Battle of Perast
commanders: Krsto Vicković vs. Mehmed Rizvanbegović
importance: A celebrated defensive victory where a tiny garrison of Venetian soldiers from Perast and allied hajduks successfully repelled a vastly superior Ottoman force from the Sanjak of Herzegovina, killing the Ottoman commander Mehmed Rizvanbegović.
casualties: 63–80+ Ottoman dead, 200–800 wounded; light defender losses

name: Siege of Thodorou
commanders: Silahdar Yusuf Pasha vs. Biagio Giuliani
importance: An opening engagement of the Cretan War where Ottoman forces captured the strategic island fortress of Agioi Theodoroi (Thodorou) off the coast of Crete. The Venetian commander Biagio Giuliani blew up the powder magazine/sewer in a desperate final act, but Ottoman troops stormed the breach, securing a vital harbor and bridgehead for the subsequent siege of Chania.
casualties: Garrison put to the sword; heavy losses from the explosion among the storming units

name: Siege of Chania (1645)
commanders: Silahdar Yusuf Pasha vs. Blasio Zulian and Venetian Garrison
importance: The opening major siege of the Cretan War where Ottoman forces besieged Venetian-held Chania for 56 days, culminating in its capture and opening the Ottoman conquest of Crete.
casualties: Heavy casualties on both sides; Venetian garrison surrendered after a brave 56-day defense

name: Siege of Rethymno
commanders: Hussein Pasha vs. Luigi Minotto and Cormaro
importance: Ottoman forces under Hussein Pasha captured the ruined and rebellious city of Rethymno, forcing the remaining Venetian garrison under Luigi Minotto to surrender the citadel following a heavy bombardment and plague outbreak.
casualties: Heavy Venetian commander and garrison losses; plague casualties among besiegers

name: Siege of Chania (1660)
commanders: Francesco Morosini and Almerigo d'Este vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: An Allied Christian campaign involving Venetian, Maltese, Papal, Tuscan, and French forces attempting to recapture Chania, which ultimately failed due to internal command disputes and successful Ottoman reinforcements.
casualties: Heavy Christian losses during initial assaults; Ottoman garrison reinforced

name: Siege of Lviv
commanders: Ottoman-Cossack-Tatar forces; Commonwealth defenders
importance: Part of the Ottoman-Commonwealth war following Kamianets.

name: Battle of Khotyn
commanders: Jan Sobieski; Hussein Pasha
importance: Restored Commonwealth prestige after Buchach.

name: Treaty of Zurawno
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
importance: Confirmed Ottoman possession of Podolia in the short term.

name: Treaty of Constantinople (1494)
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Venice
importance: Established early stable relations and commercial arrangements.

name: Treaty of Constantinople (1533)
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Habsburg Monarchy
importance: Long-lasting peace and mutual recognition of borders.

name: Treaty of Adrianople (1547)
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Ferdinand I
importance: Ferdinand I recognized Ottoman control over most of Hungary.

name: Peace of Amasya
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Safavid Iran
importance: First official peace between Ottomans and Safavids.

name: Treaty of Constantinople (1590)
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Safavid Iran
importance: Ottomans secured vast areas of the Caucasus.

name: Siege of Veszprém
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Habsburg
importance: The first engagement of the Long Turkish War, marking the resumption of large-scale hostilities.

name: Siege of Várpalota
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Habsburg
importance: Followed the fall of Veszprém, forcing the Habsburgs onto the defensive in western Hungary.

name: Siege of Győr
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Habsburg
importance: A major strategic loss for the Habsburgs; Győr was a key fortress protecting the road to Vienna.

name: Second Siege of Győr (1598)
commanders: Adolf von Schwarzenberg and Miklós Pálffy vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: A daring surprise assault and subsequent siege where Christian forces under Adolf von Schwarzenberg successfully recaptured the crucial fortress of Győr from the Ottomans, reversing their major loss from 1594.
casualties: Heavy defending Ottoman casualties during the surprise breach; moderate Christian losses

name: Second Siege of Tata (1597)
commanders: Miklós Pálffy vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Royal Hungarian and imperial forces led by Miklós Pálffy successfully captured the border fortress of Tata from the Ottoman garrison during a coordinated campaign in Royal Hungary.
casualties: Garrison losses and subsequent Ottoman recapture attempts

name: Siege of Buda (1598)
commanders: Archduke Matthias and Adolf von Schwarzenberg vs. Mihalijli Ahmed Pasha
result: Ottoman defensive victory / Lifting of the siege
importance: The first major Habsburg attempt to capture Buda during the Long Turkish War. Despite a large coalition army and artillery bombardment, unrelenting autumn rains, flooding, and stubborn defense by the Ottoman garrison forced Archduke Matthias to lift the siege.
casualties: Heavy losses due to exposure, mud, and Ottoman counter-attacks; Ottoman garrison suffered ~1,500 casualties during engagements.

name: Siege of Komárom
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Habsburg
importance: Part of the rapid 1594 Ottoman push to seize critical Danube crossings.

name: Siege of Esztergom
commanders: Habsburg (Mansfeld) vs. Ottoman Empire
importance: A major tactical success that reclaimed the strategic fortress city of Esztergom from Ottoman control.

name: Battle for Klis
commanders: Ivo Senjanin, Giovanni Alberti, and Antonio Bertucci vs. Mustafa Pijadepašić and Ibrahim-aga
importance: A major anti-Ottoman rebellion and surprise capture of the strategic Klis fortress by Uskoks, Venetian irregulars, and allied forces, followed by a massive Ottoman counter-siege and relief defeat that restored Ottoman control.
casualties: Heavy losses among the Christian garrison and relief forces; entire initial Ottoman garrison killed during the initial capture, followed by significant casualties during the 8,000-strong Ottoman counter-siege.

name: Siege of Esztergom (1594)
commanders: Archduke Matthias vs. Koca Sinan Pasha
result: Ottoman defensive victory / Lifting of the siege
importance: An Imperial-German army led by Archduke Matthias laid siege to the strategic fortress of Esztergom in the spring of 1594, but the campaign was abandoned and the siege failed after Grand Vizier Koca Sinan Pasha led a successful Ottoman relief expedition north from Belgrade.
casualties: Unspecified imperial and Ottoman relief losses

name: Siege of Visegrád
commanders: Habsburg (Mansfeld) vs. Ottoman Empire
importance: The capture of Visegrád further solidified the Habsburg hold on the Danube line and the route towards Buda.

name: Battle of Șelimbăr
commanders: Michael the Brave vs. Andrew Báthory
importance: Michael the Brave defeated the Transylvanian prince, allowing him to occupy Alba Iulia and begin his brief unification of the Romanian principalities.

name: Siege of Castelnuovo
commanders: Francisco de Sarmiento vs. Hayreddin Barbarossa & Ulamen
importance: An Ottoman army of over 50,000 men besieged and captured Castelnuovo after a brutal defense by a Spanish tercio, ending Christian attempts to control the Eastern Mediterranean
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses (~8,000 killed); almost all 3,500+ Spanish defenders killed or captured

name: Siege of Navarino (1572)
commanders: John of Austria, Álvaro de Bazán & Alexander Farnese vs. Occhiali
importance: A Holy League armada led by John of Austria failed to capture the Ottoman-held castle at Navarino and withdrew following heavy resistance and reports of large reinforcements
casualties: 750 allied troops killed; 1 Ottoman ship lost

name: Battle of Mirăslău
commanders: Michael the Brave vs. Giorgio Basta
importance: A decisive defeat for Michael the Brave that ended his rule in Transylvania and forced his temporary retreat.

name: Siege of Nagyvárad (1660)
commanders: Máté Balogh, János Rácz & Mihály Ibrányi vs. Ali Pasha & Szejdi Ahmed Pasha
importance: A 50,000-strong Ottoman army besieged and captured the strategic fortress of Várad (Oradea) after a 44-day siege, leading to the establishment of the Eyalet of Várad and the loss of Transylvanian independence
casualties: Heavy losses; garrison reduced from 850 to 300 men before surrender

name: Battle of Nagyvárad
commanders: László Rákóczy & Zsigmond Pethő vs. Kucuk Pasha (Ottoman Garrison)
importance: Fought during the Austro-Turkish War; a joint Hungarian-German force led by László Rákóczy launched a surprise attack and entered Ottoman-held Nagyvárad, but was ultimately ousted after looting the town, resulting in heavy losses and the death of Rákóczy
casualties: Heavy losses on both sides, including the death of Hungarian commander László Rákóczy

name: Siege of Pskov
commanders: Stephen Báthory & Jan Zamojski vs. Vasili Skopin-Shuisky & Ivan Shuisky
result: Disputed — tactical Russian defensive success (siege repelled) but strategic Polish-Lithuanian victory via the Treaty of Jam Zapolski
importance: Final major action of the Livonian War; a 31,000-strong Polish-Lithuanian-Hungarian-Bohemian-Wallachian-German army failed to take the city despite repeated assaults, mining attempts, and a five-month blockade, while Russian defenders (~4,000 troops and ~12,000 armed citizens) conducted 46 sallies; ended with the Treaty of Jam Zapolski, in which Russia renounced claims to Livonia and Polotsk in exchange for the return of captured territories

name: Treaty of Nasuh Pasha
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Safavid Iran
importance: First time Ottomans agreed to cede conquered territory.

name: Treaty of Busza
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
importance: Addressed Moldavian affairs and Cossack–Tatar raids.

name: Treaty of Serav
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Safavid Iran
importance: Reduced the annual silk tribute requirement.

name: Treaty of Khotyn
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
importance: Ended the war; borders remained largely unchanged.

name: Treaty of Zuhab
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Safavid Iran
importance: Defined the modern border between Iraq and Iran.

name: Peace of Vasvár
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Habsburg Monarchy
importance: Despite Habsburg victory at St. Gotthard, Ottomans kept key gains.

name: Treaty of Buchach
commanders: Ottoman Empire; Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
importance: Poland agreed to tribute and loss of Podolia (later rejected).

name: Siege of Vienna
commanders: Kara Mustafa Pasha; Ernst Rudiger von Starhemberg and Jan III Sobieski
importance: Turning point of the Great Turkish War and the end of Ottoman expansion in central Europe.
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses and abandoned camp.

name: Raid on Korneuburg (1529)
commanders: Ottoman Advance Forces vs. Local Garrison
importance: During the 1529 campaign against Vienna, Ottoman advance forces and light cavalry raided and plundered Korneuburg on the northern bank of the Danube.
casualties: Local garrison and civilian losses; widespread looting

name: Siege and Sack of Perchtoldsdorf (1683)
commanders: Ottoman Forces vs. Town Garrison and Townsfolk
importance: During the 1683 march toward Vienna, Ottoman forces besieged Perchtoldsdorf; after the town surrendered, a catastrophic massacre of the garrison and townsfolk took place.
casualties: Severe; virtually the entire garrison and townsfolk massacred after surrender

name: Raid on Baden bei Wien (1683)
commanders: Ottoman and Tatar Raiders vs. Local Inhabitants
importance: During the 1683 campaign leading up to the Siege of Vienna, Ottoman and Tatar irregular cavalry raided, sacked, and burned Baden bei Wien south of Vienna, ravaging the surrounding spa region.
casualties: Heavy civilian casualties and widespread property destruction

name: 1532 Akıncı Raids into Lower Austria
commanders: Ottoman Light Cavalry (Akıncıs) vs. Imperial Local Defenses
importance: During Suleiman the Magnificent's 1532 campaign, Ottoman light cavalry pushed ahead of the main army, systematically devastating villages, towns, and rural areas east and south of Vienna without meeting a major pitched battle.
casualties: Heavy civilian casualties, thousands of captives taken, and widespread destruction of settlements across Lower Austria

name: Raid on Metlika
commanders: Ottoman Raiders vs. Carniolan Frontier Defenses
importance: Metlika suffered its earliest recorded destructive border raid as Ottoman incursions began pushing into the Bela Krajina frontier region of Carniola.
casualties: Local civilian casualties and property damage

name: Raid and Siege of Metlika
commanders: Ottoman Akıncı Raiders vs. Metlika Garrison
importance: As part of the escalating 'turški vpadi' border wars, Metlika was heavily besieged and raided by Ottoman forces, prompting increased local defensive fortifications.
casualties: Significant structural damage and captives taken

name: Raid and Siege of Metlika
commanders: Ottoman Raiders vs. Bela Krajina Garrison
importance: Metlika faced another major military assault and siege during a wave of intensive Ottoman incursions across the southern Habsburg frontier.
casualties: Garrison and civilian losses; surrounding rural areas ravaged

name: Raid and Siege of Metlika
commanders: Ottoman Frontier Forces vs. Metlika Garrison
importance: Metlika was once again targeted and besieged during peak operational phases of the Croatian and Carniolan Military Frontier defense network.
casualties: Combat losses and structural wear on the frontier stronghold

name: Raid on Kostanjevica na Krki (1471)
commanders: Ottoman Akıncı Raiders vs. Local Inhabitants
importance: Kostanjevica na Krki suffered a devastating Ottoman raid in 1471 during the intensifying 'turški vpadi' incursions, prompting local authorities to subsequently upgrade defensive fortifications.
casualties: Local civilian casualties and property destruction

name: Raid on Kostanjevica na Krki (1580s)
commanders: Ottoman Frontier Raiders vs. Regional Defenses
importance: The town and monastery complex at Kostanjevica na Krki faced further raiding pressures during the late 16th-century escalation along the Croatian and Carniolan Military Frontier.

name: Raid on Novo Mesto (Rudolfswerth) (1471)
commanders: Ottoman Akıncı Raiders vs. Local Defenses
importance: Novo Mesto (Rudolfswerth) in Carniola suffered an initial destructive Ottoman raid during the peak of 15th-century border incursions.

name: Raid on Novo Mesto (Rudolfswerth) (1559)
commanders: Ottoman Frontier Raiders vs. Regional Defenses
importance: The strategic town of Novo Mesto experienced a renewed Ottoman raid, highlighting the ongoing vulnerability of the Carniolan interior prior to formal Captaincy reorganizations.

name: Raid on Krško (Gurkfeld) (1471)
commanders: Ottoman Akıncı Raiders vs. Local Inhabitants
importance: Krško (Gurkfeld) along the Sava river valley corridor was targeted and plundered by Ottoman irregular raiding parties.

name: Raid on Krško (Gurkfeld) (1473)
commanders: Ottoman Akıncı Raiders vs. Local Defenses
importance: Krško faced a subsequent Ottoman incursion just two years after the 1471 raid as light cavalry swept through the Windic March region.

name: Raid on Brežice (1471)
commanders: Ottoman Akıncı Raiders vs. Regional Defenses
importance: Brežice, situated near the confluence of the Sava and Krka rivers, was heavily raided during the widespread 1471 Ottoman incursions into Carniola.
casualties: Local civilian casualties and structural damage

name: Raid on Celje
commanders: Ottoman Akıncı Raiders vs. Regional Defenses
importance: The historic center of Celje in Styria was targeted and raided during the intense wave of 1471 Ottoman incursions across the southern Habsburg borderlands.
casualties: Local civilian casualties and property destruction

name: Raid on the Vipava Valley
commanders: Ottoman Akıncı Raiders vs. Regional Frontier Defenses
importance: Ottoman light cavalry executed a deep and highly destructive incursion into the Vipava Valley, pushing far toward the Karst plateau and terrorizing local settlements.
casualties: Widespread rural devastation, structural destruction, and thousands of captives taken

name: Raids on the Kočevje (Gottschee) Region
commanders: Ottoman Akıncı Raiders vs. Local Inhabitants
importance: The isolated forested region of Kočevje (Gottschee) was heavily and repeatedly targeted by Ottoman raiding parties during the peak of 15th-century border incursions, resulting in severe regional depopulation.
casualties: Significant population losses, captives abducted, and extensive property destruction

name: Raid on Ptuj (Pettau)
commanders: Ottoman Akıncı Raiders vs. Styrian Defenses
result: Town raided and surrounding area sacked
importance: Ptuj, one of the oldest towns in the region along the Drava river, suffered a major Ottoman raid during the 1479 border incursions.
casualties: Widespread property damage and local casualties

name: Raids on the Outskirts of Maribor
commanders: Ottoman Akıncı Raiders vs. Maribor Outskirts
importance: While the main walled core of Maribor successfully held, its surrounding suburbs and agricultural outskirts were threatened and heavily raided by Ottoman light cavalry during the 1480s.
casualties: Destruction of suburban properties and livestock losses

name: Fortification of Ljubljana against the Ottoman Threat
commanders: Ljubljana City Authorities vs. Ottoman Threat
importance: Although never directly besieged or taken by Ottoman armies, Ljubljana's city walls, castle defenses, and regional fortifications were extensively upgraded and maintained throughout the 15th and 16th centuries in response to the persistent Ottoman threat.

name: Raid on Brežice (1483)
commanders: Ottoman Akıncı Raiders vs. Local Garrison
importance: Brežice suffered another major destructive raid as Ottoman forces continued pressuring the crucial Sava river valley defense lines.

name: Battle of Molodi
commanders: Crimean-Ottoman vs Russia
importance: Checked northern expansion.

name: Attack on Chilia (Kilia)
commanders: Ottoman naval/land forces; Moldavian defenders under Alexandru cel Bun
importance: First recorded Ottoman military attempt to capture a stronghold in Moldavia.

name: Battle of Vaslui (Podul Înalt)
commanders: Hadım Suleiman Pasha; Stephen the Great (Ștefan cel Mare)
importance: One of the greatest Christian tactical victories against Ottoman forces in the 15th century.

name: Battle of Valea Albă (Războieni)
commanders: Mehmed II; Stephen the Great
importance: Mehmed II defeated the main Moldavian field army but failed to permanently subdue the principality.

name: Siege of Neamț Fortress
commanders: Mehmed II; Moldavian garrison defenders
importance: The fortress held out successfully, forcing Mehmed II to withdraw due to supply shortages and plague.

name: Battle of Komarno
commanders: John III Sobieski & Stefan Bidzinski vs. Nurredin-Sultan & Petro Doroshenko
importance: A premier engagement of Jan III Sobieski's autumn expedition during the Polish-Ottoman War; Crown Hetman Sobieski led a grueling 57-kilometer march in heavy rain to surprise a superior Tatar-Cossack force near Komarno, routing them into the Wereszyca river and liberating approximately 20,000 captive civilians
casualties: 9,300 Crimean Tatars and allies killed or captured; minimal Polish-Lithuanian losses

name: Battle of Trembowla
commanders: Jan Samuel Chrzanowski & Anna Dorota Chrzanowska vs. Ibrahim Shyshman
importance: A legendary defense during the Polish-Ottoman War (1672–1676); a tiny garrison of around 80 soldiers and local volunteers under Captain Chrzanowski and his resolute wife Anna Dorota successfully held the small Trembowla castle against a massive Ottoman-Tatar army for over three weeks until the approach of Jan III Sobieski's forces forced the Turks to lift the siege
casualties: Heavy garrison and defender losses; significant casualties inflicted on the besieging Ottoman-Tatar forces

name: Suleiman's Moldavian Campaign (Capture of Suceava)
commanders: Suleiman the Magnificent; Petru Rareș (deposed)
importance: Suleiman captured the capital, annexed southern Bessarabia (Tighina/Bender), and firmly asserted vassal tracking over foreign policy.
casualties: Minimal battlefield combat losses; highly strategic campaign.

name: Siege of Suceava (1497)
commanders: John I Albert vs. Stephen III
importance: Unsuccessful four-week Polish siege of Suceava that forced King John I Albert to begin retreating from Moldavia
casualties: Heavy Polish losses from resistance and disease

name: Moldavian Campaign of Bohdan Khmelnytsky
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & İslâm III Giray vs. Vasile Lupu
importance: Joint invasion of Moldavia that forced Vasile Lupu to pay heavy tribute, break his Polish alliance, and agree to the marriage of his daughter Ruxandra to Tymofiy Khmelnytsky
casualties: Heavy Moldavian losses and widespread looting/enslavement

name: Moldavian Campaign (Battle of Roșcani)
commanders: Ottoman-Wallachian coalition forces; John III the Terrible (Ioan Vodă cel Cumplit)
importance: Suppressed a major anti-Ottoman rebellion and reasserted sovereign provincial tribute authority.
casualties: Heavy Moldavian rebel forces wiped out.

name: Battle of Savra
commanders: Hayreddin Pasha; Balša II of Zeta
importance: First major Ottoman military victory in Albania; established baseline suzerainty over regional princes.

name: Occupation of Krujë
commanders: Ottoman Rumelian forces; Thopia family defenders
importance: Brought a highly critical northern Albanian fortress under direct garrison control.

name: Conquest of Vlorë, Berat and Kanina
commanders: Evrenosoglu Ali Bey; Rugina Balšić
importance: Secured southern Albania and established a critical strategic foothold on the Adriatic coast.

name: Siege of Pécs (1551)
commanders: Ottoman Empire (Sokollu Mehmed Pasha) vs. Habsburg garrison
importance: A key Ottoman offensive operation led by Sokollu Mehmed Pasha to consolidate control over the southern Hungarian border region.

name: Siege of Lippa (1551)
commanders: Habsburg (George Martinuzzi and Giovanni Battista Castaldo) vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: A significant tactical success where Christian imperial forces forced the Ottomans to abandon the city, triggering an intense Ottoman response in 1552 which led to Lippa's reoccupation.

name: Siege of Kanizsa (1543)
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Habsburg forces
importance: A failed Ottoman attempt to seize the fortress during the broad 1543 campaign season.

name: Siege of Kanizsa (1545)
