importance: Drew Spanish Mediterranean naval focus away from the Ottoman front after 1635

name: Battle of Breadfield
commanders: Pál Kinizsi, István Báthory, Vuk Branković & Basarab Laiotă cel Bătrân vs. Ali Koca Bey & Basarab cel Tânăr
importance: A combined Hungarian, Serbian, and allied army led by Pál Kinizsi and István Báthory decisively defeated a massive Ottoman-Wallachian raiding force, providing decades of security for Transylvania and southern Hungary
casualties: High Ottoman losses (~thousands killed, including Malkoçoğlu and Isa Bey); ~3,000 Hungarian/allied losses

name: Ottoman-Portuguese Red Sea trade skirmishes
commanders: Ottoman Red Sea maritime patrols vs. Portuguese privateers/traders
importance: Low-intensity skirmishing and convoy protection securing Red Sea spice and coffee trade routes against Portuguese interception.

name: Corsair raid on the Canary Islands
commanders: Barbary corsairs vs. Spanish Atlantic garrisons
importance: Demonstrated the expanding operational reach of North African corsairs into the Atlantic archipelagos.

name: Salé corsair raid on Cornwall
commanders: Salé (Moroccan) rovers vs. English coastal settlements
importance: Salé corsairs raided Mount's Bay and the Cornish coastline, highlighting the vulnerability of English shipping and shores.
casualties: Coastal property damage and captives taken.

name: Turkish Abductions (Grindavík raid)
commanders: Barbary/Salé corsairs vs. Danish-Icelandic villagers
importance: Opening phase of the 'Tyrkjaránið' (Turkish Abductions), where corsairs raided Grindavík and local Icelandic coastal settlements.

name: Sack of Vestmannaeyjar
commanders: Barbary/Salé corsairs vs. Icelandic island population
importance: The most notorious northern Atlantic corsair raid; several hundred inhabitants of the Westman Islands were abducted into North African slavery.

name: Sack of Baltimore
commanders: Murat Reis the Younger (Jan Janszoon) vs. Irish villagers
importance: Algerine corsairs sacked the coastal village of Baltimore in County Cork, Ireland, carrying almost the entire village population into captivity.

name: Corsair raids on British coastal waters
commanders: North African corsairs vs. Irish, Cornish, and Devon coastal guards
importance: Repeated corsair deep-water incursions along the Irish, Cornish, and Devon coastlines, disrupting regional commerce.

name: Salé Rovers raiding in the English Channel
commanders: Salé Rovers vs. English shipping / coastal approaches
importance: Persistent raiding by Moroccan Salé rovers into the English Channel and southwest England approaches.

name: Raid on Trabzon
commanders: Prince Selim vs. Ibrahim (Safavid)
importance: First direct military clash between the Ottomans and Safavids; Prince Selim repelled the raid and pursued them to Erzincan.

name: Selim's Counterattack on Erzincan
commanders: Prince Selim vs. Safavid regional forces
importance: Independent Ottoman counterattack into Erzincan in response to the Safavid invasion of the Dulkadirids.

name: Selim's Counterattack on Bayburt
commanders: Prince Selim vs. Safavid regional forces
importance: Continuation of Prince Selim's 1507 campaign, defeating local Safavid forces in Bayburt.

name: Raid on Antalya
commanders: Şahkulu vs. Şehzade Korkut
importance: Şahkulu raided Antalya with 400–500 men, causing Şehzade Korkut to flee and abandon his treasury.

name: Skirmish at Antalya
commanders: Serasker Hasan Pasha vs. Şahkulu's rebels
importance: Serasker Hasan Pasha secured the treasury to Antalya but was subsequently attacked, defeated, and forced to retreat.

name: Capture of Burdur & Siege of Adana
commanders: Şahkulu vs. Murad Pasha
importance: Rebels captured Isparta and attacked Burdur, killing sanjakbey Murad Pasha alongside 2,000 men; an initial siege of Adana was also launched.

name: Ambush at Kütahya
commanders: Hadım Ali Pasha & Karagöz Ahmet Pasha vs. Şahkulu
importance: Şahkulu ambushed and nearly annihilated an Ottoman army sent by Bayezid II, capturing and executing Karagöz Ahmet Pasha.
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses, senior commander executed

name: Battle of Manisa & Siege of Kütahya
commanders: Şehzade Korkut & Haydar Pasha vs. Şahkulu
importance: After a brief setback at Kütahya against Haydar Pasha, Şahkulu invaded Manisa, routed Şehzade Korkut, and killed Serasker Hasan Pasha.
casualties: High Ottoman casualties including senior leaders

name: Second Attack on Kütahya
commanders: Haydar Pasha vs. Şahkulu
importance: Şahkulu returned to Kütahya in a follow-up engagement and killed Haydar Pasha.

name: Battle near Ankara
commanders: Kâtip Ali Pasha vs. Şahkulu
importance: Major field battle where an Ottoman army of 50,000 under Kâtip Ali Pasha was defeated by the rebels, and the Ottoman commander was killed.

name: Skirmish in Karaman
commanders: Haydar Pasha & Cündî Kemal Bey vs. Şahkulu
importance: During his retreat toward Safavid territories, Şahkulu attacked Karaman, killing beylerbey Haydar Pasha and sanjakbey Cündî Kemal Bey.
casualties: Severe leadership casualties for the Ottomans

name: Battle at Sivas / Çubukova
commanders: Hadım Ali Pasha vs. Şahkulu
importance: Hadım Ali Pasha pursued Şahkulu for 14 days culminating in a fierce battle where the Ottomans were defeated and Ali Pasha was killed (though Şahkulu was also fatally wounded, breaking the revolt).
casualties: Heavy casualties on both sides; death of Grand Vizier/Commander Hadım Ali Pasha

name: Clash at Eyüyazı
commanders: Nur-Ali Khalifa vs. Hadım Sinan Pasha
importance: Nur-Ali Khalifa defeated an Ottoman army led by vizier Hadım Sinan Pasha, resulting in the death of commander Yularkıstı Sinan Pasha.

name: Attempted Capture of Urfa
commanders: Murad Bey vs. Acheh Soltan Qajar
importance: Sultan Selim's 8,000-man force under Murad Bey failed to capture Urfa and was repelled by the city's governor, with Murad Bey killed.

name: Siege and Capture of Bayburt
commanders: Bıyıklı Mehmed Bey & Mustafa Bey vs. Kara Maksud-i
importance: Joint Ottoman forces successfully besieged and captured Bayburt after the governor refused to surrender.

name: Surrender of Kiğı
commanders: Bıyıklı Mehmed Bey vs. Kiğı Governor
importance: Kiğı Castle surrendered peacefully without a siege after its governor transmitted the keys directly to Bıyıklı Mehmed Bey.

name: Battle of Ovacık
commanders: Pir Hüseyin Bey & Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha vs. Nur-Ali Khalifa & Aykutoğlu Muhammed Bey
importance: An Ottoman army of 10,000 under Pir Hüseyin Bey and Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha defeated Nur-Ali Khalifa and Aykutoğlu Muhammed Bey, resulting in the death of Nur-Ali Khalifa and the annexation of Tunceli.
casualties: Heavy Safavid casualties, Nur-Ali Khalifa killed

name: Siege and Capture of Diyarbakır
commanders: Cemşid Bey, Yiğit Ahmet, Şadi Pasha & Idris Bitlisi vs. Karahan Ustajli & Durmuş Bey
importance: An Ottoman army defeated a Safavid force of 10,000 under Karahan Ustajli and Durmuş Bey, successfully capturing the city of Diyarbakır.

name: Siege and Capture of Harput
commanders: Çerkes Hüseyin Bey & Karaçinoğlu Ahmet Bey vs. Safavid Garrison
importance: 1,000 Janissaries successfully captured Harput after a rapid 3-day siege.

name: Ambush at Sinjar
commanders: Pro-Ottoman Kurdish fighters vs. Çuka Khan (Safavid)
importance: 500 pro-Ottoman Kurdish fighters ambushed a 2,000-strong Safavid force under Çuka Khan, inflicting casualties with minimal losses.

name: Ambush at Bismil
commanders: Karahan Ustajli vs. Çerkez Hüseyin Bey & Mehmed Çelebi
importance: Karahan Ustajli ambushed an Ottoman force in revenge, annihilating the entire Ottoman contingent and killing the sanjakbey of Harput, Çerkez Hüseyin Bey, and Mehmed Çelebi.
casualties: Entire Ottoman force wiped out, senior commanders killed

name: Battle of Koçhisar
commanders: Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha vs. Karahan Ustajli
importance: Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha led 20,000 Ottomans to a decisive field victory against 6,000 Safavids, resulting in the death of the Safavid commander Karahan Ustajli.

name: Battle of Marj Dabiq
commanders: Sultan Selim I vs. Sultan Al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghawri
importance: A decisive clash ending Mamluk supremacy. Following months of diplomatic ruses, Sultan Selim I's artillery-backed forces crushed Qansuh al-Ghawri's army near Aleppo, opening the gate to the conquest of Syria and Egypt.
casualties: Catastrophic Mamluk losses; Sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri perished on the field alongside thousands of cavalrymen.

name: Siege and Capture of Mardin
commanders: Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha & Deli Husrev Pasha vs. Ustajli Süleyman Bey
importance: Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha and Deli Husrev Pasha captured Mardin after an extended siege involving heavy artillery; the Safavid commander Ustajli Süleyman Bey was killed.
casualties: Heavy garrison losses, Safavid commander killed

name: Capture of Hasankeyf
commanders: Idris Bitlisi & Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha vs. Hasankeyf Garrison
importance: Idris Bitlisi and Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha successfully besieged and captured Hasankeyf, taking its governor and defenders prisoner.

name: Capture of Mosul
commanders: Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha & Bedir Bey vs. Ahmed Bey Afshar
importance: Bıyıklı Mehmed Pasha and Bedir Bey defeated Ahmed Bey Afshar and captured Mosul, successfully concluding the Mesopotamia Campaign.

name: Siege of Van
commanders: Suleiman the Magnificent, Rüstem Pasha & Gabriel de Luetz d'Aramon vs. Shah Tahmasp I
importance: Occurred during Suleiman's second campaign of the Ottoman-Safavid War (1532–1555). The walled city of Van was besieged and heavily bombarded, with French ambassador Gabriel de Luetz providing critical advice on artillery placement.
casualties: Safavid garrison defeated and city captured

name: Capture of Bitlis
commanders: Grand Vizier Ibrahim Pasha vs. Safavid Garrison
importance: Conducted during the early incursions of the Ottoman-Safavid conflict, where Grand Vizier Ibrahim Pasha successfully attacked Safavid-held regions and recaptured the strategically vital fortified city of Bitlis.

name: Invasion of Persia by Alqas Mirza
commanders: Alqas Mirza vs. Shah Tahmasp I
importance: Alqas Mirza (Tahmasp's defected half-brother) led a 40,000-strong Ottoman-backed cavalry force to invade Persia, while Tahmasp responded with a devastating scorched-earth policy across Armenia.
casualties: Extensive regional devastation and troop losses

name: Battle near the Euphrates
commanders: Ottoman forces vs. Persian forces & Portuguese allies
importance: Portuguese forces intervened to assist the Persians, deploying tactical troops and twenty cannons to help defeat an Ottoman army near the Euphrates.

name: Fort Captures in Georgia and Tabriz Gains
commanders: Suleiman the Magnificent vs. Regional Garrisons
importance: During the continuation of the second campaign, Sultan Suleiman successfully secured various strategic forts in Georgia and captured territorial gains around Tabriz and Persian-ruled Armenia.
casualties: Garrisons captured or forced to surrender

name: Safavid Incursions in Eastern Anatolia
commanders: Safavid forces vs. Ottoman regional garrisons
result: Safavid raid success / Triggered Ottoman retaliation
importance: Safavid attacks devastated Van and Erzurum, resulting in heavy casualties among the local population and triggering Sultan Suleiman's final campaign of the war.

name: Ottoman Raid on Safavid Azerbaijan
commanders: Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent vs. Safavid forces
importance: The Ottoman army pushed deep into Safavid Azerbaijan, destroying imperial infrastructure, palaces, and gardens, and taking thousands of captives.

name: Capture of Yerevan
commanders: Ottoman imperial forces vs. Safavid garrison
importance: Yerevan was captured by Ottoman forces during the 1554 campaign phase of the third Ottoman-Safavid war.

name: Capture of Karabakh
commanders: Ottoman imperial forces vs. Safavid regional defenders
importance: Karabakh was successfully invested and captured by Ottoman forces during their strategic push into the southern Caucasus.

name: Battle of Circassia (1501 Expedition)
commanders: Şehzade Mehmed & Mehmed Giray vs. Circassian Forces
importance: Ottoman-Crimean punitive expedition destroyed; Kefe garrison wiped out and Mehmed Giray forced to flee
casualties: Entire Ottoman force (~500 men) and majority of Tatar/Cossack troops killed

name: Skirmish and Counterattack near Azov
commanders: Circassian Force vs. Auz Cherkas & Karabay
importance: Circassians used a feigned retreat to lure and destroy Azov Cossack pursuers, killing both commanders during a retaliatory raid
casualties: ~30 Azov Cossacks killed including leaders Auz Cherkas and Karabay

name: Ottoman Campaign in Western Circassia (1502)
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Western Circassia
importance: Second successive Ottoman expedition into western Circassia that ended in failure and defeat

name: Kabardian Expedition (1504)
commanders: Şehzade Mehmed vs. Kabardia
importance: Third expedition led by Şehzade Mehmed without Crimean support, which collapsed after Mehmed was poisoned on Bayezid II's orders

name: Battle of Khotyn (1509)
commanders: Mikołaj Kamieniecki vs. Copaciu
importance: Polish forces retreating from an unsuccessful siege of Suceava successfully repelled and routed a surprise Moldavian-Ottoman attack while crossing the Dniester near Khotyn
casualties: Heavy Moldavian losses, including fifty dignitaries beheaded during the pursuit

name: Battle of Brașov
commanders: Radu Șerban & György Rácz vs. Mózes Székely
importance: Wallachian and Habsburg forces decisively defeated the Ottoman-backed Transylvanian army of Mózes Székely, who was killed in the battle, allowing Radu Șerban to briefly control Transylvania
casualties: Heavy losses for Székely's army; Mózes Székely killed

name: Siege of Velikiye Luki
commanders: Stephen Báthory vs. Ivan Vasiliyevich
importance: Forces of Stephen Báthory successfully besieged and captured the Russian fortress of Velikiye Luki, cutting links between Livonia and Russia
casualties: Thousands of Russian soldiers and civilians killed; ~200 Polish-Hungarian troops killed by a secondary gunpowder magazine explosion

name: Battle of Suceava (1595)
commanders: Jan Potocki & Ieremia Movilă vs. Ştefan Răzvan
importance: A smaller Polish-Lithuanian force under Jan Potocki decisively defeated the Transylvanian-Ottoman forces of Ştefan Răzvan near Suceava during the Moldavian Magnate Wars, leading to Răzvan's capture and execution
casualties: Heavy Transylvanian losses; Răzvan captured and impaled

name: Jan Zamoyski's Expedition to Moldavia
commanders: Jan Zamoyski and Ieremia Movilă vs. Mehmed III, Gazi II Girej, and Ștefan Răzvan
result: Polish-Lithuanian victory; establishment of Moldavia as a Polish vassal state / condominium
importance: A major successful military expedition by Hetman Jan Zamoyski into Moldavia to counter Ottoman expansion, installing Ieremia Movilă as hospodar and turning Moldavia into a Polish-Ottoman condominium.
casualties: Heavy Tatar and pro-Ottoman losses; light Polish-Lithuanian losses

name: Battle of Cecora (1595)
commanders: Jan Zamoyski vs. Gazi II Girej
importance: Zamoyski fortified his army near the Prut River, successfully repelling multiple Tatar attacks and forcing Khan Gazi II Girej to sign a treaty recognizing Ieremia Movilă as hospodar.
casualties: Moderate to heavy Tatar forces; light Commonwealth losses

name: Siege of Brno (1645)
commanders: Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches & Martin Středa vs. Lennart Torstensson & Sigismund II Rákóczi
importance: A small garrison of ~1,400 defenders successfully withstood a months-long siege by 28,000 Swedish and Transylvanian troops, halting Torstensson's march on Vienna

name: Capture of Warsaw (1657)
commanders: George II Rákóczi, Gustaf Otto Stenbock & Anton Zhdanovych vs. Eliasz Jan Łącki
importance: Allied forces besieged and captured Warsaw following the betrayal of the garrison commander, leading to a temporary occupation and sacking of the city
casualties: Garrison and civilian losses during the capture and sacking

name: Siege of Danzig (1577)
commanders: Stephen Báthory vs. Danzig forces
importance: A six-month siege of Danzig by Stephen Báthory ending in a compromise after the Danzig army was defeated in a field battle, with Báthory confirming the city's special privileges in exchange for reparations and recognition
casualties: Heavy losses for Danzig's mercenary army in field engagements

name: Battle for the Sich at Mykytyn Rih
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky vs. Crown Army/Registered Cossack garrison
importance: Opening action of the uprising; defeat of the royal garrison led Registered Cossacks to defect to Khmelnytsky, who was elected Hetman shortly after
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Zhovti Vody
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Tugay Bey vs. Stefan Potocki
importance: First major battle of the uprising; Registered Cossack regiments defected mid-engagement, and the Polish camp was encircled and routed
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Korsun
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Maksym Kryvonis & Tugay Bey vs. Mikołaj Potocki & Marcin Kalinowski
importance: Both Crown and Field Hetmans captured; combined with the death of King Władysław IV, left Poland leaderless and opened the way for Khmelnytsky's westward march
casualties: Most Polish soldiers perished during the ambush and retreat

name: Siege of Lviv (first)
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky vs. city defenders of Lviv
importance: Demonstrated the reach of the Cossack army into Galicia; ransom funds were used partly to pay Tatar allies
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Pyliavtsi
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky vs. Władysław Dominik Zasławski, Mikołaj Ostroróg & Aleksander Koniecpolski
importance: Annihilation of the Polish infantry caused a panicked flight of the entire crown army and its commanders; Cossacks captured over 90 cannons and vast supplies
casualties: Polish infantry largely annihilated; Cossacks captured goods valued at 7–10 million złotys

name: Siege of Zamość
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky vs. Zamość garrison
importance: Capture of Zamość would have opened the road to Warsaw; siege ended after King John II Casimir's election and request for a ceasefire
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Siege of Bar
commanders: Not specified in the source text
result: Not specified in the source text
importance: Renewed hostilities around Bar in Podolia during the buildup to the 1649 campaign
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Siege of Zbarazh
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky vs. Adam Firlej
result: Siege lifted following the Treaty of Zboriv
importance: Polish relief force was ambushed while marching to relieve the besieged fortress, leading directly to the Battle of Zboriv
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Zboriv
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Islam III Giray vs. King John II Casimir Vasa
importance: King himself was nearly surrounded; led to the Treaty of Zboriv, granting autonomy to Kyiv, Bratslav and Chernihiv voivodeships
casualties: Crown army lost up to 7,000 men

name: Clash at Syni Vody
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Crimean Tatar raiders
importance: Direct confrontation with nominally allied Tatars who continued raiding the civilian population despite Cossack protests

name: Battle of Berestechko
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Islam III Giray vs. King John II Casimir Vasa & Jeremi Wiśniowiecki
importance: One of the largest battles of 17th-century Europe; flight of the Tatars and capture of Khmelnytsky's treasury and regalia turned the tide against the Cossacks, though the army recovered within two months
casualties: Over 8,000 Cossack soldiers perished; Poles captured most of the Cossack artillery and gunpowder

name: Confrontation at Bila Tserkva
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky vs. Commonwealth forces
importance: Both sides exhausted after Berestechko; resulting treaty limited the Cossack registry to 20,000 and restricted autonomy to Kyiv Voivodeship, though it was never ratified
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Batih
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky (Tatar cavalry) vs. Marcin Kalinowski
importance: Revenge for Berestechko; Kalinowski killed and half his hussars destroyed; followed by the mass execution of Polish prisoners known as the Batih massacre
casualties: Marcin Kalinowski and half of his hussars killed; Polish prisoners of war massacred afterward

name: Siege of Suceava
commanders: Tymish (Tymofiy) Khmelnytsky vs. Gheorghe Stefan, Transylvanian & Wallachian forces
importance: Tymish Khmelnytsky died in the siege while defending his father-in-law Vasile Lupu's claim to the Moldavian throne, ending Bohdan Khmelnytsky's dynastic ambitions in Moldova

name: Siege of Zhvanets
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Islam III Giray vs. King John II Casimir Vasa
importance: Roughly equal-sized armies (~40,000 each) blockaded each other until the Crimean khan brokered a new peace treaty signed 17 December 1653
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Cossack-Muscovite campaign in Belarus
commanders: Ivan Zolotarenko (with Muscovite forces) vs. Commonwealth garrisons
importance: 18,000-strong Cossack force occupied Bykhaw, Krychaw and Mogilev in 1654, then advanced to Svislach and Minsk in 1655, later joining Muscovite forces toward Vilnius and Grodno
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Polish-Tatar raid into Bratslav and Uman
commanders: Seweryn Potocki (with allied Tatar forces) vs. local Cossack/civilian population
importance: Devastated Podolia and delayed Khmelnytsky's planned offensive into Volhynia; forced thousands of refugees to flee to Moldova
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Okhmativ
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Vasily Sheremetev vs. Crown army
importance: Fought amid severe frost; succeeded in halting the Polish advance despite no decisive winner
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Okhmativ (1644)
commanders: Stanisław Koniecpolski and Jeremi Wiśniowiecki vs. Tugay Bey
importance: The greatest Polish Commonwealth victory over the Crimean Tatars in the first half of the 17th century. Koniecpolski successfully predicted the enemy's movements, preventing them from splitting into mobile units and inflicting a crushing defeat.
casualties: Over 4,000 Tatars killed; Polish casualties described as minimal

name: Siege of Lviv (second)
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky & Vasily Buturlin vs. city defenders of Lviv
importance: A Tatar raid into Khmelnytsky's rear forced the lifting of the siege in exchange for a payment rather than capture of the city
casualties: Not specified in the source text

name: Battle of Cornul lui Sas
commanders: Ștefan IX Tomșa & Khan Temir vs. Stefan Potocki & Constantin Movilă
importance: Decisive defeat of Stefan Potocki's private Polish-backed army during the Moldavian Magnate Wars, securing Ștefan Tomșa's rule
casualties: Heavy losses; Stefan Potocki and Elisabeta Movilă captured, Constantin Movilă drowned

name: Crimean Campaign against Kabardia
commanders: Bahadır Giray vs. Kabardian Principality
importance: Catastrophic defeat of the Crimean army under Bahadır Giray after bypassing Taman to strike Kabardia, losing two-thirds of their forces and pausing Crimean offensives
casualties: Approx. two-thirds of the Crimean army lost (~20,000 troops); minor Circassian losses

name: Battle of Udycz
commanders: Stanisław Żółkiewski vs. Khan Temir
importance: Hetman Stanisław Żółkiewski decisively defeated Khan Temir's invading Tatar horde near the Udych River
casualties: Heavy losses for Khan Temir's forces

name: Battle of Sudbischi
commanders: Devlet I Giray vs. Ivan Sheremetyev & Alexey Basmanov
importance: A heavily outnumbered Russian force under Ivan Sheremetyev and Alexey Basmanov successfully repelled multiple assaults from Devlet I Giray's massive Crimean-Ottoman army from a fortified wagon laager
casualties: Heavy Russian losses (~1,100 elite boyar children); extremely high Crimean-Ottoman losses

name: Raid and Battle of Gezlev
commanders: Zakhar Kulaga vs. Feti-Giray
importance: Zaporozhian Cossacks successfully sacked Gezlev (Yevpatoria), but were caught by Feti-Giray's fleet the next morning, resulting in Kulaga's death and capture of several Cossacks
casualties: ~30 Cossacks captured, including the death of ataman Zakhar Kulaga

name: Battle on the Dniester (1589)
commanders: Zaporozhian Cossacks vs. Ğazı Giray
importance: Cossacks intercepted returning Tatar forces from a Galician raiding expedition on the Dniester river
casualties: Heavy losses; ~9,000 Tatar raiders lost and Ğazı Giray wounded, alongside heavy Cossack casualties

name: Battle of Kalmius (1585)
commanders: Mykhailo Ruzhynsky and Jan Orishevsky vs. İslâm II Giray
importance: A multi-stage conflict where Zaporozhian Cossacks first repelled a Tatar invasion fleet at sea, followed by a counteroffensive that captured the strategic fortresses of Kalmius and Berda, seizing 40,000 horses and establishing permanent Cossack outposts in the region.
casualties: 3,000+ Tatars killed; heavy losses and capture of 40,000 horses

name: Battle of Karasubazar (1624)
commanders: Mehmed III Giray & Mykhailo Doroshenko vs. Topal Recep Pasha
importance: Ottoman invasion force landing at Kaffa was ambushed and defeated near Karasubazar by the combined Crimean-Cossack army, halting the attempt to depose Mehmed III Giray
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses; Hasan Pasha and Ibrahim Pasha killed

name: Battle of Kaffa
commanders: Petro Sahaidachny vs. Ottoman Empire Garrison
importance: A daring naval raid and surprise attack by Zaporizhian Cossacks under Petro Sahaidachny on the heavily fortified Crimean port city of Kaffa; the Cossacks defeated an Ottoman galley squadron, breached the citadel, and liberated thousands of Christian slaves
casualties: Heavy Ottoman garrison casualties and losses of captured ships

name: Raid on Tiahynka (1492)
commanders: Bohdan Glynsky vs. Ottoman-Tatar Forces
importance: First recorded campaign of the Zaporozhian Cossacks, involving a naval attack on an Ottoman-Tatar ship near Tiahyn.
casualties: Ottoman ship captured, commander and property seized, slaves freed

name: Cossack Raid on Istanbul (1615)
commanders: Petro Konashevych-Sahaidachnyi vs. Ahmed I, Hasan Pasha, Ali-Pasha
importance: Zaporozhian Cossacks on chaikas attacked the harbor of Istanbul, burned neighborhoods, and defeated the pursuing Ottoman fleet.
casualties: Enormous damage to the Ottoman fleet; heavy losses and high-ranking commanders captured

name: Cossack Raid on Perekop (1620)
commanders: Yakiv Borodavka-Neroda vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Conducted amidst deteriorating relations during the Polish-Ottoman conflict, leading to the complete looting of Varna and Perekop.

name: Cossack Raids on Istanbul (1624)
commanders: Mykhailo Doroshenko and Hryhoriy Chornyi vs. Murad IV and Damat Halil Pasha
importance: Multiple successive raids where Zaporozhian Cossacks bypassed defenses to plunder and burn Istanbul's suburbs and defeat the improvised Ottoman fleet.
casualties: Several captured; heavy losses to the Ottoman fleet

name: Cossack Raid on Istanbul (1629)
commanders: Bohdan Khmelnytsky and Ivan Sirko vs. Kskenash Pasha and Sultan Murad IV
importance: Cossacks reached the outskirts of Istanbul, plundered surrounding settlements, and successfully rescued besieged comrades before returning to the Sich.
casualties: 7 boats captured; significant damage to the Ottoman fleet with 2 galleys captured

name: Cossack Raid on Istanbul (1652)
commanders: Ivan Bogatyi vs. Mehmed IV and Melek Ahmed Pasha
importance: Don Cossacks launched a surprise raid on Istanbul's suburbs and successfully defeated an intervening Ottoman fleet on the return journey.
casualties: Light Cossack losses; many Ottomans killed and 150 captured

name: Cossack Raid on Sinop (1614)
commanders: Petro Konashevych-Sahaidachny vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: The first recorded Cossack raid into Anatolia, where the major city of Sinop was sacked, its castle captured, and galleys/arsenals destroyed.
casualties: Thousands killed; estimated 40 million gold pieces in damage, 18 boats sunk and 200 Cossacks killed

name: Battle of Tashiskari
commanders: Giorgi Saakadze & Zaza Tsitsishvili vs. Ottoman and Crimean Tatar forces
importance: Fought near Tashiskari; a Georgian force led by Giorgi Saakadze launched a surprise dawn attack and almost completely destroyed an invading Ottoman and Crimean Tatar army that had raided Kartli to capture King Luarsab II
casualties: Heavy Ottoman and Tatar losses; almost the entire invading force destroyed except for a small number who escaped

name: Battle of Köbölkút
commanders: Ádám Forgách vs. Fazıl Ahmed Pasha
importance: Fought near Köbölkút (modern Gbelce, Slovakia) during the Austro-Turkish War; an Ottoman army under Grand Vizier Fazıl Ahmed Pasha heavily defeated a Habsburg-Hungarian force under Ádám Forgách, enabling the Ottomans to capture the town and extensive territories in modern-day Slovakia
casualties: Heavy Habsburg/Hungarian losses (6,000 killed, 1,000 captured out of 8,000)

name: Battle at Jurjeve Stijene
commanders: Petar Zrinski vs. Ali-Pasha Čengić
importance: Fought in a canyon near Otočac during the Austro-Turkish War; Croatian forces under Petar Zrinski ambushed a larger Ottoman army under Ali-Pasha Čengić, inflicting heavy losses, capturing the Ottoman commander, and halting Ottoman advances into Gacka
casualties: 1,500–2,000 Ottoman killed and hundreds captured, including Ali-Pasha Čengić as a prisoner of war

name: First Battle of Novi Zrin
commanders: Miklós Zrínyi / Nikola Zrinski vs. Kanije Pasha
importance: Fought near the Novi Zrin fortress on the Mura river during the Austro-Turkish War; Croatian and Hungarian forces under Nikola Zrinski sortied from the fortress to rout Kanije Pasha's besieging army, subsequently pursuing and looting the enemy countryside

name: Battle of Vízvár
commanders: Miklós Zrínyi vs. Unknown Ottoman commander
importance: Fought at Vízvár in Csallóköz during the Austro-Turkish War; a 15,000-strong united Christian army including German regiments and led by Miklós Zrínyi ambushed and defeated the Turkish rearguard, capturing equipment, weapons, and livestock
casualties: 600 Turks killed, 20 POWs captured; Christian forces suffered only 12 casualties

name: Battle of Körmend
commanders: Franz III. Nádasdy, Jean de Coligny-Saligny & Wolfgang von Hohenlohe vs. Grand Vizier Ahmed Köprülü
importance: Fought along the Rába River during the Austro-Turkish War; a multinational Christian force successfully held the river fords against Grand Vizier Ahmed Köprülü's army, preventing an Ottoman crossing toward Vienna and setting the stage for the Christian victory at Saint Gotthard
casualties: Heavy Ottoman assault losses; French commander de Coligny wounded

name: Siege of Léva
commanders: Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches vs. Ali Pasha
importance: Fought near Léva (Levice, Slovakia) during the Austro-Turkish War; an Imperial army under Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches ambushed and routed an Ottoman relief force under Ali Pasha, resulting in the death of the Ottoman commander and the capture of artillery and weaponry
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses, including the death of commander Ali Pasha and abandonment of artillery and carts; light Habsburg casualties

name: Battle of Zsarnóca
commanders: Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches vs. Kücsük Mehmed Pasha
importance: Fought near Zsarnóca (Žarnovica, Slovakia) during the Austro-Turkish War; an Austrian force under Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches repelled and routed an Ottoman division led by Kücsük Mehmed Pasha, resulting in the death of the Ottoman commander and enabling a Habsburg offensive
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses, including the death of commander Kücsük Mehmed Pasha

name: Siege of Nitra
commanders: Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches & István Koháry vs. Ghazi Hussein & Kurd Mehmed Pasha
importance: Conducted during the Austro-Turkish War; an army under Jean-Louis Raduit de Souches besieged and recaptured the strategic fortress of Nitra from Ottoman forces after intensive artillery bombardment and a negotiated surrender
casualties: Garrison losses during sorties and bombardment; remaining Ottoman defenders granted free retreat

name: Siege of Kanizsa
commanders: Miklós Zrínyi, Wolfgang Julius von Hohenlohe & Pietro Strozzi vs. Sohrab Mehmed Pasha
importance: An unsuccessful month-long siege of the Ottoman fortress of Kanizsa by a combined Christian army led by Miklós Zrínyi; the siege was abandoned due to supply shortages, logistical delays, and the approach of the Grand Vizier's relief army, leading to a hurried Christian retreat
casualties: Unspecified losses during skirmishes and sallies; garrison successfully defended the fortress

name: Destruction of the Suleiman Bridge
commanders: Nikola VII Zrinski (Miklós Zrínyi) & Pál Esterházy vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: A major highlight of Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign during the Austro-Turkish War; Christian cavalry penetrated deep into Ottoman territory and successfully burned the vital 8-kilometer wooden bridge across the Drava River at Osijek, cutting Turkish supply lines
casualties: Minimal Christian losses; minor shelling casualties

name: Capture of Babócsa
commanders: Nikola VII Zrinski & Wolfgang Julius von Hohenlohe vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Fought shortly after the fall of Berzence during Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign; Christian forces successfully captured the strategic Ottoman-held stronghold of Babócsa, clearing the path for the rapid cavalry advance toward Szigetvár and Osijek

name: Capture of Berzence
commanders: Nikola VII Zrinski & Wolfgang Julius von Hohenlohe vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The initial objective of Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign; allied Christian forces captured the border fortress of Berzence in southwestern Hungary to establish a secure forward base of operations for the deeper push toward the Drava River

name: Siege of Pécs
commanders: Miklós Zrínyi & Wolfgang Julius von Hohenlohe vs. Kaplan Pasha
importance: Fought during Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign; Christian forces successfully sacked the lower city of Pécs but failed to capture the heavily defended citadel due to lack of heavy artillery and poor discipline, ultimately lifting the siege to destroy the Osijek bridge
casualties: Garrison losses during initial assault; heavy Christian losses during disorganized citadel assaults

name: Capture of Nádas
commanders: Independent Christian infantry detachments vs. Ottoman local garrison
importance: Captured during the secondary operations of the 1664 Winter Campaign as Christian forces systematically cleared minor Ottoman-held fortified points in the Danube-Drava confluence

name: Capture of Újvár
commanders: Independent Christian infantry detachments vs. Ottoman local garrison
importance: Secured as part of the wider Danubian offensive by detached Christian units during Miklós Zrínyi's 1664 Winter Campaign, helping clear Ottoman outposts from the area

name: Capture of Szekcső
commanders: Independent Christian infantry detachments vs. Ottoman local garrison
importance: Fought during the Winter Campaign of 1664; Christian troops captured the fortified settlement of Szekcső along the Danube to consolidate control over the region following the raid on the Osijek bridge

name: Capture of Szécs
commanders: Independent Christian infantry detachments vs. Ottoman local garrison
importance: Part of the Danube-Drava estuary operations during Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign; Christian forces occupied the stronghold of Szécs to neutralize local Ottoman resistance and sever regional communications

name: Danube-Drava Estuary Expedition
commanders: Independent Christian infantry units vs. Ottoman local garrisons
importance: Executed concurrently with the Osijek bridge raid during Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign; detached Christian infantry units pushed into the Danube-Drava confluence, successfully occupying and neutralizing the minor Ottoman fortresses of Mohács, Szécs, Szekcső, Újvár, and Nádas to secure the flanks
casualties: Minimal Christian losses; multiple minor Ottoman outposts captured or destroyed

name: Battle of Krasnobród
commanders: Jan Sobieski & Mykhailo Khanenko vs. Selim I Giray
importance: Fought during Jan Sobieski's autumn expedition in the Polish-Ottoman War; Polish and pro-Polish Cossack forces surprised a Tatar camp near Krasnobród after a grueling nocturnal march in heavy rain, destroying several Tatar units and freeing thousands of captive Polish civilians
casualties: Multiple Tatar units destroyed; civilian captives liberated

name: Battle of Niemirów
commanders: Jan III Sobieski vs. Jambet Giray (Azamet Gerej)
importance: Fought during Jan Sobieski's autumn expedition in the Polish-Ottoman War; Crown Hetman Sobieski launched a surprise front-and-rear attack on a large Crimean Tatar camp near Nemyriv, routing the invaders and liberating thousands of captured Polish nobility, peasants, women, and children
casualties: 100 Polish-Lithuanian casualties; 234 Tatars killed and 6,000 captured

name: Battle of Ladyzhyn
commanders: Mykhailo Khanenko & Karol Łużecki vs. Petro Doroshenko & Safa Giray
importance: Fought near Ladyzhyn during the Polish-Ottoman War (1672–76); a combined force of pro-Polish Cossacks and Polish-Lithuanian cavalry under Khanenko and Łużecki defeated an allied force of Crimean Tatars and pro-Doroshenko Cossacks
casualties: Heavy Polish losses during enemy counterattack, alongside opposing Tatar and Cossack casualties

name: Djidjelli Expedition
commanders: François de Vendôme (Duke of Beaufort), Count of Gadagne & Charles-Félix de Galéan vs. Kabyles & Regency of Algiers
importance: A military expedition launched by Louis XIV to seize Djidjelli as a naval base against Barbary corsairs; French forces easily captured the town initially, but internal command disputes, fierce local resistance, supply strains, and an outbreak of plague forced a complete abandonment and demolition of fortifications, followed by the tragic sinking of the returning ship La Lune
casualties: Heavy French losses through ambushes, plague, and over 700 drowned in the shipwreck of La Lune; substantial Kabyle and Algerian losses

name: Capture of Mohács
commanders: Independent Christian infantry detachments vs. Ottoman local garrison
importance: Executed during Miklós Zrínyi's Winter Campaign as detached Christian infantry units swept through the Danube-Drava region, capturing the strategically significant town and fortress of Mohács to secure the army's flank

name: Second Battle of Novi Zrin
commanders: Miklós Zrínyi & Péter Zrínyi vs. Ali Pasha
importance: Fought near the Novi Zrin fortress on the Mura river during the Austro-Turkish War; Hungarian and Croatian forces under Miklós and Péter Zrínyi decisively defeated a 16,000-strong Ottoman army, resulting in the death of Ottoman commander Ali Pasha
casualties: Heavy Ottoman casualties, including the death of commander Ali Pasha

name: Battle of Babadağ (1625)
commanders: Shahin Giray vs. Khan Temir
importance: Shahin Giray was defeated by Khan Temir's Budjak Horde following the collapse of the short-lived Zaporozhian-Crimean alliance
casualties: Heavy losses for Shahin Giray's forces

name: Battle of Kagal'nik (1646)
commanders: Semeon Romanovich Pozharskii vs. Nuraddin (Crimean Khanate)
importance: Russian force led by Pozharskii was defeated near Kagal'nik by a 10,000-strong Crimean army during the failed 1646 campaign
casualties: Heavy Russian losses and subsequent mass desertions due to hunger and demoralization

name: 1480 Sarai Raid
commanders: Vasili Nozdorovaty-Zvenigorodsky & Nur Devlet vs. Great Horde
importance: Joint Russo-Crimean raid on New Sarai while Akhmat Khan was engaged at the Ugra River, forcing his retreat and securing massive loot
casualties: Near-total destruction and capture of the Great Horde capital population/loot

name: Battle and Siege of Kalnyk
commanders: Jan III Sobieski & Mykhailo Khanenko vs. Petro Doroshenko & Tatar allies
result: Tactical Polish Victory / Strategic Cossack-Tatar Defense
importance: Crown Hetman Jan Sobieski defeated a relief force near Kalnyk but ultimately failed to capture the fortified town after a two-week siege
casualties: ~500 Tatar/Cossack troops killed in the relief clash; unknown siege losses

name: Battle of Pidhaitsi (1667)
commanders: John III Sobieski vs. Petro Doroshenko & Crimean Tatars
importance: Hetman John III Sobieski successfully defended against a massive combined Cossack-Tatar force, backed by Ivan Sirko's diversionary expedition into Crimea, leading to an armistice
casualties: Heavy casualties for the invading Tatar-Cossack forces

name: Ottoman-Crimean Invasion of Circassia (1479 Campaign)
commanders: Mengli I Giray & Cezeri Kasim Pasha vs. Peterzeqo & Tabuldu
importance: Crimean Tatars and Ottoman forces captured the strategic coastal fortresses of Anapa and Kopa, establishing early Ottoman influence in the North Caucasus
casualties: Numerous Circassians captured and enslaved; local forces scattered

name: Crimean Campaign against Circassia (1490–1491)
commanders: Mengli I Giray vs. Circassian Tribes
importance: Major campaign by Mengli I Giray launching a systematic series of subdual efforts against the Circassians and Kabardians
casualties: Significant enslavement and devastation in local territories

name: Siege of Perekop
commanders: Ivan Sirko, Grigory Kosagov, Stenka Razin, Erke Aturkay vs. Murad Giray, Karach Bey
result: Cossack-Russian-Kalmyk victory; sack and devastation of Perekop and surrounding settlements
importance: A major joint military campaign that successfully disrupted Crimean support for Poland-Lithuania during the Russo-Polish War, forcing the Khan to divert forces to defend Crimea and aiding the outcome of the siege of Hlukhiv.
casualties: Moderate losses in October; heavy Crimean/Ottoman losses with almost all defending troops killed in December

name: Siege of Ochakov (1670)
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Ottoman Empire
importance: Ivan Sirko successfully besieged and sacked Ochakov to undermine Ottoman control and demonstrate loyalty to Russia

name: 1st Raid on Ochakov (1600)
commanders: Zaporozhian Cossacks vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: An early 17th-century raid on the strategic fortress of Ochakov, marking a period of intensified Cossack aggression against Ottoman outposts.
casualties: Ottoman defensive losses; garrison successfully harassed

name: 3rd Raid on Ochakov (1660)
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Ottoman/Tatar forces
importance: Also known as the Ochakiv–Aslan campaign, this operation was launched by Ivan Sirko to preemptively disrupt a planned joint Ottoman-Crimean-Nogai invasion against the Cossack Hetmanate.
casualties: Heavy losses for Ottoman-Crimean forces; many captured and sold into slavery

name: Raid on Varna (1620)
commanders: Yakiv Borodavka-Neroda and Ivan Sirko vs. Mustafa I
importance: A coordinated campaign by Zaporozhian and Sloboda Cossacks following raids near Istanbul, resulting in the complete looting and devastation of Varna and Perekop.

name: Battle of Sich (1674)
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Mehmed IV & Selim I Giray
importance: Cossacks detected and repelled a surprise night assault by an Ottoman-Crimean army of 15,000 Janissaries and 40,000 Tatars sent to destroy the Sich

name: Wallachia Raid (1674)
commanders: Ivan Sirko and Andriy Murashko vs. Ottoman/Vassal forces
importance: A punitive raiding expedition into Wallachia conducted by Sirko's forces to disrupt Ottoman supply lines and political influence, prior to his defensive efforts at Ladyzhyn.
casualties: Significant property damage; Ottoman-allied regional forces suffered heavy losses

name: Tighina Raid (1674)
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: A strategic strike against the Ottoman fortress of Tighina (Bendery) aimed at undermining the Ottoman position in the Dniester region and signaling resistance against the expansion of Ottoman control into Right-bank Ukraine.
casualties: Ottoman garrison harassed; military stores captured or destroyed

name: Stand on the Sich (1679)
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Ottoman Empire & Crimean Khanate
importance: Joint Cossack-Russian defensive preparations successfully deterred and forced a 25,000-strong Ottoman-Tatar army to retreat from the Sich

name: Siege of Azov (1569)
commanders: Ottoman Fleet vs. Russian/Cossack Defenses
importance: Ottoman fleet besieging Azov was completely destroyed by a violent storm during the 1569 campaign
casualties: Entire Ottoman fleet lost to the storm

name: Pyatigorsk War / Expedition of the Great Horde
commanders: Sheikh Ahmed & Seid-Mahmud vs. Circassian Princes
importance: The Great Horde's campaign into Circassia and the Pyatigorye region collapsed due to famine, livestock loss, internal crisis, and Circassian resistance, forcing their withdrawal toward the Volga
casualties: Heavy losses in livestock, supplies, and strategic position for the Great Horde

name: Capture of Kołomyja
commanders: Mukha vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Rebel forces under Mukha captured the strategic town of Kołomyja during the peasant uprising in Pokuttia

name: Capture of Halicz
commanders: Mukha vs. Kingdom of Poland
importance: Rebel forces under Mukha successfully captured the fortified town of Halicz during the regional uprising

name: Campaign and Conquest of Pokuttia
commanders: Mukha vs. Polish-Lithuanian Crown Forces
importance: Extensive peasant and cossack campaign across the entire Pokuttia region, seizing control of major settlements including Kołomyja and Halicz
casualties: Heavy local noble losses and widespread property destruction

name: Battle of Ochakov (1630)
commanders: Kapudan Pasha vs. Taras Fedorovych
importance: A naval engagement during a Cossack expedition into the Black Sea where the Ottoman fleet intercepted and defeated the Zaporozhian forces near Ochakov.

name: Ochakov Campaign (1528)
commanders: Ostap Dashkevych & Przecław Lanckoroński vs. Crimean-Ottoman forces
importance: A 1,200-strong Polish-Cossack force successfully raided the Ochakov region, winning three consecutive engagements against Tatar detachments and capturing substantial loot
casualties: Heavy Tatar losses; 500 horses and 30,000 sheep captured

name: Capture of Nakhchivan
commanders: Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent vs. Safavid garrison
importance: Captured by Sultan Suleiman's main army during the campaign, resulting in the acquisition of thousands of captives and significant territorial coercion.

name: Conquest of Akhaltsikhe
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Safavid Regional Forces
importance: Ottoman forces invaded the Safavids' Caucasian territories through Ardahan and successfully captured Akhaltsikhe.

name: Siege and Capture of Tiflis
commanders: Lala Mustafa Pasha vs. Safavid / Kartli Forces
importance: Ottoman forces under Lala Mustafa Pasha captured Tiflis and forced Kartli to become a tributary vassal of the Ottoman Empire.

name: Conquest of Shirvan
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Safavid Empire
importance: The Ottomans captured Shirvan from the Safavids, securing operational control over almost all territories west of the Caspian Sea coast.

name: Conquest and Fortification of Faş (Farş) Castle
commanders: Admiral Ali Pasha vs. Regional Defenses
importance: Ottoman naval forces under Admiral Ali Pasha captured and heavily reinforced the Georgian fortress on the Black Sea coast.

name: Crimean Tatar Campaign & Counterattack in Shirvan
commanders: Adil Giray (Crimean Tatars) vs. Mirza Salman Jaberi & Hamza Mirza (Safavids)
importance: A large contingent of Crimean Tatars raided core parts of Armenia and Azerbaijan, but were met with a fierce Safavid counterattack, resulting in the defeat, capture, and execution of Adil Giray.
casualties: Heavy Crimean Tatar losses; commander Adil Giray executed

name: Invasion of Samtskhe-Saatabago
commanders: Lala Mustafa Pasha vs. Regional Forces
importance: Ottoman forces crossed the Georgian border into the Samtskhe principality to open the Caucasus theater.

name: Conquest and Division of Samtskhe
commanders: Lala Mustafa Pasha vs. Prince Manuchar II Jaqeli
importance: Following the surrender of castle keys by Prince Manuchar II Jaqeli, the Ottomans occupied Samtskhe and politically reorganized it into eight sanjaks.

name: Capture of Tbilisi / Kartli
commanders: Lala Mustafa Pasha vs. Safavid/Georgian Garrison
importance: The Ottomans captured the strategic Georgian capital of Tbilisi and subdued the Kingdom of Kartli.

name: Conquest of Sheki in Shirvan
commanders: Lala Mustafa Pasha & Alexander II of Kakheti vs. Safavids
importance: Ottoman troops, aided by Alexander II of Kakheti and his Georgian forces, conquered Sheki in Shirvan from the Safavids.

name: Siege of Shamakhi
commanders: Özdemiroğlu Osman Pasha vs. Safavid Counter-attackers
importance: Özdemiroğlu Osman Pasha successfully defended recent Ottoman conquests and inflicted a major defeat on counter-attacking Safavid forces.

name: Battle of Mollahasanli
commanders: Safavids vs. Özdemiroğlu Osman Pasha
importance: Safavid forces achieved a localized victory against the Ottomans, forcing Osman Pasha to temporarily regroup in Derbent.

name: Georgian Uprisings and Campaigns under Simon I
commanders: Simon I of Kartli vs. Ottoman Erzurum Army
importance: Simon I of Kartli led troops in sustained campaigns against the Ottoman Erzurum army, dismantling short-lived Ottoman dominance in parts of the region and restoring Safavid regional influence.
casualties: Significant military casualties on both sides

name: Defeat of the Ottoman-Crimean Tatar Force
commanders: Gazi Giray & Dal Mehmed Çelebi vs. Safavids
importance: A combined Ottoman-Crimean Tatar force was decisively defeated by the Safavids, forcing Özdemiroğlu Osman Pasha to leave a garrison at Baku and retreat to Derbent.

name: Safavid Harassment along the Caspian Shore
commanders: Piri Muhammed Beg & İmam Kulu Khan vs. Ottoman Retreating Forces
importance: Safavid forces relentlessly harassed the retreating Ottoman troops all along the Caspian shore up to the ramparts of Derbent.
casualties: Ottoman rearguard losses and logistical stress

name: Gazi Giray's Diversionary Foray & Capture
commanders: Gazi Giray vs. Safavid Forces
importance: Gazi Giray led a diversionary foray between Shabaran and Shamakhi; following betrayal by Abu Bakr Mirza's troops, Gazi Giray was captured and imprisoned in the castle of Alamut.
casualties: Tatar diversionary force defeated, commander captured

name: Invasion of Khorasan
commanders: Jalal Khan Uzbek vs. Mortaza Gholi Khan Parnak Turkaman
importance: Following unpaid annual tributes, Uzbek raiders invaded through Nesa, Abiward, and Mashhad, but were intercepted by Safavid Governor Mortaza Gholi Khan's 3,000-man Qizilbash and Qurchi force.

name: The Battle of Ashgabat / Jam Province
commanders: Safavid Qizilbash Army vs. Jalal Khan Uzbek
importance: Despite numerical superiority, Uzbek forces were heavily routed by the discipline and counter-charge of the Qizilbash army. Uzbek leader Jalal Khan was killed in action, forcing the surviving forces to retreat in disarray.
casualties: Heavy Uzbek losses; commander Jalal Khan killed

name: Capture and Destruction of Nahavand
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Shah Abbas I launched a surprise attack, recapturing Nahavand and thoroughly destroying its fortress to deny the Ottomans an advance staging base.

name: Capture of Tabriz
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: The Safavid army successfully captured Tabriz utilizing artillery; local citizens took harsh reprisals against the occupying Ottoman Turks.
casualties: Heavy occupying force and garrison casualties

name: Evacuation and Capture of Nakhchivan
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs. Ottoman Regional Forces
importance: The Safavids peacefully entered and occupied Nakhchivan immediately after it was evacuated by retreating Ottoman forces.

name: Siege of Yerevan
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs. Ottoman Garrison
result: Safavid capture of the Yerevan fortress
importance: The Safavid army laid a strategic and prolonged siege to the fortified city of Yerevan as part of Abbas I's major counter-offensive.

name: Capture of Tbilisi and Subjugation of Kartli and Kakheti
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs. Ottoman-Backed Regional Forces
importance: Safavid armies successfully captured Tbilisi, returning both the kingdoms of Kartli and Kakheti back to Safavid dependent status.

name: Safavid Capture of Yerevan
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: The Safavid army successfully captured Yerevan while the main Ottoman field army was still marching to the front.

name: Safavid Advance toward Kars and Akhaltsikhe
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs. Ottoman Defensive Forces
importance: Safavid forces advanced aggressively toward Kars before being checked and halted at Akhaltsikhe by Ottoman defensive deployments.

name: Battle near the Shore of Lake Urmia
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs. Cigalazade Yusuf Sinan Pasha
importance: The first major pitched victory for the Safavids against the Ottomans in history. Shah Abbas I utilized a masterclass in cavalry tactics to rout the Ottomans, forcing a chaotic retreat.
casualties: ~20,000 Ottoman dead; Ottoman Beylerbey Kose Sefer Pasha captured

name: Liberation of Shirvan
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs. Ottoman Regional Forces
importance: Following the total Ottoman operational collapse and the death of commander Sinan Pasha during the retreat, Shah Abbas I successfully liberated and recaptured the Shirvan province.
casualties: Ottoman regional units routed or expelled

name: Capture of Harput
commanders: Tavil Ahmed vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Taking advantage of the military vacuum on the eastern front during the Ottoman-Safavid War, rebel leader Tavil Ahmed captured the strategic city of Harput.

name: Revolt and Takeover of Baghdad
commanders: Mehmed (Tavil Ahmed's son) vs. Ottoman Authorities
importance: Tavil Ahmed’s son Mehmed successfully overthrew Ottoman authority and seized control of Baghdad.

name: Engagement against Nasuh Pasha
commanders: Mehmed (Rebel) vs. Nasuh Pasha
importance: Rebel forces under Mehmed decisively defeated the Ottoman field army led by Nasuh Pasha, who had been dispatched to restore imperial order in Iraq.

name: Ottoman Clearing of Baghdad
commanders: Imperial Ottoman Forces vs. Rebel Garrison
importance: Imperial forces re-entered and systematically cleared Baghdad of rebel control, restoring Ottoman authority in Mesopotamia.

name: Rebel Expansion in Lebanon and Syria
commanders: Fakhr-al-Din II & Canbulatoğlu Ali Pasha vs. Ottoman Authorities
importance: Fakhr-al-Din II extended his authority by aligning with rebel leader Canbulatoğlu Ali Pasha, directly challenging the Sultan's rule across Adana and the Levant.

name: Anatolian Suppression Campaigns
commanders: Grand Vizier Kuyucu Murad Pasha vs. Anatolian Rebels
importance: Grand Vizier Kuyucu Murad Pasha led brutal, large-scale military expeditions across Anatolia to crush the Jelali revolts, securing the empire's rear lines against the Safavids.
casualties: Tens of thousands of rebel casualties and executions

name: Standoff at Acıçay
commanders: Grand Vizier Kuyucu Murad Pasha vs. Shah Abbas I
importance: The opposing armies met at Acıçay (north of Tabriz) but avoided a set-piece battle due to extreme logistics, supply chain failures, and the approach of winter, forcing an Ottoman withdrawal.

name: Ambush in the Lake Urmia Region
commanders: Kuyucu Murad Pasha vs. Qizilbash Forces
importance: While retreating back toward Diyarbakır following the standoff at Acıçay, the withdrawing Ottoman forces were ambushed by Qizilbash troops in the Lake Urmia region.

name: Siege and Capture of Ganja
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Shah Abbas successfully besieged and captured Ganja as part of his major campaign to secure and reclaim Azerbaijan.

name: Siege of Shamakhi
commanders: Shah Abbas I & Allahverdi Khan vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: The capital of Shirvan was heavily besieged utilizing siege cannons brought from Ganja and bridge construction across the moat, culminating in a general assault that broke the fortress.

name: Ochakiv–Aslan Campaign (1660)
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Pasha of Silistra and Nurredin-Sultan
importance: Carried out by Zaporozhian-Don Cossacks before Easter in 1660 to preemptively disrupt a planned joint Ottoman-Crimean-Nogai invasion against the Cossack Hetmanate and Russia.
casualties: Heavy losses for Ottoman-Crimean forces; many captured and sold into slavery

name: Garrison Sally Operations at Shamakhi
commanders: Ottoman Garrison vs. Safavid Besieging Army
importance: The Ottoman garrison launched active sortie attacks from unguarded eastern and southern swampy wings, inflicting heavy losses on the besieging Iranian army.
casualties: Significant losses inflicted on the Safavid besiegers

name: Uprising and Capture of Baku
commanders: Local Baku Population vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Spurred by Shah Abbas's siege of Shamakhi, the local population and aristocracy revolted against Ottoman rule, stormed the garrison commander's palace, captured him, and beheaded the staff.

name: Battle of Kuialnyk (1672)
commanders: Ivan Sirko and Mykhailo Khanenko vs. Nurredin-Sultan and Murza Tenmambet
importance: Fought on the Kuialnyk river as Cossacks returned from a Wallachian campaign, resulting in the defeat of a combined Crimean-Budjak-Janissary force and the capture of Murza Tenmambet.
casualties: Heavy combat losses for Tatar-Turkish forces; enemy cannons exploded; key leaders captured

name: Sirko's Eastern Campaign - Budjak & Aq Kirmān (1673)
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Ottoman/Nogai forces
importance: A punitive campaign launched in response to Tatar cattle theft, beginning with the devastation of the Nogai Horde in Budjak and culminating in the siege, capture, and looting of the Ottoman fortress of Aq Kirmān (Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi).
casualties: Heavy devastation of Nogai and northern Ottoman borderlands; Aq Kirmān looted

name: Sirko's Eastern Campaign - Crimea (1673)
commanders: Ivan Sirko and Kalmyk allies vs. Selim I Giray
importance: A multi-pronged amphibious and land offensive taking advantage of a Crimean pandemic and Khan Selim I Giray's illness. Sirko captured Perekop, drove the Khan out of Bakhchysarai into the mountains, freed several thousand captives, and captured numerous Tatars, though Sirko's son Roman was killed in the fighting.
casualties: Khan driven from capital; several thousand captives freed; many Tatars captured

name: Uprising and Surrender of Derbent
commanders: Local Populace vs. Kiziroğlu Ahmet Pasha
importance: Local uprisings broke out against Turkish troops in Narinkale (Derbent), compelling castle commander Kiziroğlu Ahmet Pasha to surrender and hand over the keys directly to Shah Abbas.

name: Siege of Kızıkermen (September 1697)
commanders: Ali Pasha and Murtaza Pasha of Kaffa vs. Kızıkermen garrison
importance: Following the arrival of Ali Pasha and Murtaza Pasha on September 4, a heavy siege of Kızıkermen was launched. Despite destroying part of the wall on September 14 and attempting multiple storms, the Turks failed to capture the city and lifted the siege on September 28.

name: Siege of Erivan
commanders: Grand Vizier Öküz Mehmed Pasha vs. Shah Abbas I
importance: A sizable Ottoman army laid siege to Erivan, but Shah Abbas successfully harassed Ottoman supply lines, forcing Mehmed Pasha to lift the siege and retreat before winter, resulting in heavy losses from extreme cold.
casualties: Heavy Ottoman freezing and supply casualties

name: Halil Pasha's Invasion of Iran
commanders: Damat Halil Pasha vs. Qarachaqay Khan
importance: Damat Halil Pasha launched a new Ottoman invasion into Iran, aided by Tatar and Georgian warriors, marching toward the Azerbaijan province and Ardabil before concluding peace.

name: Safavid Scorched-Earth and Harassment Campaign
commanders: Qarachaqay Khan vs. Damat Halil Pasha
importance: Under commander-in-chief Qarachaqay Khan, Safavid forces executed a strict scorched-earth and harassing strategy, avoiding pitched battles to let winter starve and freeze out the invading Ottoman forces.
casualties: Ottoman starvation and winter exposure losses

name: Safavid Siege and Capture of Baghdad
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs. Ottoman Officer Bakr
importance: Following initial shifts in Ottoman local alliances, Safavid forces besieged Baghdad and captured it on January 14, 1624 (aided by Bakr's son Muhammad), followed by a massacre of Sunni inhabitants.
casualties: Garrison defeated; heavy Sunni civilian casualties

name: Battle of Karaharman (1625)
commanders: Kindrat Burliy vs. Topal Recep Pasha, Piyale-Uzun, Kapudan Abdi, and Janalem-Zade-Aga
importance: A major naval clash off the Karaharman coast where a combined Zaporozhian and Don Cossack fleet faced the Ottoman navy, resulting in one of the biggest defeats for the Cossack naval campaigns.
casualties: 780 Cossacks killed, 300 captured, and 270 chaikas lost; 200-300 killed on the Ottoman side

name: Crimean Campaign (1624)
commanders: Topal Recep and Canibek Giray vs. Mehmed III Giray, Shahin Giray, and Mykhailo Doroshenko
importance: An unsuccessful Ottoman military expedition to depose Mehmed III Giray in favor of Canibek Giray, thwarted near Karasubazar by combined Crimean cavalry and Zaporozhian Cossacks.
casualties: Ottoman commanders Hasan Pasha and Ibrahim Pasha killed; army forced to retreat and negotiate

name: Cossack Raid on Northern Anatolia (1616)
commanders: Petro Konashevych-Sahaidachny vs. Chikala Pasha and Ibrahim Pasha
importance: A large-scale campaign led by Sahaidachny across the Black Sea against major Ottoman ports in northern Anatolia, including Trebizond and Sinop, followed by strikes near Istanbul and a victorious clash on the return route.
casualties: Thousands killed in Istanbul and surrounding areas; Ottoman fleet suffered multiple ship losses including 3 large vessels at Sinop and the loss of Admiral Ibrahim Pasha

name: Battles of Ladyzhyn (1674)
commanders: Anastas Dmytriiv, Andriy Murashko, and Vojca Serbin vs. Kara Mustafa Pasha
importance: Two successive engagements over Ladyzhyn in Right-bank Ukraine. Cossacks initially won the first battle on July 31, but grand vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha besieged and captured the city in the second battle, leading to its total destruction.
casualties: Over 20,000 casualties; entire civilian population killed or taken captive

name: 1st Cossack Raid on Trebizond (1613)
commanders: Zaporozhian Cossacks vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: An early major maritime expedition across the Black Sea by Zaporozhian Cossacks targeting the northern Anatolian coast, successfully raiding and plundering Trebizond.
casualties: Widespread damage to Ottoman fortifications and civilian losses

name: 2nd Cossack Raid on Trebizond (1616)
commanders: Petro Konashevych-Sahaidachny vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Part of Sahaidachny's large-scale 1616 Anatolian campaign, where Cossacks took the city completely by surprise, burning Ottoman galleys nearby before moving on to Sinop and Istanbul.
casualties: Ottoman garrison defeated, coastal defense assets and ships destroyed

name: Cossack Raid on Kiliia (1602)
commanders: Petro Sahaidachny vs. Hasan-aga
importance: One of the early 17th-century Cossack maritime raids where a fleet of 30 chaykas defeated the local Ottoman fleet, plundered Kiliia, and captured multiple ships in the Danube/Dniester region.
casualties: Ottoman fleet defeated; 1 galley and several merchant ships captured

name: Ottoman-Portuguese Coalition vs. Safavids at Basra
commanders: Ottoman Pasha of Basra & Portuguese Allies vs. Imam Quli Khan
importance: The Ottoman pasha of Basra formed an alliance with Portuguese forces against a pressing Safavid army led by Imam Quli Khan, inflicting a severe defeat and forcing the Persians to retreat from Basra.

name: Safavid Conquest of Iraq
commanders: Shah Abbas I vs. Ottoman Regional Garrisons
importance: Following the fall of Baghdad, Persian forces swept across and captured most of Iraq, extending control to Kirkuk, Mosul, Najaf, and Karbala.

name: Ottoman Siege of Baghdad
commanders: Grand Vizier Hafız Ahmed Pasha vs. Safavid Garrison
result: Safavid Victory / Ottoman Lift of Siege
importance: Grand Vizier Hafız Ahmed Pasha invested Baghdad on three sides. After Persian relief forces arrived and cut supply lines, the Ottomans suffered heavy losses in a desperate attack and withdrew to Mosul.
casualties: Heavy Ottoman attacking and supply casualties

name: Battle at Mahidasht
commanders: Grand Vizier Gazi Hüsrev Pasha vs. Zainal Khan Begdeli Shamlu
importance: Grand Vizier Gazi Hüsrev Pasha invaded Persia proper and decisively routed the Persian forces under Zainal Khan in a pitched battle at Mahidasht near Kermanshah, followed by the sacking of Hamadan.

name: Ottoman Siege of Baghdad
commanders: Gazi Hüsrev Pasha vs. Safavid Garrison
importance: Hüsrev Pasha laid siege to Baghdad in November 1630 but had to lift it quickly due to the looming threat of a severe winter cutting communication and supply lines.

name: Safavid Suppression of Georgian Kingdoms
commanders: Rustam Khan vs. King Teimuraz
importance: Rustam Khan was dispatched by the Shah to subdue the defiant Georgian kingdoms of Kartli and Kakheti; King Teimuraz was defeated and forced to flee to Imereti.

name: Murad IV’s Campaign of Yerevan and Tabriz
commanders: Sultan Murad IV vs. Safavid Defenders
importance: Sultan Murad IV personally led an imperial army, capturing Yerevan (Revan) on August 8, 1635, and subsequently plundering Tabriz on September 11, 1635.
casualties: Safavid garrisons defeated and strongholds captured

name: Safavid Counter-offensive and Retaking of Yerevan
commanders: Shah Safi vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: In the spring of 1636, Shah Safi successfully counter-attacked, defeating the regional Ottoman army and retaking Yerevan.

name: Battle of Ponza
commanders: Ottoman Fleet & Gabriel de Luetz vs. Andrea Doria (Genoa)
importance: An Ottoman fleet accompanied by French ambassador Gabriel de Luetz successfully defeated a Genoese fleet commanded by Andrea Doria.
casualties: Genoese fleet defeated and ships captured

name: Raids on Naples, Sicily, and Elba
commanders: Turgut Reis, Koja Sinan & Baron Paulin de la Garde
importance: Ottoman admirals Turgut and Koja Sinan, alongside a French squadron under Baron Paulin de la Garde, raided the coasts of Naples, Sicily, and Elba before heading toward Corsica.

name: Capture of Bastia
commanders: Franco-Ottoman Allied Forces & Corsican Exiles vs. Genoese Garrison
importance: Franco-Ottoman and Corsican exile forces successfully captured Bastia as part of the opening campaign of the Invasion of Corsica.

name: Siege and Capture of Saint-Florent
commanders: Paulin de la Garde & French Forces vs. Genoese Garrison
importance: Paulin de la Garde and French forces arrived in front of Saint-Florent and swiftly captured it, establishing a firm allied foothold on the island.

name: Capture of Bonifacio
commanders: Franco-Ottoman Allied Forces vs. Genoese Garrison
importance: Allied forces successfully captured the strategic southern town of Bonifacio during the initial 1553 invasion wave.

name: Siege of Saint-Florent (Genoese Counter-Attack)
commanders: Andrea Doria (Genoa) vs. Franco-Ottoman Defenders
importance: Andrea Doria led a massive Genoese force of 15,000 men to begin recapturing the island, launching a major counter-offensive starting with the siege of Saint-Florent.
casualties: Heavy combat losses on both sides

name: Siege of Calvi
commanders: Genoese/French Forces vs. Local Garrisons
importance: During the later phase surrounding the siege of Calvi, the Turkish fleet stood by and contributed little due to shifting strategic priorities.

name: Siege and Retaking of Bastia
commanders: Genoese Forces vs. Allied Forces
importance: The Genoese forces succeeded in retaking Bastia while the Turkish fleet maintained a stance of strategic inactivity.

name: Aden Revolt and Recapture
commanders: Piri Reis vs. Ali bin Suleyman al-Tawlaki & Portuguese Allies
importance: Following a local uprising and submission of Aden to the Portuguese by rebel leaders, Admiral Piri Reis led an Ottoman fleet of 60 ships to crush the revolt, defeating local and Portuguese-backed forces and recapturing the city on February 26, 1548.
casualties: Rebel forces routed; local leader killed in combat

name: Siege of Malacca (First)
commanders: Aceh-Kalinyamat Sultanate (Ottoman-backed) & Johor Sultanate vs. Portuguese Malacca
importance: Ottomans supplied cannoneers and mercenaries to the Aceh alliance in the East Indies theater

name: Siege of Malacca (Renewed)
commanders: Aceh Sultanate (Ottoman-backed) vs. Portuguese Malacca
importance: Continued Ottoman-Acehnese pressure on Portuguese Malacca as part of a broader Anti-Portuguese League project

name: Siege of Nice
commanders: Franco-Ottoman alliance (Barbarossa) vs. Duchy of Savoy
importance: Part of the Ottoman fleet's operations in the Western Mediterranean during the Italian Wars

name: Ottoman Wintering in Toulon
commanders: Hayreddin Barbarossa
importance: Ottoman fleet used the French port as a base while devastating Spanish-allied Italian coasts

name: Expedition to Mostaganem (Count Alcaudete, 1543)
commanders: Count Alcaudete (Spain) vs. Ottoman-Algerian forces
importance: Failed Spanish attempt to strike Ottoman Algeria from Oran

name: Spanish Expeditionary Force in Hungary (Tercio Viejo de Nápoles)
commanders: Bernardo de Aldana & Giovanni Battista Castaldo vs. Northern Hungarian oligarchs, Transylvanians, Ottomans
importance: Fought in Transdanubia; suppressed robber knights, rebuilt Szolnok, briefly occupied Transylvania (1551-1556)

name: Occupation of Ottoman Transylvania
commanders: Spanish-Habsburg forces vs. John Sigismund Zápolya
importance: Briefly deposed John Sigismund Zápolya from the Transylvanian throne

name: Capture of Mahdia
commanders: Spanish fleet vs. Ottoman-Tunisian defenders
importance: Captured Ottoman fortress in Tunisia, later evacuated in 1553

name: Capture of Muscat
commanders: Piri Reis & Seydi Ali Reis vs. João de Lisboa (Portuguese Empire)
importance: An Ottoman fleet under Piri Reis attacked and captured Old Muscat from the Portuguese, serving as part of the Ottoman campaign against Hormuz and reinforcing regional control in the northwestern Indian Ocean.

name: Siege of Hormuz
commanders: Piri Reis vs. Portuguese Garrison
importance: Following the capture of Muscat, Piri Reis's Ottoman fleet moved on to lay siege to the heavily fortified Portuguese stronghold of Hormuz. After a short investment, the Ottomans found the fortress too strong to take without heavy reinforcements and soon withdrew.
casualties: Ottoman and Portuguese skirmishing losses; tactical stalemate

name: Battle of the Strait of Hormuz
commanders: Murat Reis vs. Dom Diogo de Noronha (Portuguese Empire)
importance: An Ottoman fleet attempting to transfer galleys from Basra to the Red Sea was intercepted by a Portuguese fleet in the Strait of Hormuz; despite skilled maneuvering and fierce bombardment, the Turks were forced to disengage and retreat back to Basra.
casualties: Few casualties; minor ship damage on both sides

name: Battle of the Gulf of Oman
commanders: Seydi Ali Reis vs. Dom Fernando de Meneses & Dom Antão de Noronha
importance: A catastrophic naval defeat for the Ottoman Indian fleet under Seydi Ali Reis against a large Portuguese armada, resulting in the total loss of all Ottoman galleys and a major setback for Ottoman naval ambitions in the Indian Ocean.
casualties: All 15 Ottoman galleys captured or destroyed; heavy personnel losses

name: Siege of Bahrain
commanders: Mustafa Pasha vs. Dom António de Noronha, Álvaro da Silveira & Morad Shah
importance: Mustafa Pasha, governor of the Lahsa Eyalet, attempted to seize Bahrain and its pearl trade from the Portuguese and Kingdom of Hormuz. After Portuguese naval reinforcements under Álvaro da Silveira trapped the Ottoman fleet, prolonged skirmishing, and a severe outbreak of plague, the trapped Ottoman forces surrendered, negotiated a ransom, and withdrew on November 6, 1559.
casualties: Heavy losses on both sides due to combat and plague; Ottoman forces forced to pay ransom and relinquish weapons

name: Battle of Kamaran
commanders: Sefer Reis vs. Portuguese Squadron Commanders
importance: A Portuguese squadron was ambushed and defeated off the coast of Kamaran by four Ottoman galleys under Sefer Reis, who utilized a disguised ship decoy to successfully seize two Portuguese vessels.
casualties: Two Portuguese ships captured/destroyed with total personnel losses; two ships fled to India

name: Defense of Mocha
commanders: Sefer Reis vs. Alvaro da Sylveira (Portuguese Empire)
importance: A Portuguese fleet under Alvaro da Sylveira launched a direct attack against Sefer Reis's base in Mocha. Warned of their approach, Sefer Reis met the attackers with a heavy land and naval artillery bombardment that damaged Portuguese ships and forced a retreat.
casualties: Several Portuguese ships damaged and a dozen sailors killed; tactical Ottoman success

name: Battle of Bab el-Mandeb
commanders: Sefer Reis vs. Luiz Figueira (Portuguese Empire)
importance: A punitive Portuguese expedition under Luiz Figueira was ambushed and decisively defeated near Bab el-Mandab by Ottoman corsair Sefer Reis. Figueira's flagship fusta was overrun, the commander was killed, and his men were captured, forcing the remaining Portuguese sailing ships to flee.
casualties: Portuguese commander Luiz Figueira killed, entire fusta crew captured; escort ships forced to retreat

name: Battle of Punnaikayal
commanders: Irapali (Ali), Seydi Ali Reis & Piri Reis vs. Captain Manoel Rodrigues Coutinho
importance: A joint coalition of Ottoman naval forces, Calicut Muslim fleets, Vijayanagara troops under Vitthala, and Madurai forces under Vishwanatha Nayak attacked Punnaikayal, the capital of Portuguese settlements on the Coromandel Coast. After fierce resistance, the outnumbered garrison was overrun and captured, ending Portuguese dominance over the local pearl fisheries.
casualties: Portuguese garrison captured, churches destroyed, and heavy prisoner losses

name: Battle at Diu
commanders: Sefer Reis vs. Balthazar Lobato (Portuguese Empire)
importance: Following the Ottoman defeat in the Gulf of Oman, corsair Sefer Reis sailed with four light galiots to Diu, where he established a blockade, captured and looted four heavy merchant vessels carrying 160,000 cruzados, suppressed a captive crew revolt, and successfully returned to Mocha with nine ships.
casualties: Four Portuguese merchant vessels captured, retaken, and recaptured; crew casualties during the skirmishes

name: Battle of the Bay of Velez
commanders: Salah Reis vs. Inácio Nunes Gato (Portuguese Empire)
importance: An Algerian-Ottoman fleet under Salah Reis ambushed and captured a Portuguese squadron transporting the Wattasid claimant Abu Hassan in the bay of Vélez, successfully securing the capture of the entire flotilla, its commander, and the claimant.
casualties: Entire Portuguese squadron captured (including commander Inácio Nunes Gato and Abu Hassan)

name: Plunder of Pula and Invasion of Vieste
commanders: Ottoman fleet vs. Kingdom of Naples
importance: Continued Ottoman coastal pressure on Spanish Italy

name: Bombardment of Tuscany and Invasion of Orbetello
commanders: Ottoman fleet vs. Republic of Florence
importance: Ottoman fleet failed to meet the French fleet for a planned joint operation on Corsica and withdrew

name: Battle of Taza
commanders: Salah Reis vs. Mohammed al-Shaykh (Saadi Sultanate)
importance: Salah Reis led a daring night attack with a small force against the massive Saadian camp outside Taza. The sudden detonations and swift maneuver routed Mohammed al-Shaykh's 40,000-strong army, leading to the capture and garrisoning of Taza.
casualties: Heavy rout and panic among Saadian forces; unknown exact numbers

name: Battle of Qudyat-al-Mahali
commanders: Salah Reis vs. Saadi Sultanate (Mohammed al-Shaykh)
importance: Following the victory at Taza, Salah Reis advanced on Fez and decisively defeated the Moroccan Saadi forces at Qudyat-al-Mahali in the suburbs of Fez, solidifying allied control and establishing the Wattasid ruler Abu Hassan in the city.
casualties: Saadi forces routed; heavy casualties among Moroccan troops

name: Siege of Qatif
commanders: Dom António de Noronha vs. Ottoman Garrison (Mirmaxet & Rax Xarafo)
importance: A Portuguese armada and Hormuzi auxiliary force led by Dom António de Noronha besieged the Ottoman-held fort at Qatif. After an eight-day bombardment, the Ottoman garrison attempted to flee under the cover of night, and the fort was subsequently demolished by the Portuguese.
casualties: Light casualties during bombardment; escaping Ottoman garrison pursued and killed

name: Second Siege of Diu
commanders: João de Mascarenhas & João de Castro vs. Khoja Zufar & Ottoman-Gujarati Forces
importance: A joint Ottoman-Gujarati force besieged the Portuguese garrison at Diu for nearly seven months. The prolonged siege was broken when a Portuguese relief fleet under Governor João de Castro arrived and routed the attackers, killing general Khoja Zufar and securing Portuguese dominance.
casualties: Heavy casualties; ~3,000 allied forces killed and 600 prisoners; over 200 Portuguese casualties

name: Battle of Wofla
commanders: Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi vs. Cristóvão da Gama
importance: Imam Ahmad crushed the Portuguese expeditionary force, killing most of its men, capturing their firearms, and capturing and executing Portuguese leader Cristóvão da Gama.

name: Engagement in Wogera
commanders: Gelawdewos & Portuguese Allies vs. Sayid Mehmed
importance: Allied Ethiopian and Portuguese forces defeated a group of cavalry and infantry led by the Imam's lieutenant, Sayid Mehmed, in Wogera, killing him and paving the way for the decisive confrontation.
casualties: Adal forces routed; lieutenant Sayid Mehmed killed

name: Battle of Wayna Daga
commanders: Gelawdewos & Portuguese Allies vs. Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi
importance: The large-scale, decisive final battle near Lake Tana where combined Ethiopian and Portuguese forces utterly routed the Adal-Ottoman army. Imam Ahmad was killed, breaking Adal-Ottoman dominance in the region.
casualties: Extensive Adal-Ottoman casualties; over half the army killed or captured, including 160 Ottoman arquebusiers; light Portuguese losses

name: Battle of Jarte
commanders: Cristóvão da Gama & Seble Wongel vs. Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi
importance: Fought over nearly two weeks, the outnumbered Portuguese expeditionary force and Ethiopian allies under Cristóvão da Gama decisively defeated the Adal-Ottoman army, wounding Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi and forcing his forces to retreat.
casualties: Heavy Adal-Ottoman casualties (~300 killed, several captains and Turks); light Portuguese-Ethiopian losses (11 killed, 50 wounded)

name: Fall of Agadir
commanders: Saadi Morocco vs. Portuguese garrison
importance: Portugal expelled from Agadir; led to evacuation of Azemmour and Safi and consolidation at Mazagão

name: Battle of Baçente
commanders: Cristóvão da Gama (Portugal) vs. Adal-Ottoman forces
