importance: Early victory of the Portuguese expeditionary corps aiding Emperor Gelawdewos of Ethiopia

name: Battle of Suez
commanders: Estêvão da Gama & Cristóvão da Gama vs. Davud Pasha
importance: A Portuguese fleet under Estêvão da Gama penetrated the Red Sea and attempted a surprise attack on Suez with light oar vessels; however, heavy Ottoman defenses, fortifications, and artillery under Davud Pasha repelled the assault, forcing a Portuguese retreat.
casualties: Unknown exact losses; Portuguese forces repulsed and forced to withdraw

name: Battle of El Tor
commanders: Dom Estevão da Gama & Dom Cristóvão da Gama vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Portuguese forces under Dom Estevão da Gama and Dom Cristóvão da Gama attacked and captured the port city of El Tor on the Sinai Peninsula from Ottoman forces. At the request of local monks, the city was spared from plunder, followed by a famous knighting ceremony at the foot of Mount Sinai.
casualties: Over 20 Ottoman dead; minimal Portuguese casualties (3 wounded)

name: Battle of Suakin
commanders: Dom Estêvão da Gama & Dom Cristóvão da Gama vs. Ottoman Garrison & Ruler of Suakin
importance: A Portuguese armada under Governor Dom Estêvão da Gama attacked, sacked, and razed the prosperous Ottoman-held Red Sea port city of Suakin, after surprising and routing the defending forces and camp on the mainland.
casualties: Heavy casualties and complete destruction of the Ottoman camp and city structures; rich spoils and hostages captured by the Portuguese

name: Defense of Algiers
commanders: Hasan Agha vs. Holy Roman Emperor Charles V
importance: Hasan Agha successfully repelled a massive naval and land attack led by Emperor Charles V, a major victory that local populations saw as a divine mandate for Ottoman rule.
casualties: Heavy Spanish/Imperial fleet and troop losses due to storms and combat

name: Subjugation of Kuku, Biskra, and Tlemcen
commanders: Hasan Agha vs. Local Rulers
importance: Hasan Agha extended Ottoman-Algerian dominion eastward by subjugating Kuku, extending rule southward to Biskra, and securing Tlemcen's allegiance in the west.

name: Battle of Chelif Valley
commanders: Hasan Corso vs. Saadian Morocco
importance: Hasan Corso decisively defeated a 30,000-strong Saadian Moroccan army invading Tlemcen, effectively removing them from the region and ending the Zayyanid dynasty.
casualties: Heavy Saadian casualties and complete rout

name: Capture of Tenes and Tlemcen
commanders: Oruç Reis vs. Local Rulers & Spanish Forces
importance: Oruç Reis successfully captured Tenes and Tlemcen, expanding his control and influence in North Africa

name: Spanish Counter-Attack and Death of Oruç Reis
commanders: Garcia de Tineo vs. Oruç Reis
importance: A Spanish counter-attack resulted in the defeat and death of Oruç Reis while he was besieged in Tlemcen
casualties: Heavy corsair losses, including the death of Oruç Reis

name: Selman Reis's Expedition into Interior Yemen
commanders: Selman Reis vs. Local Yemeni Forces
importance: An Ottoman military expedition led by Selman Reis successfully penetrated and asserted control over the interior regions of Yemen

name: Capture of Monastir
commanders: Corsair Forces vs. Local Garrison
importance: Corsair naval forces successfully captured the Tunisian coastal town of Monastir, consolidating Ottoman and corsair control over North African ports

name: Capture of Sousse
commanders: Corsair Forces vs. Local Garrison
importance: Corsair naval forces successfully captured the strategic Tunisian port city of Sousse, expanding regional control

name: Capture of Hammamet
commanders: Corsair Forces vs. Local Garrison
importance: Corsair naval forces captured the coastal town of Hammamet as part of their campaign along the Tunisian shoreline

name: Capture of Kelibia
commanders: Corsair Forces vs. Local Garrison
importance: Corsair naval forces captured the fortified town and harbor of Kelibia, completing their consolidation of key Tunisian coastal strongpoints

name: Algiers Naval Expedition (Charles V)
commanders: Charles V vs. Hassan Agha
importance: A massive Habsburg armada led by Emperor Charles V to capture Algiers was completely destroyed by a catastrophic storm and fierce defense, resulting in a disastrous retreat
casualties: Thousands of soldiers and sailors drowned, killed, or captured; dozens of ships lost

name: Spanish Expedition to Tlemcen
commanders: Spanish Forces vs. Zayyanid-Ottoman Forces
importance: A subsequent Spanish military expedition into the interior of Tlemcen failed to establish permanent control against local and Ottoman-backed resistance

name: Battle of Alborán
commanders: Bernardino de Mendoza vs. Corsair Fleet
importance: A Spanish naval squadron intercepted and defeated a corsair fleet returning from a raid on Gibraltar near Alborán Island
casualties: Heavy corsair losses and capture of corsair ships

name: Battle of Girolata
commanders: Giannettino Doria vs. Dragut
importance: Genoese forces caught and defeated the notorious corsair commander Dragut (Turgut Reis) in the Gulf of Girolata, capturing him and his ships
casualties: Corsair fleet captured; Dragut imprisoned as a galley slave

name: Recapture of Castelnuovo (Herceg Novi)
commanders: Hayreddin Barbarossa & Ulamen vs. Francisco de Sarmiento
importance: Ottoman forces recaptured Castelnuovo after a brutal siege, destroying the Spanish tercio garrison and ending Holy League footholds in the region
casualties: Almost all 3,500+ Spanish defenders killed; ~8,000 Ottoman casualties

name: Ottoman Invasion of Gibraltar
commanders: Corsair Raiders vs. Spanish Garrison
importance: Corsairs raided Gibraltar, capturing loot and hostages before being intercepted and defeated as they attempted to withdraw

name: Ottoman Invasion of Apulia
commanders: Hayreddin Barbarossa vs. Neapolitan/Papal Forces
importance: An Ottoman fleet raided the coast of Apulia, sacking towns and terrorizing southern Italy during the opening phase of the Ottoman-Venetian War

name: Barbarossa's Invasion of Minorca
commanders: Hayreddin Barbarossa vs. Spanish Local Defense
importance: Following the loss of Tunis, Barbarossa raided and devastated Minorca, capturing Mahón and taking numerous captives

name: Spanish Attack on Tlemcen
commanders: Spanish Forces vs. Zayyanid-Corsair Forces
importance: A Spanish military expedition aiming to take Tlemcen was successfully repelled by local and corsair defenders

name: Ottoman Conquest of Tunis
commanders: Hayreddin Barbarossa vs. Muley Hassan
importance: Hayreddin Barbarossa captured Tunis from the Hafsid ruler Muley Hassan, establishing direct Ottoman naval and political dominance in the region

name: Recapture of Koroni
commanders: Hayreddin Barbarossa vs. Spanish Garrison
importance: Ottoman forces under Barbarossa recaptured the strategic fortress of Koroni from the Spanish

name: Cherchell Campaign
commanders: Andrea Doria vs. Corsair Forces
importance: A Spanish naval and land expedition against the corsair stronghold of Cherchell was repelled with heavy losses

name: Siege of Agadir
commanders: Saadi Dynasty vs. Portuguese Garrison
importance: Saadi forces captured the fortress of Agadir, pushing back Portuguese presence in southern Morocco

name: Destruction of Spanish Relief Fleet
commanders: Ottoman-Corsair Forces vs. Spanish Fleet
importance: A Spanish relief fleet of 10 ships sent to North Africa was intercepted and destroyed by corsair forces
casualties: 10 Spanish ships destroyed and crews captured/killed

name: Touggourt and Ouargla Expedition
commanders: Salah Reis vs. Berber Principalities
importance: Beylerbey Salah Reis expanded Algerian rule deep into the Sahara, turning the Berber principalities of Touggourt and Ouargla into tributaries.

name: Capture of Fez
commanders: Salah Reis vs. Saadian Sultanate
importance: Responding to Spanish-allied Saadian attacks, Salah Reis marched all the way to Fez, capturing the city and installing Abu Hassun as an Ottoman vassal.

name: Turkish-French Raid on Piombino (1555)
commanders: Piyale Pasha & Turgut Reis (Ottoman) & French forces
importance: Part of continued coastal devastation of Calabria, Tuscany, Corsica and Liguria

name: Capture of Béjaïa
commanders: Salih Reis (Ottoman-Algeria) vs. Spanish garrison (Alonso Peralta)
importance: One of the last Spanish bases in North Africa lost; commander Alonso Peralta executed in Valladolid for surrendering

name: Peace of Augsburg
commanders: Holy Roman Empire (Catholic and Lutheran princes)
importance: Established cuius regio, eius religio; occurred amid Charles V's exhaustion from Ottoman wars, contributing to his abdication

name: Invasion and Landing at Cariati
commanders: Turgut Reis & Piyale Pasha (Ottoman, 60 ships) vs. Kingdom of Naples
importance: Preceded the conquest of Bizerte in the same campaign season

name: Conquest of Bizerte
commanders: Turgut Reis & Piyale Pasha vs. Spanish garrison
importance: Recaptured territory held by Spain since 1534

name: Franco-Ottoman Raid on Reggio and Calabria
commanders: Turgut Reis, Gabriel de Luetz d'Aramon vs. Spanish authorities
importance: Joint naval raids devastated Spanish possessions in southern Italy and demonstrated the effectiveness of the Franco-Ottoman alliance.

name: Invasion of Reggio Calabria
commanders: Turgut Reis & Piyale Pasha vs. Local Garrisons
importance: An Ottoman naval force under Turgut Reis and Piyale Pasha successfully invaded and plundered Reggio Calabria as part of a major Western Mediterranean campaign

name: Plunder of the Lipari Islands
commanders: Turgut Reis & Piyale Pasha vs. Local Garrisons
importance: The Ottoman fleet subjected the Lipari Islands to extensive plunder and devastation during their 1558 Western Mediterranean expedition
casualties: Heavy local losses and capture of numerous inhabitants

name: Capture of Massa Lubrense
commanders: Turgut Reis & Piyale Pasha vs. Local Defenders
importance: Ottoman naval forces under Turgut Reis and Piyale Pasha captured Massa Lubrense as part of their 1558 raiding campaign along the Kingdom of Naples coast

name: Capture of Cantone
commanders: Turgut Reis & Piyale Pasha vs. Local Defenders
importance: Cantone was captured and plundered by the Ottoman fleet during the 1558 Mediterranean expedition

name: Capture of Sorrento
commanders: Turgut Reis & Piyale Pasha vs. Amalfi Coast defenders
importance: The coastal city of Sorrento was successfully attacked and captured during the extensive 1558 Ottoman raids along the Neapolitan coast
casualties: Heavy local losses and widespread destruction

name: Bombardment of Piombino (1558)
commanders: Ottoman fleet
importance: Continuation of the same year's Tuscan coast campaign

name: Defeat of Knights of Malta Fleet off Malta (1558)
commanders: Ottoman fleet vs. Knights of Malta
importance: Cleared the way for the Ottoman fleet to head to the Balearic Islands

name: Capture of Ciutadella
commanders: Turgut Reis & Piyale Pasha vs. Minorcan defenders
importance: Captured the capital of Minorca after an eight-day siege

name: Battle of Tadla
commanders: Mohammed ash-Sheikh (Saadi dynasty) vs. Ali Abu Hassun (Wattasid dynasty, Ottoman-backed)
importance: Ali Abu Hassun, who had reconquered Fez earlier that year with Ottoman help under Salah Rais before the Turkish troops withdrew, was vanquished and killed by the Saadians, permanently ending the Wattasid dynasty; Mohammed ash-Sheikh subsequently entered Fez on 13 September 1554 and became the undisputed ruler of Morocco, establishing the Saadian dynasty as the country's sole ruling power
casualties: Ali Abu Hassun killed, ending the Wattasid line; broader troop losses not specified in source

name: Assassination of Mohammed ash-Sheikh
commanders: Ottoman Empire (assassin named Sahil) vs. Mohammed ash-Sheikh (Saadi dynasty)
importance: Ottoman retaliation for the loss of their Wattasid client state at Tadla; the Saadi ruler was killed by an axe-wielding assassin who decapitated him, removing the founder of unified Saadian rule in Morocco

name: Battle of Wadi al-Laban
commanders: Hasan Pasha vs. Abdallah al-Ghalib (Saadians)
importance: Fought north of Fez along Wadi al-Laban following the Ottoman campaign into Morocco and the assassination of Mohammed al-Shaykh; tactical stalemate ending with Hasan Pasha's withdrawal to counter a Spanish threat from Oran

name: Expedition to Mostaganem (1558)
commanders: Spanish forces (allied with Moroccan troops) vs. Ottoman-Algerian forces
importance: Disastrous failed Spanish attempt to conquer Algiers

name: Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis
commanders: Spain & France
importance: Ended the Italian Wars, consolidating Spanish hegemony and temporarily dismantling the Franco-Ottoman alliance

name: Permanent Ottoman-Holy Roman Empire Armistice
commanders: Suleiman the Magnificent & Emperor Ferdinand I
importance: Followed lengthy negotiations begun in 1557; freed Ottoman attention for succession struggles among Suleiman's sons

name: Battle of Lipari
commanders: Turgut Reis vs. Naples-Sicily fleet
importance: Destroyed the Naples-Sicily fleet, extending the post-Djerba Ottoman naval advantage

name: Blockade of Naples
commanders: Turgut Reis & Piyale Pasha
importance: Captured remaining Kingdom of Naples ships following the Battle of Lipari

name: Capture of Béjaïa
commanders: Salah Reis vs. Spanish Garrison
importance: Salah Reis successfully captured the strategically vital coastal stronghold of Béjaïa from Spanish control.

name: Expedition to Mostaganem
commanders: Hasan Pasha vs. Count Alcaudete
importance: Hasan Pasha decisively thwarted the invasion and expedition against Mostaganem led by the Spanish governor of Oran, Count Alcaudete.
casualties: Heavy Spanish losses including the death of Count Alcaudete's forces/commanders

name: Second Siege of Oran
commanders: Piyale Pasha & Turgut Reis vs. Spanish garrison
importance: Ottoman navy unable to take the key Spanish enclave

name: First Battle of Adana
commanders: Atabey Uzbek (Mamluk Sultanate, ~3,000 Royal Mamluks plus 9 Emirs of 1,000) vs. Ottoman Empire garrison forces
importance: After Uzbek's peace message was ignored, the Mamluks confronted an Ottoman force outside Adana and quickly routed it; part of the Mamluk counteroffensive ordered by Sultan Qaitbey to reclaim territory seized by the Ottomans in Cilicia earlier that year
casualties: Around 800 Ottomans captured, including 17 commanders, who were subsequently paraded through Damascus, Aleppo, and Cairo

name: Siege of Adana
commanders: Atabey Uzbek (Mamluk Sultanate) vs. Ottoman garrison of Adana
importance: Following their victory in the field outside the city, the Mamluks besieged Adana itself; the siege continued until the garrison ultimately surrendered after the Ottoman relief army was defeated at the Second Battle of Adana
casualties: Entire Ottoman garrison of 1,500 soldiers ultimately surrendered

name: Second Battle of Adana
commanders: Hersek-oglu (Ottoman Empire, relief army) vs. Atabey Uzbek (Mamluk Sultanate, fewer than 15,000 soldiers per captured Ottoman scouts)
importance: Sultan Bayezid II sent Hersek-oglu — son of Stjepan Vukčić of Herzegovina, raised at the Ottoman court and married to one of Bayezid's daughters — to relieve besieged Adana; his reconnaissance unit was routed first, and in the main battle the Turkmen contingents fled early while Hersek-oglu and 200 Janissaries fought on encircled until he was wounded and captured. This decisive defeat directly caused the subsequent surrender of the Adana garrison
casualties: Reported Ottoman losses of 40,000 (per source infobox); Hersek-oglu wounded and captured along with the son of the late vizier Mustafa Pasha, Kızıl Ahmed Beg (Sanjakbegi of Kengırı), and the sultan's chief pantry-keeper Süleyman Aga

name: Siege of Peñón de Vélez (1563)
commanders: Sancho Martínez de Leyva (Spain) vs. Ottoman-Moroccan base
importance: Heavy Spanish defeat besieging the Ottoman base on Morocco's northern coast

name: Recapture of Peñón de Vélez (1564)
commanders: García Álvarez de Toledo y Osorio (Spain, with Portuguese/Italian help) vs. evacuated Ottoman garrison
importance: Spain recaptured the base after Ottoman evacuation; territory remains part of Spain today

name: Great Siege of Mazagan
commanders: Portuguese defenders vs. Prince Abdallah Mohammed (Moroccan Saadi)
importance: Crucial Portuguese defensive success in Morocco

name: Capture of Tunis (Kılıç Ali Pasha)
commanders: Kılıç Ali Pasha vs. Hafsid rulers (under Spanish protection)
importance: Taken while Spain was preoccupied suppressing the Granada Revolt

name: Granada Revolt / Alpujarras War
commanders: Aben Humeya (Morisco rebels, Ottoman-supported) vs. Philip II of Spain
importance: Moriscos requested and received limited Ottoman aid; suppression allowed Spain to refocus on the direct Ottoman struggle

name: Ottoman Fleet Movements under Kılıç Ali Pasha (Messina)
commanders: Kılıç Ali Pasha vs. Holy League fleet (55 Spanish galleys)
importance: Rebuilt Ottoman navy avoided direct battle with the Allied fleet near Messina

name: Ottoman-Venetian Peace
commanders: Ottoman Empire & Republic of Venice
importance: Ended the Holy Alliance as an effective force, leaving Spain and the Ottomans facing each other alone

name: Spanish Capture of Tunis (Juan de Austria)
commanders: Juan de Austria (Spain) vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Retook Tunis while the Ottoman fleet was occupied raiding Apulia

name: Capture of Fez
commanders: Caïd Ramdan vs. Saadian Sultanate (Mohammed II)
importance: Uluj Ali's deputy Caïd Ramdan captured Fez after defeating the Saadian ruler, placing Abd al-Malik on the throne as an Ottoman vassal.

name: Sahara Campaign to Tuat
commanders: Hassan Veneziano vs. Saadi-Allied Tribes
importance: Hassan Veneziano led troops deep into the central Sahara to the oases of Tuat in response to local pleas against Saadi-allied tribes from Tafilalt.

name: Attack on Jijel
commanders: Algerian Forces vs. Kingdom of France
importance: Algerian forces successfully repelled French landing and military efforts under Louis XIV at Jijel, maintaining regional hegemony.

name: Invasion of Tunis (Maghrebi War)
commanders: Dey Hadj Chabane vs. Muradid Tunis
importance: Taking advantage of a Muradid civil war, Dey Hadj Chabane invaded Tunis and installed a puppet bey to enforce Algerian supremacy over Tunisia.

name: Sack of Orăștie
commanders: Ottoman Empire (Murad II's forces) vs. local Transylvanian defenders
importance: Ottomans seized and devastated the town following their victory at Hațeg, part of the initial 1420 incursion into Transylvania
casualties: No reliable military casualty figures survive; as a raid-and-sack rather than a defended siege, losses were likely concentrated among the civilian population rather than combatants, but no credible count is recorded

name: Siege of Brassó and Ravaging of Barcaság
commanders: Murad II (Ottoman Empire, with Dan II possibly guiding) vs. Brassó garrison and citizenry
importance: Ottoman force advanced through the Predeal Pass into Transylvania via Wallachia to punish Dan II's rival Michael I; devastated the Barcaság region while its inhabitants sheltered in the fortress. Part of a recurring pattern of Ottoman akıncı raider incursions through the 1420s using Wallachia as a staging ground
casualties: The fortified town of Brassó itself was not taken, so the garrison suffered minimal direct losses; the surrounding Barcaság countryside sustained heavy civilian and property losses from burning and pillaging, though no numerical estimate survives

name: Pippo Spano's Victory near the Bulgarian Border
commanders: Pippo Spano (Kingdom of Hungary, with troops withdrawn from Moravia) vs. Ottoman force (~15,000)
importance: Significant Hungarian success that prompted Byzantine Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos to propose a joint anti-Ottoman campaign to Sigismund; exact battlefield location near the Bulgarian border is my best estimate, not precisely sourced
casualties: The defeated Ottoman force numbered approximately 15,000; contemporary accounts describe it as a significant defeat but do not give a reliable death toll — modern historians generally treat 15th-century Ottoman-Hungarian border-war casualty figures from this period as unverifiable rather than citing a specific number

name: Defeat and Death of 'Isa Bey' Ishaković (Bosnia)
commanders: Ottoman Empire ('Isa Bey Ishaković') vs. Kingdom of Bosnia
importance: Ottoman forces under this commander were defeated and he was killed; his forces subsequently dispersed, allowing Vrboszna (Sarajevo region) to return to Bosnian control. Caveat: the well-documented Ottoman governor 'Isa-Beg Ishaković,' founder of Sarajevo, was active later (c. 1440s–1470s) and is not recorded dying in 1424 — likely a different bey of similar name or a dating inconsistency in the source article
casualties: The commanding bey was killed; the size and losses of his force are not recorded, though its subsequent dispersal implies it was significantly weakened or broken as a fighting force rather than merely defeated in the field

name: Battle of Golubac (1426)
commanders: Pippo Spano (Kingdom of Hungary) vs. Ottoman Empire
importance: Pippo Spano defeated the Turks in a pitched battle near Golubac; he suffered a stroke shortly after and died en route to Lippa, removing one of Hungary's most capable commanders
casualties: No reliable numerical figures survive for either side; the battle's significance in the sources rests on the tactical Hungarian win and the loss of Pippo Spano himself (to illness, not combat) rather than on documented troop losses

name: Cession of Golubac to the Ottoman Empire
commanders: Đurađ Branković (Serbian Despotate) vs. Ottoman Empire / Kingdom of Hungary
importance: Following the death of Despot Stefan Lazarević in 1427, his successor Đurađ Branković was bound to hand over Belgrade to Hungary but ceded the strategically vital fortress of Golubac to the Ottomans instead — directly precipitating Sigismund's major 1428 siege attempt to retake it
casualties: None — this was a diplomatic/administrative transfer of a fortress rather than a military engagement

name: Siege of Golubac (1428) and Retreat Ambush
commanders: Sigismund of Luxembourg & Stephen Rozgonyi & Zawisza the Black (Hungary, Lithuania, Wallachia — ~25,000 including 6,000 Wallachians) vs. Murad II (Ottoman Empire)
importance: Major Hungarian-led siege of the key Ottoman stronghold of Golubac (recently ceded by Serbia); Sigismund proposed a ceasefire as Murad's relief force approached, but Ottoman forces treacherously attacked during the Hungarian retreat, resulting in a massacre. Sigismund narrowly escaped thanks to Rozgonyi's intervention. Led to a three-year ceasefire and the eventual full vassalization of the Serbian Despotate
casualties: This is the one engagement in the war with a widely cited (though still imprecise) toll: several thousand of the roughly 25,000-strong Hungarian-allied army are generally described by historians as killed or captured in the retreat ambush, making it the costliest single episode of the war; Zawisza the Black was killed covering the retreat. Exact Ottoman losses from the siege itself are not recorded

name: Ottoman Raids into Transylvania (Amlaș and Făgăraș)
commanders: Ottoman akıncı raiders (Ottoman Empire) vs. local Transylvanian defenders
importance: Renewed Ottoman raiding parties devastated the Transylvanian districts of Amlaș and Făgăraș in 1432, conventionally marking the closing phase of the war before the broader conflict shifted focus toward John Hunyadi's rise in the 1430s–1440s
casualties: No reliable military casualty figures survive; as with most akıncı raids, losses fell heavily on the rural civilian population and in destroyed property rather than on organized combatant forces, and contemporary chroniclers did not quantify them

name: Barbarossa's Raid up the Italian Coast
commanders: Hayreddin Barbarossa (Ottoman fleet placed at France's disposal)
importance: Barbarossa left the Dardanelles with over 100 galleys and raided the Italian coast en route to Marseille, where he joined the French fleet under the Count of Enghien

name: Franco-Ottoman Occupation of Toulon
commanders: Hayreddin Barbarossa (Ottoman, ~30,000 men, hosted by France)
importance: Francis expelled Toulon's population (except heads of households) and handed the city to Barbarossa as a base after the Ottoman commander threatened to leave without resupply

name: Ottoman Fleet's Pillaging of the Neapolitan Coast
commanders: Hayreddin Barbarossa (Ottoman, with 5 French galleys under Antoine Escalin des Aimars)
importance: Occurred as the Ottoman fleet departed for Istanbul, France having proven unwilling to help recapture Tunis from Charles V

name: Blockade of the Kerch Strait (1655)
commanders: Ivan Sirko, Ataman Dergun, and Pavel Chesnochikhin vs. Mehmed IV Giray, Adil Giray, and Mehmed IV
importance: A strategic maritime operation by Zaporozhian and Don Cossacks to block the Kerch Strait, preventing Crimean Tatar forces from joining the Polish-Lithuanian campaign against the Cossack-Russian alliance. The campaign involved the capture of Taman and Sudak and dominated the Crimean coast for months.
casualties: 30 Cossacks killed; heavy combat losses and 400+ captured on the Ottoman-Tatar side

name: Siege of Smederevo (1437)
commanders: Murad II vs. Pongrácz of Szentmiklós, John Jiskra & John Hunyadi
importance: A combined relief army surprised and defeated Sultan Murad II's forces besieging Smederevo, halting the Ottoman invasion of Serbia

name: Ottoman Campaign into Transylvania (1438)
commanders: Sultan Murad II & Ali Bey Evrenosoğlu vs. Hungarian Forces
importance: A retaliatory 45-day Ottoman invasion led by Sultan Murad II and Ali Bey Evrenosoğlu following the previous Hungarian raids; the expedition devastated southeastern Hungary and Székely Land, setting the stage for the subsequent conquest of Serbia
casualties: Heavy Hungarian losses and destruction across Transylvania

name: Battle of Mediaș
commanders: Ali Bey Evrenosoğlu vs. Hungarian Forces
importance: Fought during Ali Bey's raid into Székely Land; an Ottoman force of 20,000 sipahi and akinji defeated 12,000 Hungarians near Mediaș, putting them to the sword and capturing multiple Hungarian counts and their banners
casualties: Heavy Hungarian casualties (~12,000 force defeated; around 15 counts captured)

name: Ottoman Border Raids in the Banat
commanders: Ottoman Raiding Parties vs. Hunyadi Brothers
importance: Simultaneously with the siege of Smederevo, Ottoman raiding parties crossed the Danube to harass southern Hungary up to Timișoara, managed only with difficulty by the Hunyadi brothers

name: Occupation of the Morava Region
commanders: Murad II vs. Serbian Forces
importance: Sultan Murad II's army invaded and occupied the Morava region of Serbia during their major 1439 campaign

name: Encounter near Császártöltés
commanders: John Hunyadi & Nicholas of Ilok vs. Isa Bey Ishaković
importance: John Hunyadi and Nicholas of Ilok intercepted and decisively defeated the Ottoman force led by Isa Bey Ishaković near Császártöltés after the Ottomans raided local villages, thwarting threats against Belgrade
casualties: Heavy Ottoman casualties; enemy lines shattered

name: Mezid Pasha's Raid and Invasion of Transylvania
commanders: Mezid Pasha vs. John Hunyadi & Nicholas of Ilok
importance: An Ottoman army under Mezid Pasha invaded Transylvania to pillage and seize riches, devastating the Maros River valley before confronting Hunyadi's gathering forces

name: Battle of the Ialomița River (1442)
commanders: John Hunyadi vs. Şehabeddin Pasha
importance: John Hunyadi's greatest battlefield victory; well-equipped heavy cavalry and Hussite wagon forts shattered the massive Ottoman punitive expedition led by Rumelian governor Şehabeddin Pasha, destroying the belief in Ottoman invincibility and paving the way for the Long Campaign
casualties: Massive Ottoman casualties, including multiple sanjak beys and elite janissaries

name: Battle of Marosszentimre (Sântimbru)
commanders: John Hunyadi & György Lépes vs. Mezid Pasha
importance: An impulsive assault by Bishop György Lépes against the Ottoman vanguard near Ampoi Creek led to a trap by Mezid Pasha's main force; Hunyadi managed to break through the encirclement, but Bishop Lépes was killed
casualties: Heavy Hungarian losses, including the death of Bishop György Lépes

name: Siege of Hermannstadt (Sibiu)
commanders: Mezid Pasha vs. John Hunyadi, Nicholas of Ilok & City Garrison
importance: Mezid Pasha's siege of Sibiu was met with fierce resistance from the citizens before John Hunyadi and Nicholas of Ilok arrived with a relief force on March 23, 1442, setting the stage for the decisive counter-attack
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses during the failed siege

name: Battle of the Iron Gate
commanders: John Hunyadi vs. Mezid Bey
importance: Comprising the initial engagement at Sântimbru and the decisive counter-attack at the Iron Gate Pass of Transylvania, John Hunyadi crushed Mezid Bey's Ottoman force, killing Mezid and his son and marking Hunyadi's third major victory over the Ottomans
casualties: Heavy Ottoman casualties, including commander Mezid Bey and his son

name: Siege of Šabac (1521)
commanders: Suleiman I & Ahmed Pasha vs. Kingdom of Hungary garrison
importance: Suleiman the Magnificent and Ahmed Pasha captured the Šabac fortress as a crucial preliminary step before the siege of Belgrade, killing all defenders and ordering major structural improvements and a pontoon bridge across the Sava

name: Battle of Szávaszentdemeter (1523)
commanders: Pál Tomori vs. Ferhad Pasha
importance: Pál Tomori led Hungarian forces to a severe defeat against Ottoman raiding forces in Syrmia near Sremska Mitrovica, providing a temporary morale boost and checking Ottoman incursions

name: Raid/Siege of Golubac (1481)
commanders: Pál Kinizsi vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Pál Kinizsi led a successful cross-border raiding and military campaign into Ottoman territory, defeating local forces and liberating Christian captives from Golubac
casualties: Ottoman regional losses and garrison casualties

name: Serbia Expedition (1477)
commanders: Mehmed II & Mihaloğlu Ali Bey vs. Hungarian Garrisons
result: The Ottomans won, capturing the Hungarian-built fortresses of Haram Ram and Koyluca Kulič.
importance: Sultan Mehmed II launched a surprise winter expedition into Serbia in response to Hungarian castle-building near the Danube-Sava confluence, forcing the surrender of a key Hungarian river fortress after bypassing or breaking outer defenses
casualties: 500 casualties for the steadfast garrison; garrison granted safe passage upon surrender

name: Siege of the Hungarian River Fortress (Serbia Expedition)
commanders: Mehmed II vs. Hungarian Garrison
importance: As part of the 1477 Serbia Expedition, Mehmed II besieged a stubborn Hungarian fortress near Smederevo, filling its defensive ditch with timber before the garrison surrendered under a safe-passage agreement

name: Siege of Šabac (1476)
commanders: Matthias Corvinus vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: King Matthias Corvinus successfully captured the strategic Ottoman-held fortress of Šabac after a grueling and hard-fought siege

name: Siege of Zvornik
commanders: Matthias Corvinus & Emeric Zápolya vs. Mahmud Pasha, Mihaloğlu Ali Bey & Skender Pasha
importance: King Matthias Corvinus besieged Zvornik during his campaign to counter Mehmed II's actions in Bosnia, but the arrival of Ottoman relief forces and harsh winter conditions forced the Hungarian army into a disastrous, disorderly retreat, abandoning all their artillery
casualties: Many Hungarian soldiers killed or captured; heavy material and artillery losses

name: Siege of Jajce
commanders: Sultan Mehmed II vs. King Matthias Corvinus & Hungarian Garrison
importance: Amidst the grand struggle for the crown of Bosnia, the formidable sovereign Mehmed II laid siege to the majestic fortress of Jajce with a mighty host and imperial siege train, only to see his grand assault shattered by the unyielding valor of the garrison; upon learning of the approach of the illustrious King Matthias Corvinus, the baffled Sultan was forced to cast his royal cannons into the river and flee in ignominious retreat
casualties: Heavy Ottoman casualties; loss of royal siege artillery

name: Siege of Jajce
commanders: Matthias Corvinus & Emeric Zápolya vs. Yusuf Bey & Ottoman Garrison
importance: Following the Ottoman conquest of Bosnia and the execution of King Stephen Tomašević, King Matthias Corvinus led a swift counter-offensive, recapturing Jajce and establishing the northern Bosnian banates to halt Ottoman expansion
casualties: Garrison surrendered; ~400 Ottoman soldiers integrated into the Black Army

name: Battle of Pozazin
commanders: Michael Szilágyi & Gergely Lábatlani vs. Mihaloğlu Ali Bey & Skander Bey
importance: Ottoman forces under Ali Bey lured Michael Szilágyi into a devastating ambush east of Smederevo near Pojejena, resulting in a Hungarian defeat and the capture and subsequent execution of the prominent Hungarian leader Michael Szilágyi on orders of Sultan Mehmed II
casualties: Heavy Hungarian losses; capture and execution of Michael Szilágyi

name: Battle of Tahtalu / Užice
commanders: Mehmed the Conqueror & Mahmud Pasha Angelović vs. Kingdom of Hungary forces
importance: A Hungarian army crossing the Danube to exploit the autumn season was ambushed near Užice and Tahtalu after dispersing to plunder, suffering catastrophic losses and prisoners; this defeat left Serbia vulnerable and paved the way for the final annexation of the Serbian Despotate
casualties: Most of the Hungarian army killed or taken prisoner

name: Battle of Kruševac (1454)
commanders: John Hunyadi & Đurađ Branković vs. Firuz Bey
importance: Following Sultan Mehmed II's withdrawal from the siege of Smederevo, John Hunyadi and Despot Đurađ Branković ambushed and defeated the remaining Ottoman rear guard under Firuz Bey near Kruševac, capturing Firuz Bey and launching a retaliatory raid into Ottoman territory
casualties: Entire Ottoman rear guard destroyed or captured; commander Firuz Bey taken prisoner

name: Lower Danube Campaign (1445)
commanders: John Hunyadi, Vlad II Dracul, Mircea II & Walerand de Wavrin vs. Ottoman Empire
result: Hungarian Retreat / Campaign Success in Capturing Fortresses
importance: A joint expedition by Hungary, Wallachia, Burgundy, and the Papal States along the Lower Danube; the allies captured Turtucaia and Giurgiu and crossed into Bulgaria before withdrawing due to the advancing season and Sultan Murad II's return to Europe

name: Siege of Turtucaia (1445)
commanders: John Hunyadi, Vlad II Dracul & Walerand de Wavrin vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Captured without great difficulty by the allied Christian fleet and land forces during the Lower Danube Campaign

name: Siege of Giurgiu (1445)
commanders: John Hunyadi, Vlad II Dracul & Walerand de Wavrin vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Successfully captured by the allied Christian forces during their advance down the Danube

name: Siege of Little Nikopol (1445)
commanders: John Hunyadi, Vlad II Dracul & Walerand de Wavrin vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: The allies laid siege to Little Nikopol on the left bank of the Danube before deciding to cross into Bulgarian territory for further operations

name: Battle of Aleksinac
commanders: John Hunyadi vs. Ottoman Forces
importance: Following the Battle of Nish during the Long Campaign, Hunyadi intercepted an Ottoman outflanking force attempting to attack the king's camp near Aleksinac, boosting his men's morale to defeat the larger enemy force

name: Battle of Zlatitsa Pass
commanders: John Hunyadi & Władysław III vs. Murad II, Kasım Pasha & Turahan Beg
importance: Fought during the Long Campaign at the fortified Zlatitsa Pass in harsh winter conditions; the Ottoman forces successfully checked the Christian advance, forcing Hunyadi to withdraw while utilizing wagon forts to protect the retreating army
casualties: Heavy weather-related and combat hardships on both sides

name: Peace of Szeged
commanders: Władysław III & John Hunyadi vs. Murad II
importance: A ten-year peace treaty concluded between the Kingdom of Hungary and the Ottoman Empire, establishing territorial concessions and a temporary cessation of hostilities before being broken by the resumption of the Crusade of Varna

name: Battle of Melstica
commanders: John Hunyadi vs. Ottoman Forces
importance: An initial clash during the Christian retreat from Zlatitsa where Ottoman forces pursued the retreating crusader army near the beginning of their march back to friendly territory

name: Battle of  Pass
commanders: John Hunyadi & Władysław III vs. Ottoman Forces & Mahmud Çelebi
importance: Fought during the night under a full moon as part of the Long Campaign return march; Hunyadi successfully ambushed and routed pursuing Ottoman forces, capturing prominent commanders including Mahmud Bey, the Sultan's son-in-law
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses; multiple commanders captured including Mahmud Çelebi

name: Siege of Srebrenik (1442)
commanders: John Hunyadi vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: John Hunyadi led a successful campaign into Bosnia, defeating Ottoman forces and relieving/capturing the strategic fortress of Srebrenik as part of his series of triumphs in 1442

name: Raid on Kruševac
commanders: Franko Tallóci, John Ország & John Marczaly vs. Ali Bey
importance: A deep Hungarian incursion over 100 kilometers into Ottoman territory led by Franko Tallóci; the raiders routed Ali Bey's pursuing forces, crippled the Ottoman river fleet, and marked the first major offensive shift in Hungarian strategy before King Sigismund's death
casualties: Heavy casualties inflicted on Ottoman forces and pursuing troops

name: Battle of Çamurlu
commanders: Mehmed Çelebi & Stefan Lazarević vs. Musa Çelebi
importance: The final conflict of the Ottoman Interregnum fought near Samokov; Mehmed Çelebi defeated his brother Musa Çelebi with the aid of Serbian and Byzantine allies, reuniting the Ottoman Empire and becoming Sultan Mehmed I
casualties: Musa Çelebi defeated, captured, and strangled; heavy losses on both sides

name: Battle of Doboj
commanders: János Maróthi, János Garay & Pál Csupor vs. Ottoman and Bosnian coalition (Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić)
importance: Fought in the Bosna Valley as part of the Hungarian–Ottoman War (1415–1419); a Turkish-Slavic coalition decisively defeated the Hungarian army, capturing three major Hungarian generals (Maróthy, Garay, and Csupor) and paving the way for Turkish consolidation in Bosnia
casualties: Decimation of the Hungarian army; three Hungarian generals captured

name: Battle of Radkersburg
commanders: Nikola IV Frankopan vs. Ahmed Beg
importance: An Ottoman raiding expedition into Styria led by Ahmed Beg was met with fierce resistance and decisively defeated by Nikola IV Frankopan and allied forces

name: Wallachian Campaign (1395)
commanders: Mircea the Elder vs. Sultan Bayezid I
importance: Sultan Bayezid I's major punitive expedition into Wallachia to enforce direct vassalage and punish Mircea the Elder for supporting anti-Ottoman coalitions and aligning with Hungary

name: Battle of Rovine
commanders: Mircea the Elder vs. Sultan Bayezid I & Stefan Lazarević
importance: The climactic engagement of the 1395 Wallachian campaign fought near the Argeș River; Mircea's forces heavily contested the invading Ottoman host using terrain and archers, resulting in fierce fighting where notable Ottoman vassals like King Marko perished, successfully halting total Ottoman conquest
casualties: Heavy casualties for both armies; death of King Marko and Constantine Dragaš

name: Siege of Nicopolis
commanders: King Sigismund, John, Count of Nevers & Enguerrand VII de Coucy vs. Doğan Bey & Ottoman Garrison
result: Inconclusive / Lifted due to Battle of Nicopolis
importance: The crusader army besieged the formidable, well-supplied fortress of Nicopolis along the Danube; lacking heavy siege engines, they attempted a blockade which was ultimately interrupted by the arrival of Sultan Bayezid I's relieving army, leading directly to the decisive open-field battle

name: Siege of Čestin
commanders: King Sigismund vs. Serbian/Ottoman forces
importance: Successfully besieged and captured the castle of Čestin in northern Serbia during Sigismund's early campaigns to secure the southern frontier

name: Siege of Borač
commanders: King Sigismund vs. Serbian/Ottoman forces
importance: Successfully captured the fortress of Borač in northern Serbia as part of Sigismund's military operations in the region

name: Siege of Turnu Măgurele
commanders: István Kanizsai & Mircea the Elder vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Captured by Hungarian and Wallachian forces during the 1395 counterattack, pushing Ottoman forces back to the Danube

name: Hungarian Seizure of the Vidin Territories
commanders: Louis I of Hungary vs. local Bulgarian rulers
importance: Louis intervened in Bulgaria's internal conflicts and seized the territories around Vidin, reorganizing them into the Vidin province and treating Bulgaria thereafter as his 'right of inheritance'; the campaign's accompanying spread of Roman Catholicism provoked opposition from the southern Slavic states

name: First Anti-Turkish Campaign (1366)
commanders: Louis I of Hungary (with allied states) vs. Ottoman forces
importance: Hungary's first coalition campaign against the Ottomans in the Balkans; despite the reported success, Hungarian rule in northern Bulgaria was never consolidated, forcing Louis to establish the Vidin province as a vassal state under Ivan Stratsimir

name: Expulsion of Hungarians from Northern Bulgaria and Conquest of Severin
commanders: Vladislav I of Wallachia (allied with Ivan Shishman) vs. Kingdom of Hungary
importance: Ended Hungarian rule in northern Bulgaria and saw the conquest of the Banate of Severin; this reversal directly opened the way for the subsequent Ottoman offensive into the Balkans

name: Battle of Maritsa
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Bulgarians and their Serbian allies
importance: The Ottomans annihilated the Bulgarian-Serbian coalition, reducing Ivan Shishman to a vassal of the Sultan and marking a major turning point that opened the Balkans to sustained Ottoman offensives, setting the stage for the 1375–1377 Hungarian-Ottoman war
casualties: Bulgarian-Serbian forces annihilated (no numerical figure given in source)

name: Battle of Mezősomlyó
commanders: Nicholas I Garai, palatine of Valjevo (Kingdom of Hungary) vs. Ottoman and Bulgarian reinforcements of Vladislav's army
importance: A great victory won by Louis's forces as his army pushed into the Romanian interior via Mezősomlyó during the opening phase of the 1375 campaign

name: Hungarian Defeat in Wallachia (1375)
date: 1375 (after the Transylvanian Saxon desertion in late July)
commanders: Kingdom of Hungary vs. Romanians (Wallachians), supported by the Ottomans
importance: The Hungarian army, weakened after the desertion of the Transylvanian Saxons at Székelyzsombor, re-entered Wallachia and was defeated by the Romanian-Ottoman coalition

name: First Székely Uprising
commanders: Székely commoners vs. John Sigismund Zápolya
importance: A major revolt by Székely commoners protesting unlawful taxation and predatory lending, which led to the dismantling of the commoners' autonomy and their reduction to serfdom.

name: Battle of Budačka
commanders: Herbard VIII von Auersperg vs. Ferhad Pasha
importance: The Habsburg-Croatian border force was routed, and Commander Herbard VIII von Auersperg was killed; the ransom from his capture was reportedly used to build the iconic Ferhadija Mosque in Banja Luka.
casualties: Heavy (~200 killed, many enslaved on the Christian side)

name: Battle of Slunj
commanders: Jobst Joseph von Thurn and Tamás Erdődy vs. Ferhad Pasha Sokolović
importance: A major ambush and tactical success by Germanic and Croatian forces against a vastly superior Ottoman army under Bosnian Beglerbeg Ferhad Pasha.

name: Ottoman Incursion into Southern Transylvania (Temesköz)
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Kingdom of Hungary
importance: The first direct Ottoman attack on Hungary proper, crossing the Temesköz into southern Transylvania; successfully repulsed by Louis's forces, though Peter Himfi, castellan of Orosva, was killed and his niece Margaret was kidnapped by the Ottomans during the fighting
casualties: Peter Himfi killed; Margaret Himfi kidnapped

name: Hungarian Campaign into Bulgaria against Ivan Shishman (1377)
commanders: Louis I of Hungary vs. Ivan Shishman (reinforced by Ottoman Turks)
result: Disputed — some historians credit Louis with victory, others consider the campaign to have fallen short of its goals
importance: Hungarians invaded Bulgaria and confronted Ivan Shishman's Ottoman-reinforced army; regarded by some historians as ending the war in Hungary's favor since Ottoman activity in the Balkans reportedly slackened for years afterward

name: Hungarian Engagement with Voivode Radu I of Wallachia
commanders: Kingdom of Hungary vs. Radu I of Wallachia
importance: Fought as the Hungarian army marched through Wallachia during the 1377 campaign; Radu I, Vladislav I's successor, opposed the march but the engagement produced no clear winner

name: Louis I's Conquest of Halych
commanders: Louis I of Hungary vs. Lithuanian-held forces in Halych
importance: Not part of the Ottoman conflict itself, but occurred immediately after Louis diverted his attention from the Balkans; Halych, long coveted by Hungarian kings, was annexed as the Voivodeship of Ruthenia

name: Battle of Nicopolis (1366)
commanders: Louis I of Hungary vs. Ottoman Empire forces
importance: Fought as part of the first Hungarian-Ottoman War (1366–1367); King Louis I defeated the Ottoman forces near Nicopolis, securing the survival of the newly established Vidin border province, though the outcome remains a point of divergence with Turkish sources

name: Ottoman Attack on Lepanto
commanders: Turahanoğlu Ömer Bey (Ottoman Empire) vs. Venetian garrison
importance: Ömer Bey very nearly succeeded in taking the strategically important Venetian fortress of Lepanto; part of the pretext escalation leading to the outbreak of war
casualties: No reliable figures survive; the attack is described as nearly successful but ultimately repelled, without a documented casualty count on either side

name: Ottoman Capture of Argos (First)
commanders: Isa-Beg Ishaković (Ottoman Empire, Governor of the Morea) vs. Venetian-held Argos
importance: Ottoman governor of the Morea took the Venetian-held town by treachery, escalating tensions that led directly to Venice's declaration of war later that year
casualties: No documented casualties; the town was taken through betrayal/treason rather than direct assault, suggesting minimal fighting

name: Alliance of Venice and Matthias Corvinus
commanders: Republic of Venice & Matthias Corvinus (Kingdom of Hungary)
importance: First of two allied treaties (with the Papacy and Burgundy following on 19 October) forming the crusading coalition against the Ottomans, with plans to divide Balkan territories among allies upon victory
casualties: N/A — diplomatic agreement, not a military engagement

name: Alliance of Venice, the Papacy, and Burgundy
commanders: Republic of Venice & Pope Pius II & Duke Philip the Good of Burgundy
importance: Expanded the anti-Ottoman crusading coalition; envisioned Venice gaining the Morea and Epirus, Hungary gaining Bulgaria/Serbia/Bosnia/Wallachia, Skanderbeg's principality expanding into Macedonia, and a restored Palaiologan Byzantine Empire
casualties: N/A — diplomatic agreement, not a military engagement

name: Venetian Recapture of Argos
commanders: Alvise Loredan (Republic of Venice) vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Venetians retook Argos and refortified the Isthmus of Corinth, restoring the Hexamilion wall with cannon emplacements as part of the opening offensive of the war
casualties: No reliable figures survive for this recapture

name: Siege of Acrocorinth
commanders: Alvise Loredan (Republic of Venice) vs. Ottoman defenders and Ömer Bey's forces
importance: Venetians suffered a major defeat resulting in the wounding and subsequent death of Marquis Bertoldo d'Este; forced to abandon the siege and retreat to the Hexamilion and Nauplia
casualties: Marquis Bertoldo d'Este mortally wounded and later died; broader Venetian losses in the repeated clashes are described by contemporary chroniclers as significant, but no reliable numerical total survives in modern historiography

name: Ottoman Reconquest of the Morea (Mahmud Pasha's Campaign)
commanders: Mahmud Pasha Angelović (Ottoman Empire) vs. retreating Venetian forces
importance: Ottomans marched swiftly on the Isthmus, catching the demoralized, dysentery-ridden Venetian army as it withdrew to Nauplia; the Hexamilion wall was razed, Argos fell again, and Ottoman authority was restored across much of the Morea
casualties: No pitched battle occurred, as the Venetian force was already withdrawing when the Ottomans arrived; Venetian losses to dysentery and desertion in the preceding weeks were reportedly severe, though no verified figure exists

name: Siege of Mistra (1464)
commanders: Sigismondo Malatesta (Republic of Venice) vs. Ottoman garrison, relieved by Ömer Bey
importance: Malatesta, newly appointed Venetian land commander in the Morea, failed to take the castle and abandoned the siege as Ömer Bey's relief force approached
casualties: No reliable figures survive; Malatesta's limited mercenary and stratioti forces reportedly suffered attrition from the extended siege, but no numerical total is documented

name: Venetian Siege of Mytilene (Lesbos)
commanders: Orsato Giustinian (Republic of Venice) vs. Ottoman garrison, relieved by Mahmud Pasha's fleet
importance: Venetian admiral besieged the Lesbian capital for six weeks before the arrival of an Ottoman relief fleet forced his withdrawal; a second attempt shortly after also failed, and Giustinian died at Modon on 11 July
casualties: Orsato Giustinian died of illness/other causes shortly after (11 July 1464, at Modon), not in battle; no documented combat casualty figures for the siege itself

name: Venetian Demonstrations before the Dardanelles
commanders: Jacopo Loredan (Republic of Venice) vs. Ottoman defenses
importance: Giustinian's successor spent the rest of the year in ultimately fruitless shows of force before the Straits without achieving a breakthrough
casualties: None recorded; described as demonstrations of force rather than direct engagements

name: Venetian-Hospitaller Confrontation over Mamluk Merchants
commanders: Republic of Venice (Jacopo Loredan) vs. Knights Hospitaller of Rhodes
importance: Hospitaller seizure of a Venetian convoy carrying Moorish merchants nearly dragged the Mamluk Sultanate into the war on the Ottoman side; Venice sailed to Rhodes to recover the merchants, averting a wider Christian-on-Christian war

name: Kladas Brothers' Campaign in the Southern Peloponnese
commanders: Krokodeilos Kladas & Epifani Kladas (Maniot stratioti, Venetian-allied) vs. Ottoman forces
importance: The Maniot Kladas brothers brought Vardounia and surrounding lands into Venetian possession, with Epifani serving as governor
casualties: No figures survive; described as a localized guerrilla/stratioti campaign rather than a set-piece battle

name: Venetian Capture of Imbros, Thasos and Samothrace
commanders: Vettore Cappello (Republic of Venice) vs. Ottoman garrisons
importance: Marked the reinvigoration of the Venetian war effort under Cappello's leadership, taking key northern Aegean islands before sailing into the Saronic Gulf
casualties: No figures survive; these lightly-garrisoned islands appear to have fallen with minimal resistance based on the ease implied in the sources

name: Cappello's Attack on Athens
commanders: Vettore Cappello (Republic of Venice) vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Cappello landed at Piraeus and marched on Athens but failed to take the Acropolis, forcing his retreat toward Patras
casualties: No reliable figures survive for the failed assault itself

name: Battle of Patras (1466)
commanders: Jacopo Barbarigo (Republic of Venice) vs. Ömer Bey (Ottoman Empire, 12,000 cavalry)
importance: Ömer Bey's cavalry drove off the outnumbered Venetian besiegers; six hundred Venetians fell and a hundred were taken prisoner out of a force of 2,000, and Barbarigo himself was killed and his body impaled
casualties: 600 Venetians killed and 100 taken prisoner out of a 2,000-man force (per the source text, this is one of the war's better-documented casualty figures); Jacopo Barbarigo killed and his body impaled; Ottoman losses not recorded

name: Relief Attempt at the Acropolis of Athens
commanders: Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck vs. Ottoman relief army from Thebes
importance: During the ongoing siege of the Acropolis, Königsmarck successfully repulsed a relief attempt sent by the Ottoman army from Thebes, sealing the fate of the garrison which capitulated the following day.

name: Siege of the Acropolis
commanders: Francesco Morosini and Otto Wilhelm Königsmarck vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Venetian forces besieged the Ottoman garrison on the Acropolis of Athens; a mortar shell hit the Parthenon (used as a powder magazine), causing a catastrophic explosion that destroyed much of the ancient temple before the garrison surrendered.
casualties: 300 killed in the Parthenon explosion; heavy losses among the garrison

name: Battle of Derventa
commanders: Louis William, Margrave of Baden-Baden, Count Friedrich Magnus zu Castell, and Nikola II Erdődy vs. Pasha Siyavuş (Sziavusz Pasha) of Bosnia
importance: During the Great Turkish War, Louis of Baden launched a surprise night attack against the Bosnian Ottoman army near Derventa. Although the Imperial force discovered it was heavily outnumbered and initially struggled against Ottoman cavalry on elevated ground, the timely flank attack by Count Friedrich Magnus zu Castell turned the battle into a decisive victory. The defeat shattered Bosnian Ottoman resistance in the region, enabling the Habsburg advance across northern Bosnia, the capture of Zvornik later that month, and securing the southern flank of the main Habsburg offensive that culminated in the capture of Belgrade in 1688.
casualties: Holy Roman Empire: about 200 killed. Ottoman Empire: about 5,000 killed and 2,000 captured.

name: Siege of Belgrade
commanders: Maximilian II Emanuel, Elector of Bavaria, and Prince Eugene of Savoy vs. Yeğen Osman
importance: A major victory of the Great Turkish War, the Habsburg army besieged and captured Belgrade, the Ottoman Empire's principal fortress in Europe since 1521. After crossing the Sava under heavy fire and establishing a bridgehead, Imperial forces gradually tightened the siege. Yeğen Osman withdrew most of his field army to Smederevo and Niš, leaving the garrison isolated. On 6 September, Maximilian personally rallied wavering troops during the final assault, supported by Prince Eugene of Savoy, leading to the capture of the fortress. The fall of Belgrade gave the Habsburgs control of one of the most strategically important cities in the Balkans and opened the way for further advances into Ottoman Serbia, although the Ottomans recaptured the city in 1690.
casualties: Holy Roman Empire: about 4,000 killed or wounded. Ottoman Empire: about 5,000 killed, with the surviving garrison surrendering.

name: Cappello's Retaliatory Attack near Patras
commanders: Vettore Cappello (Republic of Venice) vs. Ömer Bey (Ottoman Empire)
importance: Cappello attempted to avenge the disaster at Patras but was heavily defeated; he retreated demoralized to Negroponte, where he fell ill and died on 13 March 1467
casualties: Described as a heavy defeat, but no numerical figure survives; Cappello himself survived the battle but died of illness roughly eight months later

name: Ottoman Campaign in Albania and Construction of Elbasan
commanders: Sultan Mehmed II (Ottoman Empire) vs. Skanderbeg (League of Lezhë/Albanians)
importance: Major Ottoman campaign resulting in the construction of the fortress of Elbasan in an alleged 25 days, cutting Albania in half and isolating Skanderbeg's highland base from Venetian holdings in the south
casualties: No battle casualties recorded; this was primarily a construction/fortification campaign rather than a combat engagement

name: Skanderbeg's Relief of Croia and Defeat of Ballaban Pasha
commanders: Skanderbeg (League of Lezhë) vs. Ballaban Pasha (Ottoman Empire)
importance: Skanderbeg's forces sallied from the highlands, defeated Ballaban Pasha, and lifted the Ottoman siege of Croia (Krujë) before attacking (but failing to capture) Elbasan
casualties: Ballaban Pasha, the besieging Ottoman commander, was killed in this engagement according to Albanian and Ottoman chronicle traditions (notably recorded by the near-contemporary chronicler Marin Barleti); broader troop losses on both sides are not reliably quantified

name: Mehmed II's Second Albanian Campaign
commanders: Sultan Mehmed II (Ottoman Empire) vs. Skanderbeg (League of Lezhë)
importance: Mehmed II again attacked Albanian strongholds while raiding Venetian possessions to keep them isolated; the Ottomans again failed to take Croia and failed to subjugate the country, though they overthrew Tomornitsa; a subsequent plague outbreak sapped local resistance
casualties: No reliable figures survive; the plague outbreak that followed likely caused greater losses to the Albanian resistance than the fighting itself, though it is not a combat casualty in the strict sense

name: Siege of Negroponte (Chalcis)
commanders: Sultan Mehmed II (Ottoman Empire) vs. Venetian defenders
importance: After a protracted and bloody siege, the well-fortified city fell to Ottoman troops, bringing the entire island of Euboea under Ottoman control — one of the war's most significant Venetian losses
casualties: This is one of the best-documented atrocities of the war: contemporary and near-contemporary accounts describe a large-scale massacre following the city's fall, with much of the garrison and civilian population killed or enslaved (chronicler estimates run into the low thousands, though exact figures are disputed among historians). The Venetian bailo Paolo Erizzo was executed by the Ottomans after the surrender — according to a widely repeated but disputed tradition, by being sawn in half, in reprisal for failing to honor surrender terms he believed had been agreed

name: Ottoman Siege of Shkodra (1474)
commanders: Sultan Mehmed II (Ottoman Empire) vs. Venetian-Albanian garrison
importance: Ottoman forces sent to take the strategically vital fortress of Shkodra failed to capture it, a significant defensive success for the remaining Venetian-controlled Albanian garrisons
casualties: Later Albanian/Venetian chronicle traditions (notably Marin Barleti, writing decades afterward) claim very heavy Ottoman losses in repeated failed assaults, with some accounts citing figures in the thousands; these numbers are considered by modern historians to be significantly inflated and are not treated as reliable

name: Siege of Shkodra (1478–1479)
commanders: Sultan Mehmed II (personally leading, Ottoman Empire) vs. Venetian-Shkodran defenders
result: Venetian-Shkodran defensive success (city held until ceded by treaty)
importance: Mehmed II personally led this major siege; the Venetians and Shkodrans resisted repeated assaults and held the fortress until it was ceded by treaty rather than falling by force
casualties: The defending garrison (traditionally estimated at somewhere between 1,500 and 2,500 Venetian and Albanian troops under commanders including Antonio Loredan) suffered severe attrition from disease and starvation during the prolonged blockade rather than from direct assault, since the city was never stormed; Ottoman assault casualties in the failed attacks are cited in various chronicle traditions but are not considered reliably quantified by modern historians

name: Ottoman Conquest of the Despotate of Epirus
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Leonardo III Tocco (Despotate of Epirus)
importance: With Epirus excluded from the peace treaty and left undefended after its ruler alienated Venice by courting Naples, the Ottomans conquered the last surviving rump Byzantine state, intending it as a base for a planned invasion of Italy
casualties: No reliable figures survive; the conquest is generally described as achieved with little resistance given the Despotate's isolation and lack of external support

name: Night Attack at Târgoviște
commanders: Vlad III the Impaler vs. Sultan Mehmed II
result: Wallachian Tactical Success / Ottoman Strategic Advance
importance: A famous night raid launched by Vlad III on the Ottoman encampment near Târgoviște in an attempt to assassinate Sultan Mehmed II; although the assassination failed, the psychological shock and subsequent discovery of the 'Forest of the Impaled' forced the Ottoman army to retreat
casualties: Heavy casualties on both sides; thousands of Ottoman troops and captives

name: Battle of Polog
commanders: Skanderbeg, Moisi Arianit Golemi & Hamza Kastrioti vs. Ibrahim Pasha
importance: Fought in the fields of Polog near Tetovo during Skanderbeg's Macedonian campaign; despite severe storms, Skanderbeg launched a surprise cavalry night/dawn raid into the Ottoman camp, slew Ibrahim Pasha in single combat, and routed the enemy forces
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses (estimated between 3,000 and 10,000 killed); light Albanian losses (~300)

name: Battle of Argeș
commanders: Mircea I of Wallachia vs. Sultan Bayezid I & Stefan Lazarević
importance: Fought along the Argeș River after Bayezid I invaded Wallachia in response to Mircea's refusal to pay tribute; intense Wallachian harassment preceded a major clash on October 10, setting the stage for the subsequent Battle of Rovine

name: Clashes at Severin (1419)
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Michael I of Wallachia
importance: Opening clash of the Ottoman-Wallachian conflict, provoked by Michael I's refusal to continue his predecessor Mircea the Elder's tribute payments and his attempt to form an anti-Ottoman alliance; set the stage for the much larger 1420 punitive campaign

name: Wallachian Campaign of 1420 (Main Invasion)
commanders: Sultan Mehmed I & Dan II (Ottoman Empire and Wallachian opposition, 60,000–80,000 troops) vs. Michael I of Wallachia
importance: Mehmed I personally led this massive expedition, declared a 'holy war,' exploiting Hungary's preoccupation with the Hussite Wars to leave Michael I without allies; the Ottoman fleet simultaneously moved to capture Danube and Pontic fortresses while the ground army plundered the country and took many slaves
casualties: Heavy Wallachian losses with many enslaved (per source); Ottoman losses unspecified

name: Ottoman Capture of Isaccea and Enisala
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Wallachian garrisons
importance: Capture of these Danube/Dobrujan fortresses forced Voivode Michael I to flee and seek Hungarian aid, directly precipitating his final confrontation with his Ottoman-backed rival Dan II

name: Battle Between Michael I and Dan II
commanders: Dan II (Ottoman-backed) vs. Michael I of Wallachia
importance: Michael I, fleeing after the fall of Isaccea and Enisala, was caught and confronted by his Ottoman-backed rival Dan II; Michael I was killed in the ensuing battle, along with the subsequent murder of his family members, effectively ending his reign and clearing the way for Dan II's ascension
casualties: Michael I of Wallachia killed; his family members subsequently murdered

name: Battle of Turnu
commanders: Vlad III the Impaler vs. Sultan Mehmed II
importance: An amphibious crossing operation and subsequent battle near Turnu / Nicopolis; Janissaries crossed the Danube by night under heavy fire, and after initial Wallachian resistance and artillery fire, Mehmed deployed heavy artillery to bombard Vlad's forces, forcing the Wallachian army to retreat and allowing the full Ottoman army across
casualties: Around 250 Janissaries killed plus heavy Wallachian casualties

name: Ambush and Defeat of Hamza Pasha and Yunus Bey
commanders: Vlad III (Vlad the Impaler, Wallachia) vs. Hamza Pasha & Yunus Bey (Ottoman Empire)
importance: The Ottoman commanders' plan to ambush and capture Vlad along the Danube backfired when their own force was defeated by Wallachian troops; both commanders were captured and sent as prisoners to Târgoviște, where they were subsequently impaled — a key opening move in Vlad's broader campaign to destabilize Ottoman defenses along the river
casualties: Hamza Pasha and Yunus Bey captured and later impaled; broader Ottoman troop losses not specified in source

name: Vlad the Impaler's Raids Across the Southern Danube
commanders: Vlad III (Vlad the Impaler, Wallachia) vs. Ottoman settlements and garrisons south of the Danube
importance: Following the elimination of Hamza Pasha and Yunus Bey, Vlad's forces raided settlements across the southern Danube, described by chronicler Laonikos Chalkokondyles as 'completely destroying the inhabitants, together with their women and children,' burning everything in their path; part of Vlad's strategy to eliminate Ottoman defenses on both banks and deter future punitive campaigns
casualties: Widespread civilian and garrison casualties per chronicler accounts; Vlad's own later claim (see Sack of Giurgiu entry) put total kills at 23,884 across the whole expedition

name: Sack of Giurgiu
commanders: Vlad III (Vlad the Impaler, Wallachia) vs. Ottoman garrison of Giurgiu
importance: Vlad, speaking fluent Turkish, tricked the garrison commander of the strategic fortress of Giurgiu into opening its gates; the Ottoman garrison was subsequently slaughtered and the fortress sacked, marking the climax and conclusion of the Danube expedition. In his February 1462 letter to Matthias Corvinus, Vlad claimed to have killed over 23,884 Turks and Bulgarians across the entire campaign, though this figure — like most self-reported medieval battle counts — is treated with caution by modern historians. The provocation directly led Sultan Mehmed II to personally lead an army into Wallachia to oust Vlad from power
casualties: Entire Ottoman garrison of Giurgiu slaughtered; Vlad's self-reported campaign-wide total of 23,884 Turks and Bulgarians killed (per his own letter, not independently verified)

name: Battle of Buzău
commanders: Vlad III the Impaler vs. Sultan Mehmed II, Mahmud Pasha & Mihaloğlu Ali Bey
importance: Fought during Mehmed II's 1462 Wallachian campaign; Vlad attempted to ambush encumbered akıncı forces under Ali Bey, but Mehmed II's main army and Mahmud Pasha arrived to trap the Wallachians, annihilating the bulk of Vlad's army with thousands killed or captured
casualties: Devastating Wallachian losses (~5,300 killed and 1,000 captured out of a 7,000-man force); Ottoman raider and relief unit casualties

name: Battle of Snagov
commanders: Vlad III the Impaler & Stephen III of Moldavia's retinue vs. Basarab Laiotă & Ottoman Forces
result: Ottoman-Basarab Victory / Death of Vlad III
importance: The final engagement of Vlad the Impaler near Snagov; his outnumbered force of about 2,000 was cornered and destroyed by a combined Turkish-Basarab army, resulting in Vlad's death, the massacre of his Moldavian retinue, and his head being sent to Sultan Mehmed II
casualties: Destruction of Vlad's 2,000-man force, including Vlad III himself and his Moldavian retinue

name: Battle of Beirut (1520)
commanders: Christoph le Mignon (Kingdom of France, 15 ships, 800 men) vs. Janbirdi al-Ghazali (Ottoman Empire)
importance: A French flotilla originally dispatched to reinforce the Knights Hospitaller at Rhodes against a rumored Ottoman attack instead diverted to sack Beirut after Sultan Selim I's death delayed Ottoman attention elsewhere; the French bombardment failed to silence the harbor tower, and their landing force was ambushed by Ottoman troops under Janbirdi al-Ghazali, resulting in the death of the expedition's commander and most of his men after roughly ninety minutes of fighting. News of the victory reached Damascus and Cairo, while the disaster contributed to French King Francis I's declining enthusiasm for crusading, alongside his growing concerns about encirclement by Germany and Spain. Ironically, only five days later Janbirdi al-Ghazali learned of Selim I's death and Suleiman the Magnificent's succession, prompting him to revolt against the new Sultan — a rebellion that led to his own downfall
casualties: 484 French soldiers killed, including commander Christoph le Mignon; survivors escaped back to the ships; the Ottoman commander had the heads of the dead decapitated and displayed on the city wall's battlements. Ottoman casualties not specified in source

name: Kunicki's Expedition on the Right-bank and Moldavia
commanders: Stefan Kunicki(Right-bank Cossacks) vs. Ottoman Empire and Crimean Khanate
result: Cossack-Polish Campaign / Ottoman-Tatar Counter-offensive resulting in a Cossack victory
importance: A military expedition led by Right-bank Cossack Hetman Stefan Kunicki into Right-bank Ukraine and Moldavia following the Battle of Vienna, aimed at dislodging Ottoman forces and rallying local anti-Ottoman support
casualties: Heavy casualties and losses on both sides during subsequent engagements and Tatar counter-raids

name: Battle of Sırpsındığı
commanders: Hacı İlbey vs. Allied Christian Coalition (Serbian, Bulgarian, Wallachian, Bosnian, Hungarian & Crusader forces)
importance: A surprise night raid and rout conducted by Ottoman akıncıs under Hacı İlbey against a coalition army encamped near the Maritsa River close to Adrianople; the first major allied attempt to push the Ottomans from the Balkans, resulting in massive casualties (particularly among Serbs) and paving the way for Adrianople to become the Ottoman capital
casualties: Heavy casualties for the allied army, with many soldiers killed or drowned in the Maritsa River

name: Fall of Philadelphia
commanders: Bayezid I, Manuel II Palaiologos & John VII Palaiologos vs. Philadelphia garrison and citizens
importance: The conquest and surrender of Philadelphia, the last independent Byzantine city in Asia Minor; forced to submit after a brief siege when citizens saw Byzantine imperial banners flying alongside Ottoman standards among the besieging forces
casualties: Unspecified garrison and civilian surrender terms

name: Battle of Dubravnica
commanders: Vitomir & Crep (representing Prince Lazar of Serbia) vs. Ottoman Empire forces
importance: The first recorded Ottoman incursion into Prince Lazar's territory, resulting in a localized Serbian victory that temporarily halted Ottoman raids until 1386

name: Battle of Pločnik
commanders: Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović & Miloš Obilić vs. Kula Şahin Bey
importance: Fought near Pločnik; Serbian forces capitalized on dispersed and looting Ottoman akıncı units, routing Şahin Bey's central force and inflicting heavy losses as the first major defeat of the Ottomans in South Slavic lands
casualties: Heavy Ottoman losses (estimated over 60% of the force destroyed, including thousands of akıncis)

name: Siege of Ohrid
commanders: Çandarlızade Ali Pasha vs. Ohrid garrison and Albanian forces
importance: A successful siege conducted by Ottoman forces under Çandarlızade Ali Pasha against Ohrid, resulting in the surrender of the city and the beginning of Ottoman domination in the region
casualties: Heavy Albanian losses during the conflict and subsequent surrender terms

name: First Siege of Thessalonica (1383–1387)
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Manuel II Palaiologos (Byzantine Empire)
importance: Thessalonica surrendered after a lengthy siege, along with Christopolis and Chrysopolis; initially granted autonomy in exchange for the haraç poll tax, establishing the first period of Ottoman control over the city

name: Ottoman Capture and Destruction of Chrysopolis
commanders: Sultan Bayezid I (Ottoman Empire) vs. Byzantine defenders
importance: Bayezid I's punitive response to Manuel II's escape from Ottoman custody and coronation as emperor; the city was captured by storm and largely destroyed, part of the same offensive that saw Thessalonica submit again to Ottoman rule

name: Treaty of Gallipoli (1403)
commanders: Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos (Byzantine Empire) & Süleyman Çelebi (Ottoman Empire)
importance: In exchange for supporting Süleyman in the Ottoman succession struggle following the Battle of Ankara, Manuel II secured the return of Thessalonica, part of its hinterland, the Chalcidice peninsula, and the coastal region between the Strymon and Pineios rivers

name: Musa Çelebi's Attack on Thessalonica
commanders: Musa Çelebi (Ottoman pretender) vs. Byzantine Thessalonica
importance: Attack by a rival Ottoman pretender during the Ottoman civil war period, occurring during the relatively peaceful autonomous rule of Despot Andronikos Palaiologos under the supervision of Demetrios Leontares

name: Ottoman Siege of Thessalonica (Burak Bey, 1422)
commanders: Burak Bey (son of Evrenos, Ottoman Empire, with Balkan marcher-lords) vs. Despot Andronikos Palaiologos (Byzantine Empire)
importance: Opening Ottoman assault of the conflict; ravaged Thessalonica's suburbs and the western portion of Chalcidice, directly leading to Andronikos's eventual decision to hand the city over to Venice due to Byzantine inability to provide manpower or resources for its defense

name: Handover of Thessalonica to Venice
commanders: Despot Andronikos Palaiologos (Byzantine Empire) & Republic of Venice
importance: Six Venetian galleys and one Byzantine galley entered Thessalonica's harbor, greeted by a jubilant population seeking security from roughly 5,000 blockading Ottoman troops; the transfer was accepted by Venice's Great Council on 7 July 1423 and set the terms for the six-year Ottoman-Venetian conflict that followed

name: Ottoman-Byzantine Peace of 1424
commanders: Sultan Murad II (Ottoman Empire) & Emperor John VIII Palaiologos (Byzantine Empire)
importance: The Byzantines returned almost all lands gained in 1403 and, reduced to Constantinople and its environs, became tributary vassals to the Ottomans once more, freeing Murad to focus more fully on the Thessalonica question

name: Venetian Expedition to Macedonia and Burning of Ierissos
commanders: Fantino Michiel (Republic of Venice, 10 galleys) vs. abandoned Ottoman positions
importance: Venetians found Ierissos abandoned by its Ottoman garrison but stocked with provisions, which they loaded aboard before burning the town and five other nearby forts, en route to the more contested action at Christopolis

name: Battle of Christopolis (1425)
commanders: Alvise Loredan & Fantino Michiel (Republic of Venice) vs. Ismail Bey (Ottoman Empire, 400 sipahis)
importance: After an initial repulsed landing attempt led by Alvise Loredan, the Venetians mustered their full force and overcame Ottoman resistance in a four-hour battle, killing Ismail Bey and 41 Turks and taking 30 prisoners; the Venetians then fortified the site with a garrison of 80 foot soldiers and 50 crossbowmen
casualties: 41 Turks killed including commander Ismail Bey; 30 taken prisoner

name: Ottoman Recapture of Christopolis
date: c. 20 days after the Venetian capture, 1425
commanders: Ottoman Empire (10,000–12,000 men) vs. Venetian garrison (80 foot soldiers, 50 crossbowmen)
importance: A much larger Ottoman relief force stormed the recently fortified castle; the small Venetian garrison could not escape, with half killed and the rest taken prisoner, reversing the earlier Venetian gain
casualties: Half of the Venetian garrison killed, the rest taken prisoner; Ottomans lost around 800 men in the roughly 20-day effort to retake the fort

name: Ottoman Raids around Thessalonica and Zetouni
commanders: Sultan Murad II (Ottoman Empire) vs. Byzantine and Venetian-held territory
importance: Launched in response to John VIII's formal accession as Emperor upon Manuel II's death, reflecting Murad's deep hostility toward John; struck both around Thessalonica and Zetouni (Lamia) in Central Greece

name: Venetian Occupation and Fortification of Kassandreia
commanders: Fantino Michiel (Republic of Venice) vs. Ottoman-threatened territory
importance: Undertaken in response to Thessalonian complaints about Ottoman raids on the Kassandra Peninsula; Michiel refortified the fort and strengthened the area with two smaller forts

name: Capture of Platamon Castle
commanders: Fantino Michiel (Republic of Venice) vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Michiel captured the castle by storm after setting fire to its main bailey when the Ottoman garrison refused to surrender; the site was repaired but likely abandoned soon after, as it is not mentioned again in sources

name: Pseudo-Mustafa's Raids from Thessalonica
commanders: Pseudo-Mustafa (pretender claiming to be Mustafa Çelebi, with Turkish followers) vs. Murad II's forces
result: Inconclusive; raids halted by Venetian order
importance: A pretender claiming to be Bayezid's son gathered a following in Thessalonica and launched raids against Murad's forces; after both Mustafa and the Venetian captain were nearly captured during one raid, the Great Council ordered such raids stopped and the city gates kept shut on 3 September 1425

name: Major Ottoman Assault on Thessalonica (1426)
commanders: Ottoman Empire (reportedly 30,000 men) vs. Bernardo Loredan & Jacopo Dandolo (Republic of Venice, 700 crossbowmen, 5 galleys)
importance: A major Ottoman attack was repelled with the help of five Venetian galleys possibly armed with small cannons; occurred amid failed peace negotiations in which the Ottomans insisted on control of Kassandra and Chortiatis as springboards for future conquest
casualties: Over 2,000 Turks killed before the assault failed, according to the Venetian commanders' report to the Great Council

name: Crimean Campaign of 1675
commanders: Ivan Sirko, Frol Minaev, Kasbulat Cherkassky, Mazan Batyr vs. Selim I Giray
result: Decisive allied victory; widespread destruction of Crimean territory and defeat of Khan Selim I Giray's forces
importance: A major punitive campaign led by Ataman Sirko and allied Russian, Don, Kalmyk, and Kabardian forces in retaliation for winter attacks on the Sich, inflicting catastrophic personnel losses on the Khanate.
casualties: 10,000 Tatars killed, 6,000 captured; very light allied losses (13 dead)

name: Establishment of the Belgorod Line
commanders: Tsardom of Russia
result: Successful creation of a massive defensive fortification network
importance: Advanced Russian defense systems that pushed frontier forts 300 km south of the older Abatis Line, dramatically improving the protection of southern Russian lands against nomadic incursions.

name: Establishment of the Izium Line
commanders: Tsardom of Russia
result: Successful southward expansion of Russian defensive fortifications
importance: A major defensive construction initiative that pushed Russian forts further south, establishing outposts within 150 kilometers of the Black Sea steppes and boxing in nomadic raiding routes.

name: Sack of Bakhchysarai
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Selim I Giray
result: Total destruction of the Khan's capital
importance: Cossack and allied forces breached the Crimean interior, sacked and burned the Khanate capital of Bakhchysarai, and put everything to fire and sword after the Khan retreated to the mountains.
casualties: Heavy local and defending garrison losses

name: Sack of Perekop
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Selim I Giray
