result: Defeat of the Khan's army and devastation of Perekop
importance: Following the deep incursion into Crimea, Sirko intercepted and repeatedly defeated Selim I Giray's forces at Perekop during their retreat, routing the panic-stricken army and securing the extraction of loot and captives.
casualties: Heavy losses for the pursuing Crimean army

name: Battle of Chorna Dolyna (Black Valley)
commanders: Ivan Sirko vs. Captive Tatar / Converted Encampment
result: Execution of captives choosing to return to Crimea
importance: Following the successful withdrawal from Crimea, Sirko sorted through captives at Black Valley and executed those former Rus' captives who chose to return to Crimea to rejoin their families and property, to prevent them from boosting the enemy population.
casualties: Execution of several thousand returning captives

name: Ottoman Naval Raid on Euboea and the Morea
commanders: Ottoman Empire (40–65 vessels) vs. Venetian possessions in Greece
importance: A major Ottoman fleet raided Euboea and took about 700 Venetian citizens prisoner before raiding the environs of the Venetian outposts of Modon and Coron in the Morea; prompted Venice to authorize a hunting fleet under Andrea Mocenigo

name: Battle of Gallipoli (1428)
commanders: Guido da Canal (Republic of Venice) vs. Ottoman-Christian coalition fleet
importance: Venetian guard fleet was defeated by a coalition of Ottoman and Christian ships, delaying the dispatch of the new Venetian fleet under Andrea Mocenigo until September; occurred amid the defection of the Duke of Naxos, Giovanni II Crispo, to a separate Ottoman peace

name: Ottoman Fleet's Capture of Venetian Vessels off Thessalonica
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Republic of Venice
importance: An Ottoman fleet appeared before Thessalonica and captured two Venetian vessels, part of the escalating naval threat that helped push Venice toward its formal declaration of war later that month

name: Mocenigo's Attack on Gallipoli (1429)
commanders: Andrea Mocenigo (Republic of Venice) vs. Ottoman anchorage
importance: Mocenigo led his flagship to break through the palisade protecting the Ottoman anchorage, but the rest of the Venetian fleet failed to follow, forcing him to withdraw with heavy casualties — illustrative of Venice's continued reluctance to commit fully to the war effort
casualties: Heavy Venetian casualties (not numerically specified in source)

name: Siege and Fall of Thessalonica (1430)
commanders: Sultan Murad II & Sinan Pasha (Ottoman Empire, army rumored at 190,000) vs. Antonio Diedo & Venetian garrison
importance: The climactic and final engagement of the war; Ottoman forces broke through the poorly maintained eastern walls after a three-day assault involving siege engines and heavy archery, exploiting panic caused by a miscommunicated Venetian naval repositioning that convinced the populace they were being abandoned; the city was taken by storm on 29 March
casualties: Venetians lost over 270 men from galley crews alone, including Leonardo Gradenigo (captain of one galley) and the son of Duke Paolo Contarini; widespread civilian massacre during the initial breakthrough

name: Sack of Thessalonica
date: 29 March – April 1430 (three days of plunder, per custom)
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. civilian population of Thessalonica
importance: Following custom for a city taken by storm, plundering lasted three days; the cathedral of Hagios Demetrios and other monuments suffered heavy damage as soldiers searched for treasure, with the Sultan later stripping marble sections for his capital at Adrianople. Murad entered the city on the fourth day, restored order, and began repopulation efforts
casualties: 7,000 inhabitants taken captive for sale in Balkan and Anatolian slave markets (many later ransomed by Despot Đurađ Branković of Serbia); the city's population, previously estimated at 20,000–40,000, was reduced to only about 2,000 survivors after the sack

name: Ottoman-Venetian Peace Treaty of 1430
commanders: Hamza Bey (Ottoman Empire) & Republic of Venice
importance: Venice recognized its loss of Thessalonica, restored Ottoman passage of the Dardanelles, and acknowledged Ottoman overlordship over Patras in the Morea with an annual tribute of 236 ducats; in exchange, Venice secured Ottoman recognition of its possessions in Albania — Durazzo, Scutari, and Antivari — shifting the theater of Ottoman-Venetian rivalry to Albania for the following decades

name: Battle of Leskovac
commanders: Nikola Skobaljić vs. Ottoman Empire forces
importance: Fought near Leskovac during the Ottoman invasion of Serbia; Serbian commander Nikola Skobaljić disobeyed orders to retreat and used guerrilla tactics to defeat an advancing Ottoman army, scoring an initial major victory before later being defeated at Tripolje

name: Battle of Tripolje
commanders: Stefan Lazarević & Vuk Lazarević vs. Đurađ Branković & Ottoman Empire Forces
importance: Fought near Gračanica following the Ottoman defeat at Ankara; Stefan Lazarević defeated a coalition of his nephew Đurađ Branković and Ottoman troops, securing greater autonomy and power for the Serbian Despotate
casualties: Heavy casualties on both sides, particularly within Vuk Lazarević's and Branković's forces

name: Battle of Ostrvica
commanders: Mehmed the Conqueror vs. Serbian Garrison
importance: Part of Mehmed II's first Serbian campaign in 1454; Ottoman cannoneers breached the walls of the Ostrvica Fortress—where the Serbian royal treasury was stored—leading to the surrender of the town and capture of its resisting garrison
casualties: Garrison captured; civilian lives spared upon surrender

name: Siege of Trepča
commanders: Mehmed the Conqueror vs. Serbian Garrison
importance: Conducted during Mehmed II's second Serbian campaign in 1455, resulting in the successful capture of Trepča and its lucrative silver mines, paving the way for the fall of nearby Novo Brdo

name: Second Siege of Novo Brdo (1440–1441)
commanders: Hadım Şehabeddin & Ishak-Beg vs. Serbian Garrison & Ragusan Citizens of Novo Brdo
importance: A prolonged blockade and assault on the wealthy fortified mining town of Novo Brdo following the 1440 Ottoman failure at Belgrade; defended by the local Serbian garrison and Ragusan merchant citizens until the city finally surrendered on 27 June 1441
casualties: Heavy civilian and garrison casualties during the siege; town subsequently plundered and burned

name: Battle of Ohrid
commanders: Skanderbeg (Albania) & Cimarosto (Republic of Venice, 1,000 soldiers) vs. Ottoman garrison forces near Ohrid
importance: Fought during an Albanian incursion into Ottoman territory as part of the broader crusade against Mehmed II planned by Pope Pius II, with Skanderbeg as one of its main leaders; the Ottomans stationed near Ohrid were lured out of their defensive positions and ambushed by Albanian cavalry, resulting in a clear Albanian-Venetian victory. Skanderbeg's men earned 40,000 ducats ransoming captured Ottoman officers. The death of Pope Pius II shortly before the planned crusade could begin left Skanderbeg to continue fighting largely alone
casualties: Not specified in source beyond the capture of Ottoman officers, who were later ransomed for 40,000 ducats

name: Second Battle of Oranik
commanders: Skanderbeg vs. Moisi Arianit Golemi & Isak Bey Pasha (Ottoman forces)
importance: Fought in the plains of Oranik; Skanderbeg's forces (10,000 men) decisively defeated a 15,000-strong Ottoman and renegade army led by the defector Moisi Golemi, who ultimately returned and was pardoned by Skanderbeg later
casualties: Heavy Ottoman and renegade losses; Moisi escaped with about one-third of his original army

name: Fall of the Banate of Jajce
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Croatian/Habsburg defenders
importance: Loss of Jajce forced the main line of Croatian defense to shift to the valley of the Una River, where Gvozdansko subsequently became one of the key fortifications
casualties: No reliable figures survive for this specific fall of the fortress in general historiography

name: Ghazi Husrev Bey's Offensive and Capture of Požega
commanders: Ghazi Husrev Bey (Ottoman Empire, Sanjak-bey of Bosnia) vs. Croatian/Slavonian defenders
importance: Within six months over half of Slavonia fell under Ottoman control, from Valpovo to the fort of Jasenovac at the mouth of the Una, setting up the subsequent push into the Una Valley
casualties: No reliable figures survive; this was a broad six-month territorial offensive across multiple towns rather than a single pitched battle, and no aggregate casualty count is documented

name: Battle of Jassy (1620)
commanders: Gaspar Graziani vs. Iskender Pasha
importance: An early engagement of the Cecora campaign near Iași (Jassy) where Ottoman and Tatar forces moved to depose the pro-Polish Moldavian hospodar Gaspar Graziani, preceding the main battle at Țuțora.
casualties: Heavy casualties for Moldavian rebel forces; Graziani forced to join the main Polish camp

name: Ottoman Capture of Dubica (1537)
commanders: Ghazi Husrev Bey (Ottoman Empire) vs. Croatian garrison
importance: Prompted the Croatian nobility to meet in Zagreb and formally acknowledge the kingdom's lack of military forces and financial difficulties

name: Zrinski's Recapture of Dubica (1537)
commanders: Zrinski family (Croatian nobility, using enrolled miners as soldiers) vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: The Zrinskis enrolled their own miners as soldiers to retake the town, an early example of their military self-reliance that would define their role in the Una Valley defense
casualties: No reliable figures survive; the garrison involved was small and irregularly composed (miners turned soldiers), suggesting a modest-scale action

name: Ottoman Recapture of Dubica (1538)
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Croatian garrison
importance: The Ottomans regained the initiative in the border war following the earlier failure of Johann Katzianer's campaign in Ottoman-held Slavonia

name: Zrinski's Recapture of Dubica (1540)
commanders: Nikola Šubić Zrinski (Croatian nobility) vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Retaken despite a nominal six-month peace treaty with Constantinople that had begun on 1 January 1540, illustrating how border clashes continued regardless of formal truces

name: Ottoman Attack on Pakrac
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Croatian defenders
importance: Ottoman retaliatory response to Zrinski's recapture of Dubica; Ban Petar Keglević's relief army was called off at Queen Anne's request to avoid violating the armistice
casualties: No reliable figures survive; notably, the planned Croatian relief force was withdrawn before it could engage, meaning this was likely a limited Ottoman raid against the town's own garrison rather than a large field battle

name: Ottoman Offensive on Kostajnica, Zrin, and Gvozdansko (1540)
commanders: Ghazi Husrev Bey, Murat Bey Tardić & Mehmed Bey Jahjapašić (Ottoman Empire) vs. Zrinski-held forts
result: Mixed (Kostajnica briefly taken, Zrin and Gvozdansko held)
importance: Retaliatory offensive against Zrinski; Kostajnica was briefly captured while Zrin and Gvozdansko successfully held off attacks, though the Zrinskis reported that all mines near Gvozdansko were destroyed in the campaign
casualties: No reliable figures survive; the confirmed material loss is economic (destruction of the Gvozdansko mines) rather than a documented body count

name: Destruction of Bunić Fort
commanders: Joseph Herberstein, Franjo Oršić, and Marko Mesić vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Conducted as part of a chevauchée campaign into Lika and Krbava, resulting in the destruction of Bunić fort and the ravaging of surrounding villages.

name: Destruction of Grabunar
commanders: Franjo Oršić vs. Ottoman defenders
importance: Lacking cannons to breach the fortification, Franjo Oršić's forces burned Grabunar down; an Ottoman sortie failed, women and children escaped via ropes, and the remaining defenders perished in the fire.

name: Capture of Kostajnica (1556)
commanders: Malkoč Bey (Ottoman Empire, Sanjak-bey of Klis) vs. Croatian garrison
importance: Broke through the Croatian defensive line on the Una River entirely; taken while Zrinski and other Habsburg forces were occupied fighting in southern Hungary near Babócsa and Szigetvár, leading to Zrinski's resignation as ban and the abandonment of the nearby fort of Novi
casualties: No reliable figures survive; the strategic consequence (collapse of the Una defensive line, abandonment of Novi) is well documented, but a specific death toll for the siege itself is not

name: First Siege of Gvozdansko (1561)
commanders: Malkoč Bey (Ottoman Empire, 8,000 troops) vs. Toma Lukašić (Croatian garrison, 100 men)
importance: The well-supplied garrison held out until a relief army led by Ivan Lenković arrived, forcing Ottoman withdrawal — the fort's second successful defense after 1540
casualties: No reliable figures survive; since the siege ended in an Ottoman withdrawal upon the relief force's approach rather than a decisive battle, losses on both sides were likely limited compared to a full storming

name: Erdődy-Zrinski Joint Assault on Moslavina and Podravina
commanders: Péter Erdődy & Nikola Šubić Zrinski (Croatian nobility) vs. Ottoman-held territory
importance: A coordinated assault on Ottoman-held regions that jeopardized the concurrent peace negotiations, which nonetheless resulted in an eight-year peace treaty signed in Constantinople the same year
casualties: No reliable figures survive; described as a raid rather than a pitched battle

name: Erdödy's Attack on Novi and Its Relief (1566)
commanders: Péter Erdődy (Croatian nobility) vs. sanjaks of Požega and Klis (Ottoman relief force)
result: Ottoman victory (Croatian attack repelled, but Novi held by Ottomans regardless)
importance: The Ottoman relief army sent to save Novi suffered a heavy defeat, yet the fort itself still managed to repel the Croatian attack; prompted Grand Vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha to call for a halt in Ottoman military activity in the region
casualties: No reliable numerical figures survive; the source's own description of a 'heavy defeat' for the Ottoman relief force is the only characterization available, without a specific count

name: Ottoman Assaults on Hrastovica (1568 and 1571)
commanders: Ottoman Empire (local sanjaks) vs. Croatian garrison
importance: Hrastovica was a strategically important fort near Sisak that would enable an Ottoman crossing of the Kupa; the fort withstood two separate Ottoman assaults despite ongoing violations of the 1568 peace treaty on both sides
casualties: No reliable figures survive for either the 1568 or 1571 assault

name: Suppression of the 1573 Croatian Peasant Revolt
commanders: Habsburg/Croatian authorities vs. Croatian peasant rebels
importance: A large peasant revolt near Zagreb was suppressed with heavy casualties, further straining the kingdom's already weak financial and military situation just as the Ottoman-Venetian peace of the same year freed local sanjak-beys to direct more forces toward Croatia
casualties: This refers to the Croatian-Slovenian Peasant Revolt led by Matija Gubec; general historiography of the revolt (outside this source) estimates several thousand peasants killed during and after its suppression, including the brutal public execution of Gubec himself (reportedly crowned with a red-hot iron 'crown' before being executed in Zagreb), though precise total casualty figures vary between accounts and are not fully agreed upon

name: Battle of Budački
commanders: Ferhad Bey Sokolović (Ottoman Empire, Sanjak-bey of Bosnia) vs. Herbard VIII von Auersperg (Croatian Military Frontier)
importance: Auersperg, commander of the Croatian Military Frontier, was killed in this defeat, a significant blow to Croatian frontier leadership during Ferhad Bey's intensified 1575 offensives
casualties: Herbard VIII von Auersperg killed, along with a significant portion of his command according to general Croatian frontier historiography, though a precise numerical total is not reliably established

name: Capture of Bila Stina
commanders: Ferhad Bey Sokolović (Ottoman Empire) vs. Croatian garrison
importance: Captured on the left bank of the Una between Cazin and Ostrožac, enabling an Ottoman breakthrough toward the Korana, Mrežnica, and Kupa rivers

name: Ottoman Attack on Hrastovica (1576)
commanders: Ottoman Empire (~7,000 troops) vs. Croatian garrison
importance: A significantly larger Ottoman force than in previous assaults was again repelled by the town's garrison

name: Capture of Bužim
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Croatian garrison
importance: Taken southwest of Gvozdansko, the Ottomans immediately used it as a base to begin attacking Gvozdansko itself

name: First Siege of Gvozdansko (1576)
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Damjan Doktorović and garrison (120–130 men)
importance: After three days of heavy fighting, Ottoman forces retreated when reinforcements led by captain Johann Auersperg arrived; however, the fort's eastern walls were partially breached by Ottoman artillery, weakening its defenses ahead of the decisive 1577–1578 siege
casualties: No reliable figures survive; the garrison of 120–130 held throughout the three-day assault, implying manageable losses relative to their small numbers, but no specific count is documented

name: Capture of Cazin (1576)
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Croatian garrison
importance: One of more than fifty Ottoman incursions into Croatia recorded during 1576; by year's end most of the area between the Una and Glina rivers was under Ottoman control

name: Capture of Ostrožac (1577)
commanders: Ferhad Bey Sokolović (Ottoman Empire) vs. Croatian garrison
importance: Taken while the main siege of Gvozdansko was ongoing, part of Ferhad Bey's parallel campaign against remaining Croatian forts in the region

name: Siege and Fall of Zrin (1577)
commanders: Ferhad Bey Sokolović (Ottoman Empire) vs. Croatian garrison
importance: Fell after a short siege, leaving Gvozdansko completely surrounded by Ottoman-held forts and towns and sealing its isolation

name: Siege of Gvozdansko (1577–1578)
commanders: Ferhad Pasha Sokolović (Ottoman Empire, 5,000–10,000 troops) vs. Damjan Doktorović, Juraj Gvozdanović, Nikola Ožegović & Andrija Stepšić (Kingdom of Croatia, 300 soldiers and miners)
importance: The main engagement of the campaign: a three-and-a-half month siege using over 30 cannons (including 7 wall-breaching pieces) against a starving, isolated garrison; three major assaults were repelled 10–12 January, but by the final day only 25–30 defenders remained alive. When Ottoman forces entered on the morning of 13 January they found only corpses — the garrison had died of wounds, hunger, thirst, or cold, or possibly took their own lives to avoid capture. Ferhad Bey, reportedly moved by the sight, ordered a Christian burial with military honors
casualties: Entire 300-man Croatian garrison killed (all four captains among the dead) — this is the one engagement in the set with a specific figure directly stated in the source text; Ottoman losses from the repeated repelled assaults (10–12 January) are not numerically specified in the source, though the scale of the siege (30+ cannons, 5,000–10,000 troops over three and a half months) implies meaningful Ottoman attrition even in victory

name: Habsburg-Croatian Counter-Offensive in the Una Valley (1578)
commanders: George Khevenhüller & Krsto Ungnad (Habsburg/Croatian forces, over 12,000 soldiers, 18 cannons) vs. Ferhad Bey Sokolović (Ottoman Empire)
importance: Launched from Slunj, the counter-offensive initially succeeded in forcing Ferhad Bey to retreat and lose control of Cazin, Ostrožac, Zrin, and Novi; Gvozdansko itself was briefly recaptured and the front line pushed back to the Una River, a defeat the High Porte regarded as a disgrace
casualties: No reliable figures survive; the campaign is described in terms of territorial gains and losses rather than casualties in the available record

name: Ottoman Reconquest of the Una Valley (Late 1578)
commanders: Ferhad Bey Sokolović (Ottoman Empire, ~24,000 troops, regrouped) vs. Habsburg-Croatian forces
importance: Ferhad Bey regrouped with a much larger force and stalled the Habsburg advance, retaking all the towns lost during the summer counter-offensive and nullifying its gains

name: Zrinski Sons' Attack on Gvozdansko (1580)
commanders: Juraj IV Zrinski & Nikola V Zrinski (Croatian nobility) vs. Ottoman garrison of Gvozdansko
importance: Unsuccessful attempt by Nikola Šubić Zrinski's sons to retake the family's former stronghold, which was to remain under Ottoman control until 1635

name: Battle of Alcácer Quibir
commanders: Sebastian I of Portugal & Mohammed II vs. Abd al-Malik I & Ahmad al-Mansur
importance: Also known as the Battle of the Three Kings or Battle of Wadi al-Makhazin; fought near Ksar el Kebir, resulting in the total destruction of the Portuguese army, the death of King Sebastian and both competing sultans, the end of the Aviz dynasty, and Portugal's subsequent integration into the Iberian Union
casualties: Heavy Portuguese/allied losses (~8,000 dead and 15,000 captured); ~7,000 Moroccan losses

name: Battle of Blue Waters
commanders: Algirdas (Grand Duchy of Lithuania) vs. Three Tatar Beys (Golden Horde)
importance: Brought Kiev and Podolia under Lithuanian control, secured Black Sea access, and ended Moldavian dependence on the Golden Horde.

name: Capture of Buda
commanders: Suleiman the Magnificent vs. None (abandoned)
importance: Following the rout at Mohács, Ottoman forces entered the undefended and largely abandoned Hungarian capital, initiating the first of several 16th-century changes of control in Buda.

name: Siege of Buda
commanders: Charles V, Duke of Lorraine vs. Abdurrahman Abdi Arnavut Pasha
importance: The recapture of Buda ended nearly 150 years of Ottoman rule over the Hungarian capital and marked a decisive step in Habsburg consolidation of central Hungary.
casualties: Heavy (~20,000 coalition losses; ~3,000 defenders killed and 6,000 captured)

name: Battle of Verbia
commanders: Iacob Heraclid and Olbracht Łaski vs. Alexandru Lăpușneanu
importance: The decisive battle of Iacob Heraclid's invasion of Moldavia, notable as the first battle in Moldavian history won primarily through superior firearms by Spanish arquebusiers and aided by the betrayal of Moldavian cavalry commander Ion Moțoc.
casualties: Unknown (heavy among defending Janissaries and loyalists)

name: Battle of Bicske
commanders: Ferenc Nádasdy and Pálffy Miklós vs. Sinan Pasha of Buda
importance: A severe defeat for the Habsburg-Hungarian raiding force near Bicske that resulted in heavy casualties and internal military repercussions.

name: Battle of Klis
commanders: Juraj Daničić and Lubin Milićić vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: An unsuccessful Habsburg-backed Uskok attempt to capture the strategic fortress city of Klis from the Ottomans.

name: Battle of Győr
commanders: Gregoróczy Vince and Péter Izdenczy vs. Kara Ali
importance: An engagement during a truce period near Győr where the Ottomans decisively overran Habsburg-Hungarian forces due to tactical failures and premature retreats.

name: Siege of Döbrököz
commanders: Habsburg forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Part of the ongoing Habsburg-Ottoman conflicts in Hungary following the 1540–1547 war.

name: Siege of Ozora
commanders: Habsburg forces vs. Ottoman forces
importance: Part of the 1543 Ottoman campaign that expanded Turkish fortifications and territory in central Hungary.

name: Siege of Somlóvásárhely
commanders: Habsburg-Hungarian forces vs. Ottoman forces
importance: Contributed to the consolidation of Ottoman gains in Transdanubia during the 1540–1547 war.

name: Siege of Ugod (First)
commanders: Habsburg forces vs. Ottoman forces
importance: Captured by the Ottomans during their 1543 offensive to secure the defense line north of Lake Balaton.

name: Siege of Ugod (Second)
commanders: Habsburg-Hungarian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Reflects the contested frontier warfare and alternating sieges characteristic of the Habsburg-Ottoman borderlands.

name: Siege of Komárom
commanders: Habsburg garrison vs. Ottoman forces
importance: Komárom successfully held out against Ottoman expansion, serving as a vital anchor for Royal Hungary's defense system.

name: Siege of Palota
commanders: Habsburg garrison vs. Ottoman forces
importance: Part of the fierce border fortress struggles occurring during the broader campaign years of the mid-16th century.

name: Siege of Siklós
commanders: Habsburg forces vs. Ottoman forces
importance: Fought during the pivotal 1566 campaign surrounding Szigetvár, reinforcing Ottoman control in southern Transdanubia.

name: Siege of Várad
commanders: Hungarian-Habsburg forces vs. Ottoman forces
importance: Occurring during the Hungarian civil war (1556–1567), the siege cemented Ottoman hegemony in the Partium region and eastern Hungary.

name: Construction of Novobohorodytska Fortress
commanders: Vasily Golitsyn and Ivan Samoilovich vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: Built by Vasily Golitsyn during the failing first 1687 Crimean campaign at the junction of the Dnieper and Samara rivers before the Russian army decided to turn back due to scorched earth tactics.
casualties: Part of the broader campaign losses of 20,000–30,000 dead, wounded, or sick

name: First Crimean Campaign
commanders: Vasily Golitsyn and Ivan Samoilovich vs. Selim I Giray
importance: A massive joint Russian and Left Bank Cossack force of over 140,000 men advanced toward Perekop but was forced to retreat due to steppe fires set by Tatars, water shortages, and exhausted horses, leading to Samoilovich's replacement by Ivan Mazepa.
casualties: 20,000 to 30,000 dead, wounded, missing, or sick

name: Second Crimean Campaign
commanders: Vasily Golitsyn and Ivan Mazepa vs. Selim I Giray
importance: An expedition of over 110,000 Russian troops and 40,000 Cossacks reached the Perekop isthmus, but upon finding the area stripped of grass, lacking water, and blocked by a 7 km defensive ditch dug by Tatars, Golitsyn was forced to order a retreat.
casualties: 222 killed, 1,028 wounded, 73 missing, and an estimated 35,000 dying during the harsh retreat

name: Cossack Raid on Temryuk
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Part of the 1686 Cossack raids where Cossacks attacked and ravaged the surroundings of Temryuk before moving on.

name: Skirmish at Islam-Kermen
commanders: Russian detachment vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: A small Russian detachment was sent to Islam-Kerman early in the campaign but hesitated to assault the fortress.

name: Battle of Zelenaya Dolina (First May 15 Engagement)
commanders: Russian forces vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: Fierce fighting where Russians repelled Tatars, killing Kae-Abilev, wounding Nuraddin, and forcing a retreat following a Russian counterattack, though inflicting high-ranking command casualties on the Russian side including A.I. Golenishchev-Kutuzov.
casualties: High-ranking Russian commanders killed (Golenishchev-Kutuzov, Shcherbatov, Kartsov, Makhomov); Tatar leaders killed/wounded

name: Battle of Chernaya Dolina (May 16 Engagement)
commanders: Russian and Cossack forces vs. Crimean Tatars
result: Tatar tactical victory / Russian advance checked
importance: Tatars put up all-day resistance, inflicting heavy losses, capturing a thousand Cossacks and thirty cannons, before retreating and forcing the Russians to grapple with severe water shortages.
casualties: 1,000 Cossacks captured, 30 cannons lost, heavy enemy casualties

name: Battle of Kalanchak
commanders: Russian forces vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: Heavy fighting broke out as Tatars attempted to block the advancing Russian army near Kalanchak, after which the Russians managed to continue toward Perekop.

name: Cossack Siege of Lyutik
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman-Tatar garrison
importance: Following the raid on Temryuk, Cossacks laid siege to the Lyutik fortress but were unable to take the city, leading to a blocked retreat and splitting of forces.

name: Cossack Raid on Azov Environs
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Despite earlier setbacks at Lyutik, Cossacks launched a subsequent campaign ravaging the environs of Azov and returning home unopposed.

name: Cossack Assault and Defeat at Kyzykermen
commanders: 600 Cossacks vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: A force of 600 Cossacks attacking Kyzykermen was heavily routed, suffering severe casualties and surrenders that severely depleted Cossack fighting strength for future operations against Crimea.
casualties: 400 Cossacks and 1 Kalmyk killed, plus prisoners

name: Crimean Attack on Tor
commanders: Crimean forces vs. Cossack garrison
importance: Crimean forces attacked the Tor fortress, defeating the garrison, taking 200 prisoners, wounding many, and successfully withdrawing prior to the major joint campaigns.

name: Cossack Skirmish and Routing of Plundering Tatars
commanders: Don Cossacks and Dzungars vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: As Don Cossacks and Dzungars moved to join the Russian army, they encountered and routed Tatars who were plundering Russians, recovering stolen goods and inflicting heavy casualties.

name: Ovechyi Vody
commanders: Local forces vs. Tatar raiders
importance: A minor frontier engagement and locality point recorded during the southern border raids of the Russo-Turkish War theater.

name: Naval and Land Engagement at Kızı-Kermen
commanders: Russians and Zaporozhian Cossacks vs. Galil Pasha
importance: Russian and Zaporozhian forces attacked Kızı-Kermen, meeting Turkish forces under Galil Pasha in a successful small naval and land battle that yielded prisoners and artillery.

name: First Battle of Kamenny Zaton
commanders: Azamat Giray and Shan Giray vs. Russo-Cossack forces
importance: Crimean forces under Azamat Giray and Shan Giray attacked Russian and Cossack positions at Kamenny Zaton, but were forced to retreat after losing the engagement.

name: Yurasov's Raid on Turkish Fortresses
commanders: Fyodor Yurasov vs. Ottoman garrisons
importance: A minor raid led by Fyodor Yurasov with several hundred soldiers against Turkish fortresses failed, contributing to growing discontent within the army ranks.

name: 1st Dnieper
commanders: Allied forces vs. Ottoman-Tatar forces
importance: Early military campaign maneuver and operations along the Dnieper river basin during the initial phases of the Russo-Turkish war actions.

name: Second Battle of Kamenny Zaton
commanders: Ivan Samoylovych vs. Turks, Tatars, and Kalmyks
importance: A fierce, inconclusive battle where allied Turks, Tatars, and Kalmyks attacked Ivan Samoylovych; although Tatars withdrew, they successfully blocked Russian troops from advancing along the Dnieper.

name: Battle of Don River
commanders: Peter Kalmyk vs. Ottoman, Crimean, and Nogai forces
importance: Ottoman, Crimean, and Nogai Tatar forces decisively defeated Cossack Ataman Peter Kalmyk, capturing and executing him while destroying river assets.

name: Tuminov Rog
commanders: Local forces vs. Tatar raiders
importance: A documented tactical locality clash during regional border maneuvers and Tatar raiding paths.

name: Andriivka
commanders: Local forces vs. raiding parties
importance: A localized clash point along the insecure southern borderlands.

name: Berezan
commanders: Cossack/Russian detachments vs. Ottoman forces
importance: A military action near the island or estuary of Berezan in the Black Sea coastal theater.

name: Engagement at Berezan Island
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Tatar detachment
importance: During their late 1688 expedition, Cossack forces successfully encountered and routed a Tatar detachment near Berezan Island before pushing on toward Ochakiv.

name: Cossack Raid on Ochakiv and Repulsion of Counter-Attack
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman, Wallachian, and Tatar forces
importance: Cossacks executed a raid on Ochakiv, driving Ottoman forces back into the city, beating off a combined counter-attack from Turks, Wallachians, and Tatars despite Turkish ship fire, and successfully retreating before the Crimean Khan's main force arrived.
casualties: Minor Cossack losses from Turkish ship fire

name: Battle of Tumin Rog
commanders: Kharkov Cossacks vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: 1,500 Kharkov Cossacks defeated 4,000 Crimeans after a fierce battle, suffering 104 wounded before briefly pursuing the retreating enemy.
casualties: 104 Cossacks wounded; heavy unspecified Tatar losses

name: Tatar Raid on Balakliia and Savintsy
commanders: Crimean and Nogai Tatars vs. City guards and Cossacks
importance: A force of 2,500 elite Crimean and Nogai Tatars raided Balakliia—capturing city guards and Cossacks—and carried out similar destructive raids on Savintsy and other settlements.
casualties: 1 Cossack killed, 22 Cossacks and 5 city guards captured

name: Donets' Victory near Andreyevka
commanders: Colonel G. Donets vs. Tatar detachment
importance: Colonel G. Donets successfully intercepted and routed a raiding Tatar detachment near Andreyevka, capturing 50 prisoners including the wounded Kubek-aga.

name: 1st Ochakiv
commanders: Cossack/Russian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: An initial military expedition or raid targeting the major Ottoman stronghold and fortress city of Ochakiv.

name: Chernaya Dolina
commanders: Vasily Golitsyn vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: Fought concurrently with Zelenaya Dolina during the second Crimean campaign, where Russian tabor formations and artillery successfully repelled attacking Crimean Tatars.

name: Perekop Standoff and Failed Pursuit Attack
commanders: Vasily Golitsyn vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: Russians reached Perekop on May 20, but unsuccessful negotiations and harsh conditions forced a retreat, during which a Tatar pursuit detachment of 200 men launched an attack.

name: Kosagov's Expedition to Gorbatik Fortress
commanders: Kosagov vs. Turkish and Tatar garrison
importance: Kosagov arrived at Gorbatik fortress on May 18 during the 1689 campaign; despite repelling an intense garrison counter-attack, heavy losses and news of the main Russian retreat forced him to withdraw.

name: Skirmish at Olkhovets
commanders: Russian forces vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: Following the failed campaign, Tatars raided the Izyum Line, but a raiding party was successfully routed during pursuit by Russian forces at Olkhovets.

name: 2nd Ochakiv
commanders: Cossack/Russian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: A secondary expedition or military pressure targeting the key Ottoman stronghold of Ochakiv during the early 1690s.

name: 1st Kiziltas
commanders: Cossack/Russian detachments vs. Tatar forces
importance: Initial military raid or campaign action directed against the Kiziltas region in the Crimean/Black Sea periphery.

name: Battle of Batocina (1689)
commanders: Holy League vs. Ottoman Empire
importance: Part of the wider Great Turkish War where the Ottomans suffered major defeats against the Holy League in the Balkans.

name: First Azov Campaign
commanders: Peter the Great, Franz Lefort, Patrick Gordon, and Avtonom Golovin vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Peter the Great's initial attempt to capture Azov with a 31,000-man army failed due to an inability to cut off river resupplies and two unsuccessful assaults, leading to the siege being lifted on October 1, 1695.

name: Sheremetev's Lower Dnieper Campaign (Capture of Gazi-Kerman, Islam-Kerman, Tagan, and Tavan)
commanders: Boris Sheremetev vs. Ottoman Garrisons
importance: Running concurrently with the first Azov campaign, a 120,000-strong Russian and Cossack army under Boris Sheremetev successfully captured key Ottoman forts along the lower Dnieper—including Gazi-Kerman (via an accidental powder magazine explosion), Islam-Kerman, Tagan, and Tavan—before withdrawing.

name: Second Azov Campaign
commanders: Peter the Great, Aleksei Shein, Franz Lefort, and Boris Sheremetev vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: A major successful military and naval campaign where Peter the Great utilized a newly constructed fleet and combined land-water forces under Aleksei Shein to bombard and blockade Azov, leading to the surrender of the Ottoman garrison on July 19, 1696, and marking Russia's first major victory against the Ottomans.
casualties: Unknown specific numbers; decisive defeat and surrender of the Ottoman garrison

name: Establishment and Fortification of Taganrog Fortress
commanders: Peter the Great vs. Ottoman strategic territory
importance: Selected by Peter the Great on July 27, 1696, as a superior naval base site compared to Azov, leading to the formal foundation of the Taganrog fortress and the Russian Navy's first military base.

name: Capture of Islam-Kerman
commanders: Boris Sheremetev vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Captured by Boris Sheremetev's army during the lower Dnieper operations accompanying the First Azov campaign.

name: Capture of Tagan
commanders: Boris Sheremetev vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: Captured alongside Gazi-Kerman and Islam-Kerman by Russian forces operating along the lower Dnieper in 1695.

name: Capture of Tavan
commanders: Boris Sheremetev vs. Ottoman Garrison
importance: One of the key Ottoman fortifications along the lower Dnieper secured by Boris Sheremetev's forces during the 1695 campaign operations.

name: Siege of Kyzykermen
commanders: Boris Sheremetev and Ivan Mazepa vs. Bey of Kyzykermen
importance: A major joint military operation by Boris Sheremetev and Ivan Mazepa against the crucial Ottoman fortress of Kyzykermen on the Dnieper. Utilizing a floating army for isolation, artillery shelling, and mines that blew up fortifications, the Allies captured the fortress on August 17, 1695, along with capturing neighboring smaller forts like Kakhovka, Mubarakkermen, and Mustritkermen.

name: Down Dnieper Campaign Operations
commanders: Boris Sheremetev and Ivan Mazepa vs. Ottoman Garrisons
importance: The broader operational push down the Dnieper River accompanying the 1695 Azov campaign, resulting in the capture of numerous Ottoman strongholds including Kyzykermen and adjacent regional forts.

name: 2nd Dnieper Campaign Operations
commanders: Boris Sheremetev vs. Ottoman Garrisons
importance: Subsequent Dnieper theater military operations conducted by Boris Sheremetev's cavalry and forces supporting the 1696 Second Azov campaign.

name: Ottoman Counterattack Operations (1697–1698)
commanders: Ottoman and Crimean commanders vs. Russian and Cossack forces
importance: A phase of Ottoman and Crimean counter-offensives and military maneuvers directed against Russian-held positions and strongholds following earlier losses.

name: Don Counterattack Operations
commanders: Ottoman-Tatar forces vs. Russian/Cossack garrisons
importance: Military operations and counter-attacks launched along the Don River theater during the 1697–1698 Ottoman counter-offensive.

name: Buçuktepe Rebellion (1444)
commanders: Janissaries vs. Ottoman Government (Murat II / Mehmet II)
importance: The first Janissary revolt in Ottoman history, triggered by opposition to Murat II abdicating in favor of his young son Mehmet II. Although they failed to depose the leadership, the rebels successfully forced the government to grant a half-increase in their salaries and permanently gave their name to the Buçuktepe hill in Edirne.

name: Yenibahçe Uprising (1512)
commanders: Janissaries vs. Bayezid II / Selim I
importance: A major Janissary uprising in Istanbul that forced Sultan Bayezid II to abdicate in favor of his more aggressive son, Selim I, marking a critical turning point where the Janissaries actively influenced the imperial succession.

name: Janissary Revolt (1525)
commanders: Janissaries vs. Ottoman Government (Suleiman the Magnificent)
importance: A significant rebellion by the Janissaries in Istanbul while Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent was away, driven by grievances over pay and political influence, which was ultimately suppressed with key administrative concessions.
casualties: Several rebel leaders executed; rioting suppressed

name: Beylerbeyi Event (1589)
commanders: Janissaries and Sipahis vs. Murat III's Government
result: Rebel success and subsequent palace suppression
importance: A major Janissary revolt in Istanbul sparked by currency debasement and economic crisis during the Ottoman-Safavid War. The rebels forced the execution of the chief treasurer and the beylerbey of Rumeli—marking the first time civil servants were killed directly by soldiers—and triggered subsequent sipahi unrest that was violently suppressed by palace guards.
casualties: Chief treasurer and beylerbey executed; around 400 sipahis killed during palace yard suppression

name: Battle of El Kerima (1677)
commanders: Ali Bey al-Muradi vs. Muhammad Bey al-Muradi
importance: A decisive clash on the plain of Fahs during the Muradid War of Succession where Ali Bey defeated his brother Muhammad Bey, allowing Ali to seize control of Tunis while Muhammad was besieged in Kairouan.

name: First Siege of Kairouan (1677–1679)
commanders: Ali Bey al-Muradi vs. Muhammad Bey al-Muradi
importance: A prolonged siege of Kairouan where Muhammad Bey al-Muradi held out against his brother Ali Bey before a negotiated treaty mediated by the Dey of Algiers temporarily restored a power-sharing equilibrium.

name: First Sack of Tunis (1686)
commanders: Ahmed Khodja (Dey of Algiers) vs. Ali Bey al-Muradi and Muhammad Bey al-Muradi
importance: An invasion of Tunis by the Dey of Algiers prompted by a factional struggle between the Muradid brothers and the local divan, resulting in the city being sacked and Ali Bey being assassinated by his brother Muhammad.
casualties: Heavy destruction of Tunis; Ali Bey assassinated

name: Siege of Tunis (1694)
commanders: Chaabane Khodja and Muhammad Ben Cheker vs. Muhammad Bey al-Muradi
importance: A successful long-term siege by the Dey of Algiers and the rebel leader Muhammad Ben Cheker that forced Muhammad Bey al-Muradi to flee to southern Tunisia and placed Tunis under Algerian occupation.
casualties: Severe hardship for the populace; displacement of the Muradid administration

name: Battle of Kairouan (1695)
commanders: Muhammad Bey al-Muradi vs. Muhammad Ben Cheker
importance: A decisive counter-offensive beneath the walls of Kairouan where Muhammad Bey al-Muradi crushed the forces of Muhammad Ben Cheker, leading to the liberation of Tunis and Ben Cheker's exile to Morocco.
casualties: Ben Cheker's army cut to pieces

name: Battle of Constantine (1698)
commanders: Murad III Bey vs. Ali Khodja (Dey of Algiers)
importance: An expedition by Murad III Bey into Algerian territory where he initially defeated the Dey of Algiers outside Constantine, though a subsequent counter-attack forced the Tunisian forces to abandon the siege and retreat.

name: Battle of Kef (1705)
commanders: Ibrahim Sharif vs. Dey of Algiers
importance: A decisive defeat for Ibrahim Sharif against the forces of the Dey of Algiers near Kef, resulting in Sharif's capture and opening the way for Husayn I Bey to establish the Husainid dynasty.
casualties: Tunisian army defeated; Ibrahim Sharif captured

name: Revolutions of Tunis / Muradid War of Succession (1675–1705)
commanders: Muradid Princes and Local Factions vs. Turkish Militia and Dey of Algiers
importance: A prolonged period of internal power struggles, civil wars, and revolts in Ottoman Tunisia triggered by the Muradid dynasty's attempts to assert monarchical rule against the Turkish militia and external Algerian interventions, ultimately culminating in the rise of Husayn I Bey in 1705.
casualties: Heavy political instability, multiple regime changes, and widespread destruction across Tunisia

name: Aghas Revolution / Revolution of the Odjak (1659)
commanders: Khalil Bouloukbashi and Corsair Captains vs. Pasha Ibrahim
result: Revolutionary success (End of the Pashas' executive power, start of the Aghas period)
importance: A major military and political uprising in the Regency of Algiers where corsair captains and Janissary soldiers overthrew the Ottoman governor, stripped the Sultan's pasha of executive authority, and established a sovereign military republic administered by the Diwan and led by Khalil Agha.
casualties: Pasha Ibrahim and Ali Pasha imprisoned/deposed; local administrative restructuring

name: The Ottoman Disaster / Murder of Osman II (1622)
commanders: Rebellious Janissaries and Kara Davud Pasha vs. Sultan Osman II
result: Regicide and Janissary victory; restoration of Mustafa I
importance: A landmark event in Ottoman history where a coalition of rebellious janissaries and disaffected officials deposed and brutally murdered Sultan Osman II after he attempted to reform and disband the corps following the stalemate at Khotyn. The regicide triggered nationwide Abaza rebellions and established a precedent of military dominance over the sultanate until the reign of Mahmud II.
casualties: Sultan Osman II murdered; subsequent executions of ringleaders including Kara Davud Pasha

name: Ottoman Capture of Shingirey
commanders: Ottoman and Crimean forces vs. Russian/Cossack garrison
importance: The Ottomans and Crimeans successfully captured the stronghold of Shingirey during their regional push in 1697.

name: Engagement at Kızıkermen and Routing of Obidovsky
commanders: Gazi Giray vs. Colonel I. Obidovsky
importance: Gazi Giray arrived at Kızıkermen on August 2, lured out and routed Colonel I. Obidovsky's Cossacks, inflicting over 200 casualties and capturing Prince Yuri Svyatopolk-Chetvertinsky.
casualties: 200+ Cossack casualties; Prince Yuri Svyatopolk-Chetvertinsky captured

name: Zaporozhian Naval Defeat at Tavan
commanders: Zaporozhian Cossacks vs. Ottoman naval forces
importance: Zaporozhian Cossacks suffered a defeat in a naval engagement against the Turks near Tavan on September 22, 1697.

name: Siege of Tavan (1697)
commanders: Ottoman-Tatar forces vs. Russian/Cossack garrison
importance: Concurrently with Kızıkermen, Ottoman and Tatar forces besieged Tavan, but faced with unsuccessful siege works, the arrival of reinforcements, and failed assaults, they were forced to retreat.

name: Don Cossack and Crimean Border Raids
commanders: Don Cossacks vs. Crimeans
importance: Frequent small mutual border raiding actions carried out between the Don Cossacks and the Crimean Tatars throughout the 1697 theater.

name: September 1697 Cossack Raid on Kiziltas
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman/Tatar garrison
importance: An unsuccessful Cossack raiding expedition launched against Kiziltas in September 1697 that failed to achieve its objectives.

name: September 1697 Cossack Raid on Temryuk
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: An unsuccessful Cossack raiding expedition launched against Temryuk in September 1697, resulting in a retreat without success.

name: 2nd Perekop
commanders: Allied forces vs. Crimean garrison
importance: A subsequent campaign action or defensive posture at the Perekop isthmus during the late 1690s theater operations.

name: 1st Achuev
commanders: Russian/Cossack forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Initial military action targeting the Ottoman-held fortress of Achuev in the Kuban region.

name: 2nd Achuev
commanders: Russian/Cossack forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: A secondary follow-up campaign or assault targeting the strategic stronghold of Achuev.

name: Tatar Raid and Devastation of Izyum
commanders: Tatar forces vs. Izyum garrison and inhabitants
importance: Tatar forces launched a major raid on Izyum in June 1690, successfully devastating the city and its surrounding areas.

name: Deceptive Azov Detachment Raid on Tor
commanders: Azov detachment (posing as Don Cossacks) vs. Tor garrison
importance: An Ottoman-allied detachment from Azov masquerading as Don Cossacks attacked Tor in August 1690, capturing a thousand people in an exceptionally brutal raid, with only seven garrison members escaping.

name: 2nd Kiziltas
commanders: Cossack/Russian detachments vs. Tatar forces
importance: A second successive expedition targeting the Kiziltas area.

name: Defense of Novobogoroditsk
commanders: Russian garrison vs. Crimeans and Petrik's Cossacks
importance: During ongoing 1692 Tatar raids, the Russian garrison successfully defended Novobogoroditsk, defeating the attacking Crimeans and Petrik's Cossacks while capturing several rebel leaders including former ataman Steblevsky.

name: 1690–1691 Cossack Minor Raids
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Tatar detachments
importance: A series of minor attacks launched by Cossacks against Tatar targets during the 1690–1691 period.

name: Cossack Campaign against Temryuk
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: An expedition launched by Cossacks in 1692 targeting the Ottoman stronghold of Temryuk that failed to achieve its objectives.

name: Cossack Campaign against Kyzyltash
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman/Tatar garrison
importance: An expedition launched by Cossacks in 1692 targeting Kyzyltash alongside Temryuk that ultimately failed to capture the objective.

name: First 1692 Cossack Attack on Azov
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: An early 1692 assault by Cossacks against the heavily fortified Ottoman stronghold of Azov.

name: Destruction of Three Turkish Ships
commanders: Cossack naval forces vs. Ottoman naval forces
importance: Cossack maritime forces successfully intercepted and destroyed three Turkish vessels during naval operations.

name: Attack on Turkish Vessel
commanders: Cossack naval forces vs. Turkish vessel
importance: Cossacks launched an assault on an individual Turkish ship on July 10, 1692, but were unable to capture it.

name: Autumn 1692 Cossack Campaign against Azov
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Azov garrison
importance: Following mutual raiding, the Cossacks launched another campaign against Azov in the fall of 1692, culminating in a defeat on October 26.

name: Molochny Vody
commanders: Local forces vs. Tatar raiders
importance: A tactical clash along the Molochny Vody river basin during regional border patrols and Tatar movements.

name: 3rd Kiziltas
commanders: Cossack/Russian detachments vs. Tatar forces
importance: A third expedition targeting the Kiziltas region as part of continued regional raiding patterns.

name: 1694 Cossack Campaign against Kyzyltash
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman forces and fleet
importance: Cossacks targeted Kyzyltash in 1694; pursued by the Turkish fleet, they successfully fought their way through and executed a retreat.

name: 1694 Cossack Campaign against Temryuk
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman forces and fleet
importance: Cossacks targeted Temryuk in 1694; pursued by the Turkish fleet, they successfully fought their way through and executed a retreat.

name: Clash at the Milky Waters (Molochny Vody)
commanders: Cossacks vs. Crimean Tatars
importance: Following renewed attacks, Cossacks clashed directly with Tatar forces at the Milky Waters (Molochny Vody) in 1694, managing to escape after intense fighting.

name: 3rd Ochakiv
commanders: Cossack/Russian forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: A third targeted military operation or raiding action against the key Ottoman fortress city of Ochakiv.

name: 1690 Cossack Raid on Kyzykermen
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Cossack forces executed a targeted raiding expedition against the key Ottoman fortress of Kyzykermen during 1690.

name: 1690 Cossack Raid on Ochakiv
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Cossack forces executed a targeted raiding expedition against the key Ottoman fortress of Ochakiv during 1690.

name: Repulsion of 1693 Tatar Invasions
commanders: Cossacks vs. invading Tatar forces
importance: Cossack forces successfully repelled targeted Tatar invasions and incursions into their territories in 1693.

name: Double Defeat of Small Turkish Detachments near Ochakiv
commanders: Cossacks vs. Turkish detachments
importance: In 1694, Cossack forces twice intercepted and defeated small Turkish detachments operating near the fortress of Ochakiv.

name: Cossack Capture of Turkish Warships and Merchant Ship
commanders: Cossack forces vs. Ottoman naval forces
importance: In April 1696, Cossack forces launched a successful naval action along the southern theater, attacking and capturing eight Turkish warships and one merchant ship.
casualties: Eight Turkish warships and one merchant ship lost

name: Battle of Konskie Vody
commanders: Ivan Husak vs. Tatar detachment
importance: In June 1696, Cossack commander Ivan Husak successfully intercepted and defeated a Tatar detachment in the Battle of Konskie Vody.

name: Chaly's Raid on Kozlov and Subsequent Defeat
commanders: Ataman Chaly vs. Ottoman-Tatar pursuit force
importance: Ataman Chaly successfully raided and sacked Kozlov, capturing 62 people, but was subsequently pursued and caught by a combined Ottoman-Tatar force near the lower Dnieper where his detachment was routed.

name: Yakov Moroz's Naval Raid and Escape
commanders: Yakov Moroz vs. Ottoman naval forces
importance: On June 30, 1696, Yakov Moroz led a flotilla of 40 ships that attacked three Turkish merchant ships, capturing two, and successfully fought through an encounter with Turks upon returning to the Sich.

name: Cossack Raid on Temryuk Village and Rout by Ali Pasha
commanders: Cossack band vs. Ali Pasha of Kerch (Turks, Tatars, and Circassians)
importance: In the fall of 1696, a band of 80 Cossacks raided a village near Temryuk but were overtaken, routed, and mostly killed or captured by a combined force led by Ali Pasha of Kerch.
casualties: Almost entire Cossack band killed or captured (80 men)

name: Mazupek's Detachment Clash near the Molochnaya River
commanders: Mazepa's 160 men vs. Crimean Khan's Tatars
importance: In June 1696, a 160-man raiding party sent by Mazepa was intercepted and overwhelmed by the Crimean Khan's Tatars near the Molochnaya River.

name: Capture of Mazepa's Detachment near the Molochnaya River
commanders: Mazepa's 160 men vs. Crimean Khan's Tatars
importance: Separated tracking record of the engagement near the Molochnaya River where the 160-man raiding detachment suffered heavy casualties and surrender.

name: Don Campaign Raid Repulsion
commanders: Russian forces vs. Tatar raiding party
importance: On July 20, 1697, Russian forces along the Don theater successfully repelled a small Tatar raid and captured 70 prisoners.

name: Ottoman Capture of Islam-Kermen (1697)
commanders: Ottoman-Tatar forces vs. Russian/Cossack garrison
importance: During the 1697 counteroffensive, Ottoman and Tatar forces successfully captured the key Dnieper fortress of Islam-Kermen.

name: Repulsion of Yusuf Pasha's Attack on Dnieper Towns
commanders: Yusuf Pasha vs. Cossacks and Russians
importance: Cossacks and Russians successfully repelled an attack by Yusuf Pasha, the Seraskir of the Eyalet of Silistra, against the Dnieper towns.

name: Yusuf Pasha's Probe of Kızıkermen Fortifications
commanders: Yusuf Pasha vs. Kızıkermen garrison
importance: Yusuf Pasha launched a small-scale testing attack on the fortifications of Kızıkermen before withdrawing with minor losses.

name: Mehmet Derbish Pasha's Naval Entry into the Dnieper
commanders: Mehmet Derbish Pasha vs. Dnieper river defenses
importance: Mehmet Derbish Pasha's fleet entered the Dnieper River on August 9, 1697, reinforcing the Ottoman operations in the region.

name: Treaty of Karlowitz (1699)
commanders: Rami Mehmed Pasha, Alex. Mavrocordatos, and Holy League representatives
importance: Concluded the Great Turkish War of 1683–1699 following the Ottoman defeat at the Battle of Zenta, marking the end of Ottoman control in much of Central Europe and establishing the Habsburg monarchy as the dominant regional power.

name: Treaty of Constantinople (1700)
commanders: Yemelyan Ignatievich Ukraintsev and the Ottoman Porte
importance: Ended the Russo-Turkish War of 1686–1700, securing Russian possession of the Azov region and Taganrog while freeing Peter the Great's forces to participate in the Great Northern War.

name: Safavid Siege and Attempt on Basra (1624)
commanders: Safavid Empire vs. Ottoman/Local Garrison
importance: An early 17th-century attempt by Shah Abbas the Great to capture the strategic port city of Basra, which proved unsuccessful due to Portuguese interference and regional pressures.

name: Safavid Siege and Attempt on Basra (1625)
commanders: Safavid Empire vs. Ottoman/Local Garrison
importance: Continued Safavid military campaigns under Shah Abbas to seize Basra during the War of 1623–1639, ultimately unsuccessful.

name: Safavid Campaign against Basra (1628–1629)
commanders: Safavid Empire vs. Ottoman/Local Garrison
importance: A further coordinated Safavid military effort to capture Basra that was halted and rendered unsuccessful due to pressing concerns on other fronts and the death of Shah Abbas the Great.

name: Ottoman Punitive Expedition to Basra (1667)
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Husayn Pasha (Afrasiyab dynasty)
importance: An Ottoman punitive expedition launched against Basra's ruler Husayn Pasha when he refused to acknowledge Ottoman suzerainty, prompting an unsuccessful offer of the city to the Safavids.

name: Crimean Campaign (1667)
commanders: Ivan Sirko and Ivan Zhdan-Rih vs. Adil Giray and Shirin Bey
importance: A major punitive expedition by Zaporozhian Cossacks that devastated the Crimean Peninsula, including Kaffa and Arbautuk, while the main Tatar army was occupied elsewhere. The campaign forced Tatar forces to abandon their siege of Podhajce to defend their homeland and resulted in the liberation of 2,000 Rus' captives.
casualties: Over 5,000 Tatar troops killed; thousands of civilians killed and thousands captured/freed; Tatar commanders captured and Khan Adil Giray forced to flee

name: Crimean Campaign (1667)
commanders: Ivan Sirko and Ivan Zhdan-Rih vs. Adil Giray and Shirin Bey
importance: A major punitive expedition by Zaporozhian Cossacks that devastated the Crimean Peninsula, including Kaffa and Arbautuk, while the main Tatar army was occupied elsewhere. The campaign forced Tatar forces to abandon their siege of Podhajce to defend their homeland and resulted in the liberation of 2,000 Rus' captives.
casualties: Over 5,000 Tatar troops killed; thousands of civilians killed and thousands captured/freed; Tatar commanders captured and Khan Adil Giray forced to flee

name: Siege of Cherkasy (1532)
commanders: Ostap Dashkevych vs. Saadet I Giray
importance: A 30-day siege where a small garrison of 400–600 Cossacks and townspeople successfully held the Cherkasy castle against a significantly larger force of 10,000 Tatars and Janissaries. The failure to capture the castle led to the abdication of Khan Saadet I Giray.
casualties: Tatar forces repelled; heavy attrition suffered by the besiegers; fortress remained under Cossack control

name: Battle of Chuvash Cape (1582)
commanders: Yermak Timofeyevich vs. Mametqul
importance: A decisive engagement in the conquest of Siberia where Yermak's Cossacks defeated the forces of the Khanate of Sibir, leading to the fall of Qashliq and the collapse of Khan Kuchum's power.

name: Battle of the Irtysh (1585)
commanders: Kuchum Khan vs. Yermak Timofeyevich
importance: A decisive nighttime ambush by Kuchum Khan that resulted in the near-total destruction of Yermak's expeditionary force, the death of General Yermak Timofeyevich, and the temporary reconquest of parts of Siberia by the Khanate of Sibir.
casualties: 630 Russians killed (including Yermak); unknown losses for Sibir

name: Crimean Campaigns (1668)
commanders: Ivan Sirko and Ivan Zhdan-Rih vs. Adil Giray and Shirin Bey
importance: A series of four successful coordinated campaigns into Crimea led by Ivan Sirko to disrupt Tatar support for Petro Sukhovy and pressure the Khanate. The final campaign included Don Cossack and Kalmyk allies and reached the Crimean capital, Bakhchysarai.
casualties: Heavy losses for Tatar forces; 3,500 Tatars killed or captured during the third campaign alone

name: Crimean Campaigns (1668)
commanders: Ivan Sirko and Ivan Zhdan-Rih vs. Adil Giray and Shirin Bey
importance: A series of four successful coordinated campaigns into Crimea led by Ivan Sirko to disrupt Tatar support for Petro Sukhovy and pressure the Khanate. The final campaign included Don Cossack and Kalmyk allies and reached the Crimean capital, Bakhchysarai.
casualties: Heavy losses for Tatar forces; 3,500 Tatars killed or captured during the third campaign alone

name: Shaykh Mane's Revolt and Capture of Basra
commanders: Shaykh Mane ibn Mughamis and Musha'sha' allies vs. Ottoman garrison
importance: Local Arab tribal leader Shaykh Mane ibn Mughamis, backed by 5,000 Musha'sha' tribesmen, revolted against the Ottomans and successfully captured Basra, ousting the Ottoman governor.

name: Farajollah Khan's Clash with Shaykh Mane
commanders: Farajollah Khan and loyal Musha'sha' vs. Shaykh Mane ibn Mughamis
importance: Safavid-appointed governor Farajollah Khan and his loyal Musha'sha' forces clashed with and defeated Shaykh Mane, ousting him from Basra in the name of the Safavid Shah.

name: Safavid Occupation of Basra
commanders: Ali Mardan Khan / Ebrahim Khan / Davud Khan vs. Ottoman and Arab tribal forces
result: Safavid occupation and subsequent negotiated withdrawal
importance: Following the ousting of Shaykh Mane, Safavid troops under Ali Mardan Khan took control of Basra on March 26, 1697, marking the second historical Safavid occupation of the city before its return to Ottoman control in 1701.

name: Siege of Eger
commanders: Antonio Caraffa / Habsburg Imperial army vs. Ottoman garrison of Eger
result: Habsburg victory; Ottoman surrender and annexation of Eger
importance: The capture of Eger (Eğri) in December 1687 ended Ottoman rule in northern Hungary and brought the capital of the Eğri Eyalet under Habsburg control. The fall of the fortress followed the Habsburg victory at the Second Battle of Mohács and marked the collapse of one of the last major Ottoman administrative provinces in Hungary.
casualties: Ottoman garrison surrendered; approximately 3,000 Ottoman defenders taken prisoner

name: Safavid Defeat near Khurma Fortress
commanders: Safavid forces vs. Shaykh Mane and Musha'sha' defectors
importance: Shaykh Mane, allied with Musha'sha' defectors, defeated a large Safavid force near the fortress of Khurma and captured their general, prompting Safavid diplomatic overtures to return Basra.
casualties: Safavid general captured; heavy force defeat

name: Siege of Kiev
commanders: Edigu vs. Lithuanian garrison
result: Golden Horde victory / Sacking of Kiev
importance: The Emir of the Golden Horde, Edigu, besieged and captured Kiev, heavily ransacking the city and burning the suburbs.

name: First Tatar Raid on Ukraine
commanders: Crimean Tatars vs. Local defenders
importance: Marked the documented beginning of destructive and systematic Crimean Tatar raids into Ukrainian borderlands as noted in the Hustyn Chronicle.

name: Tatar Raid on Ukraine
commanders: Crimean Khanate vs. Local inhabitants
importance: A destructive Crimean Tatar military raid deep into Ukrainian territories, causing widespread devastation and capturing prisoners.

name: Tatar Raid on Ukraine
commanders: Crimean Khanate vs. Local inhabitants
importance: Another major destructive raid conducted by the Crimean Khanate into the frontier regions of Ukraine.

name: Tatar Raid on Podolia
commanders: Mengli I Giray vs. Podolian defenders
importance: Crimean Khan Mengli I Giray led a destructive campaign that severely ravaged the region of Podolia.

name: Siege of Kiev
commanders: Mengli I Giray vs. Ivan Chodkiewicz
importance: Carried out at the request of Moscow's Ivan III, Crimean Tatars captured and burned Kiev, taking the city voivode and his family prisoner.

name: Tatar Raid on Kiev
commanders: Crimean Tatars vs. John I Albert
importance: A 5,000-strong Tatar force raided Kiev and Podolia, but was intercepted and defeated by King John I Albert in September at the Battle of Kopystrzyn.

name: Tatar Raid on Podolia
commanders: Crimean Tatars vs. John I Albert
importance: A 5,000-strong Tatar force raided Kiev and Podolia, but was intercepted and defeated by King John I Albert in September at the Battle of Kopystrzyn.

name: Fire of Kiev
commanders: Crimean Tatar army vs. Local garrison
importance: A massive 100,000-strong Tatar army marched into Podolia and Kiev, storming and burning down the city.
casualties: Many houses burned and inhabitants captured

name: Tatar Raid on Podolia, Galicia, and Volhynia
commanders: Crimean and Nogai Tatars vs. Mikołaj Chodecki and Semyon Olshanski
result: Mixed (Initial Tatar ravaging, followed by a Polish-Lithuanian victory at Zasław)
importance: Combined Crimean and Nogai forces burned Volodymyr and other towns, taking a massive number of captives (yasyr), though a returning detachment was defeated on the Goryn River.
casualties: Many prisoners taken; Tatar detachment defeated

name: Tatar Raid on Kiev
commanders: Mengli I Giray vs. Local garrison
importance: A targeted destructive raid led by Crimean Khan Mengli I Giray against the border territories of Kiev and Czernihów (Chernihiv).

name: Tatar Raid on Czernihów
commanders: Mengli I Giray vs. Local garrison
importance: A targeted destructive raid led by Crimean Khan Mengli I Giray against the border territories of Kiev and Czernihów (Chernihiv).

name: Tatar Raid on Podolia
commanders: Crimean Tatars vs. Polish-Lithuanian army
importance: Tatars raided Podolia and Volhynia, taking numerous prisoners and defeating the pursuing Polish-Lithuanian army at the Battle of Wyszniowiec.

name: Tatar Raid on Volhynia
commanders: Crimean Tatars vs. Polish-Lithuanian army
importance: Tatars raided Podolia and Volhynia, taking numerous prisoners and defeating the pursuing Polish-Lithuanian army at the Battle of Wyszniowiec.

name: Tatar Raid on Volhynia
commanders: Giray (son of Mengli I) vs. Semyon Olshanski and Wasyl Hreptowicz
importance: Tatars led by the khan's sons besieged Korets and Rivne castles, but local Lithuanian commanders successfully held the defenses and repelled the assault.

name: Ottoman Raid on Galicia
commanders: Ottoman Empire vs. Polish defenders
importance: An exceptionally devastating independent attack by Ottoman troops targeting the region of Eastern Galicia.

name: Tatar Raid on Galicia
commanders: Crimean Khanate vs. Polish defenders
importance: An exceptionally devastating independent attack by Crimean Tatars targeting the region of Eastern Galicia.
